docs.title: Why this site exists
docs.text:
Interview preparation usually breaks down the same way. You start with Transformers, realise you need RNNs, go back to LSTMs, then jump forward to RAG and MCP, and the picture never comes together.

The fix is to learn AI/ML as one story. Every technique exists because an earlier one failed at something. If you know each method's weakness, you know why the next one was invented, and the order explains itself. That chain of weaknesses is also exactly what interviewers probe: "Why not an RNN?", "Why divide by √d?", "Why RAG instead of fine-tuning?"

docs.title: The storyline in four acts
docs.text:
1. The toolkitFoundationsMath, ML fundamentals and metrics that every later topic reuses.
  2. 1950s–2000sAct I · Learn from featuresPeople design the features; models learn weights on top of them.
  3. 2006–2016Act II · Learn the featuresBecause hand-made features capped accuracy.
  4. 2017–2022Act III · Attention and scaleBecause RNNs were slow and forgot.
  5. 2022–nowAct IV · Align, ground, actBecause LLMs only continue text.
  6. ThroughoutProductionMLOps and system design: making any of it work for real users.

docs.title: How every topic is written
docs.text:
Each topic answers the same seven questions, in the order you should use when answering in an interview:

  1. Problem before it: what existed, and why it wasn't good enough.
  2. Core idea: one sentence of intuition.
  3. How it works: the mechanism, then the math interviewers expect.
  4. Strengths.
  5. Weaknesses: where it breaks, which is usually the follow-up question.
  6. What came next, and why: the bridge to the next topic.
  7. Interview questions: with answers hidden until you click, so you can test yourself first.

Your progress stays in your browser

Every study page has a status control under its title: Not started, Learning, Confident. The My Progress page totals them, and the Flashcard Drill remembers which questions you knew. Nothing leaves your browser; export it from My Progress to move it to another device.

docs.title: AI Agents
docs.text:
TL;DR

An agent is an LLM running in a loop: it decides the next action, calls a tool, observes the result, and repeats until the goal is met. Many problems are better served by workflows (fixed code paths that call LLMs: chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator–workers, evaluator–optimizer); use an agent when the path can't be known in advance. Agents need tools, memory, planning and verification, and they fail through loops, compounding errors and unsafe actions, so reliability comes from bounded loops, checks, permissions and end-to-end evaluation.

Where this fits

Before: Tool Calling and Reasoning Models. This page: putting them in a loop. Next: MCP & A2A standardize tool and agent connections; Context Engineering and Harness Engineering make long-running agents work.

  • Prompting 2020One call, no actions.
  • Chain-of-thought 2022Reasoning, but no access to the world.
  • ReAct 2022Interleave reasoning with actions and observations.
  • Function calling 2023Structured tool requests, supported natively.
  • Agent loops and workflows 2023–2024Models choose their next step; patterns for composing calls.
  • Coding, research and computer-use agents 2024–2026Long tasks with many tools, sub-agents and verification.

docs.title: What makes something an agent
docs.text:
Level Who controls the flow Example Single LLM call Your code Classify a ticket Workflow Your code, with several LLM calls on predefined paths Extract fields → validate → draft a reply Router The model picks one of a few predefined paths Send a question to billing, technical or sales flows Agent The model decides which actions to take and when it's done Fix a failing test in a repository; research a question across sources

Use the simplest level that works. Agents trade cost, latency and predictability for flexibility. They're worth it when the number of steps and the path depend on what's discovered along the way.

docs.title: Workflow patterns
docs.text: Pattern How Good for Prompt chaining Fixed sequence; each call's output feeds the next, with checks between steps Draft → review → translate; outline → write Routing Classify the input, then send it to a specialized prompt or model Support triage; sending easy queries to a cheap model Parallelization Run independent sub-tasks at once (sectioning), or the same task several times and vote Checking content against several policies; robust classification Orchestrator–workers A coordinating LLM breaks the task down dynamically and delegates to workers, then combines Code changes touching an unknown number of files; multi-source research Evaluator–optimizer One call generates, another evaluates against criteria, loop until good enough Translation, writing to a rubric, code that must pass checks

docs.title: The agent loop
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    G["Goal + context"] --> R["Model reasons<br/>about the next step"]
    R --> D{"Done?"}
    D -->|"no"| A["Call a tool"]
    A --> O["Observe the result<br/>(output, error, test results)"]
    O --> R
    D -->|"yes"| V["Verify, then answer"]

ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) made this explicit: alternate a Thought (reasoning about what to do), an Action (a tool call) and an Observation (the result), so reasoning guides actions and observations ground reasoning. Modern agents do the same with native tool calling, and reasoning models do much of the thinking internally.

Every loop needs stopping conditions: the goal is verified as met, a step or token budget is reached, the same action fails repeatedly, or a human must decide.

docs.title: Planning and reflection
docs.text:
• Plan-and-execute: write a plan first (a to-do list), then execute steps, updating the plan as results come in. Makes long tasks more coherent and easier to inspect.
  • Decomposition: split the goal into sub-goals small enough to verify.
  • Re-planning: revise when an observation invalidates the plan.
  • Reflection / self-critique: after an attempt, critique it against the goal and try again (Reflexion stores these lessons as text memory).
  • Search: explore several candidate actions or plans and evaluate them (tree search variants); costly, useful when mistakes are expensive and a good evaluator exists.
  • Verification beats confidence: the strongest agents check their work against something external: run the tests, re-query the database, compare against the source.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Kind What it holds How Short-term (working) The current conversation, recent tool results The context window Scratchpad Plans, to-do lists, intermediate notes A file or structured state the agent reads and updates Long-term episodic What happened in past sessions Logs or summaries, retrieved when relevant Long-term semantic Facts about the user, project or domain Notes files, vector stores, knowledge graphs Procedural How to do recurring tasks Instructions, skills or playbooks loaded when needed

Design questions: what gets written (and who approves it), how it's retrieved (recency, relevance, explicit lookup), how it's kept small (summarization, expiry), and privacy (what may be stored about users). Long tasks depend on compaction: summarizing older context so the window doesn't overflow. See Context Engineering.

docs.title: Multi-agent systems
docs.text:
Topology How Notes Orchestrator with sub-agents A lead agent delegates focused sub-tasks to sub-agents, each with its own clean context and tools, and combines their condensed results The most common and useful pattern Pipeline / handoffs Specialized agents pass work along (intake → research → drafting) Clear responsibilities; errors propagate Debate or critique Agents argue or review each other Can improve reasoning and catch errors; costly Peer network Agents message each other freely Hard to control and debug

When multi-agent helps: breadth-first tasks that parallelize (researching many sources at once), tasks whose context would overflow one window, and separation of concerns (a reviewer that didn't write the code). Costs: many times the tokens of a single agent, coordination failures (duplicated or conflicting work, lost information in handoffs), and harder debugging. For tightly coupled tasks such as editing one codebase, a single agent with good tools often wins.

docs.title: Frameworks
docs.text: LangGraph, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, AutoGen, the OpenAI Agents SDK, the Claude Agent SDK, Google's Agent Development Kit and others provide loops, tool registries, state, memory, tracing and multi-agent orchestration. They speed up building, but hide the loop. Interviewers expect you to be able to write the core loop yourself (call model → run tools → append results → repeat with limits) and to explain the state, prompts and tools underneath any framework.

docs.title: Why agents fail, and the fixes
docs.text:
Errors compound. If each step succeeds with probability 0.95, a 20-step task succeeds end to end with probability \(0.95^{20} \approx 0.36\). Reliability per step, checkpoints and verification matter more than raw capability.

Failure What it looks like Mitigations Loops Repeats the same failing action Step budgets, duplicate-action detection, better error messages Compounding errors An early wrong assumption derails everything Verify after key steps, re-plan, keep plans visible Premature "done" Declares success without checking Require evidence (tests pass, record exists); a separate verifier Goal drift Loses track of the original task over a long run Restate the goal, keep a to-do list, compaction that preserves goals and decisions Tool misuse Wrong tool, invented arguments Tool design, validation, examples Context overflow Huge tool outputs crowd out what matters Truncate and summarize results, sub-agents, compaction Unsafe actions Deletes, sends or pays without authorization Least privilege, confirmation for side effects, sandboxes Prompt injection Content it reads redirects its behavior Treat tool results as data, restrict capabilities, human approval Cost blow-ups Runaway token usage Budgets per task, cheaper models for sub-steps, caching

docs.title: A design checklist
docs.text:
1. Define the goal, success criteria and how success is verified.
  2. Start with a workflow; move to an agent only where the path is genuinely dynamic.
  3. Design a small set of well-described tools, acting with the user's permissions.
  4. Bound the loop: steps, tokens, time, cost.
  5. Decide which actions need human approval.
  6. Plan context: what's always loaded, what's fetched on demand, how history is compacted.
  7. Add tracing of every step.
  8. Build an end-to-end evaluation suite of realistic tasks and grade outcomes, not just final text. See Evaluating LLM Systems.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Explain the ReAct loop.

ReAct interleaves reasoning and acting: the model writes a thought about what it needs, chooses an action (a tool call with arguments), receives an observation (the tool's result), and repeats until it can answer. Reasoning makes actions purposeful, and observations ground the reasoning in real data, reducing hallucination compared with reasoning alone. Today it's implemented with native tool calling inside a bounded loop.

Workflow vs agent: when do you actually need an agent?

Use a workflow when the steps are known in advance: you get predictability, lower cost, easier testing and debugging. Use an agent when the number and order of steps depend on what's discovered along the way, such as debugging code, open-ended research, or support cases that require investigating several systems. Even then, keep agents bounded and consider hybrid designs: a workflow that calls an agent for one dynamic step.

Describe the common workflow patterns.

Prompt chaining: a fixed sequence of calls with checks between them. Routing: classify the input and send it to a specialized path or model. Parallelization: split independent subtasks across concurrent calls, or run the same task several times and vote. Orchestrator–workers: a coordinating model decomposes the task at runtime and delegates to workers. Evaluator–optimizer: one model generates and another critiques against criteria, iterating until it passes.

How do you give an agent memory?

Short-term memory is the context window, managed with compaction so older turns become summaries. Working memory is a scratchpad the agent maintains, such as a plan or to-do file. Long-term memory is stored outside the model: notes files, a vector store of past interactions or facts, or a knowledge graph, written deliberately and retrieved when relevant. Decide what is worth storing, how it's retrieved, how it's pruned, and what's allowed for privacy.

Single-agent vs multi-agent: trade-offs.

A single agent keeps all context in one place: simpler, cheaper, easier to debug, and better for tightly coupled work. Multi-agent systems give each sub-agent a focused, clean context and can parallelize, which helps breadth-heavy tasks and those exceeding one context window, and allows independent review. The costs are several times more tokens, coordination problems and information lost in handoffs. Use an orchestrator with sub-agents only where the task splits naturally.

How do you stop an agent from looping forever?

Hard limits on steps, tokens, wall-clock time and cost; detection of repeated identical actions or errors; tool errors that explain what went wrong and suggest alternatives; a plan the agent must update so it notices lack of progress; escalation to a human when stuck; and evaluation of loop rates on test tasks. The loop's exit conditions should be explicit in the harness, not left to the model.

Why do agents fail on long tasks even when each step looks easy?

Errors compound: per-step success rates multiply, so 95% per step gives about 36% over 20 steps. Long tasks also accumulate context, so important early information gets buried or summarized away, and the agent may drift from the goal. Mitigations: verification checkpoints, plans and to-do lists, compaction that preserves goals and decisions, sub-agents for isolated sub-tasks, and smaller, testable steps.

How do you make an agent verify its own work?

Give it checks grounded outside the model: run tests, linters and type checkers for code; re-query the database after a write; compare an answer's claims against retrieved sources; validate outputs against a schema. Require evidence before it can declare success, and use a separate evaluator prompt or model with explicit criteria for subjective work. Self-critique alone, without external signals, helps less.

What are the security risks of agents, and how do you mitigate them?

Agents read untrusted content and take actions, so prompt injection can turn them against users: exfiltrating data, sending messages, deleting resources. Excessive permissions magnify any mistake. Mitigate with least-privilege tools acting as the user, human approval for consequential actions, sandboxed execution, network and data egress restrictions, separating untrusted content from instructions, monitoring and audit logs, and red-team testing. See Guardrails & Security.

Design an agent that triages and resolves customer support tickets.

Clarify scope (which actions are allowed: refunds, plan changes) and success metrics (resolution rate, CSAT, escalation rate, cost per ticket). Start with a workflow: classify the ticket and route; for complex cases use an agent with tools such as account lookup, order history, policy search (RAG) and draft-reply, acting with the customer's permissions. Require approval for refunds above a threshold. Bound steps, log every action, hand off to humans with a summary. Evaluate on historical tickets with known resolutions, then shadow-mode on live traffic before letting it act.

How would you evaluate an agent?

With a suite of realistic tasks whose outcomes can be checked: the final state (tests pass, ticket resolved correctly, record updated once) rather than just the final message. Track success rate, steps, tokens, latency and cost per task, safety violations, and behavior when tools fail. Run each task several times because agents are stochastic, review transcripts of failures, and re-run the suite on every change to prompts, tools, models or the harness.

Common mistakes

  • Reaching for a multi-agent framework when a workflow or a single call would do.
  • No step or cost limits.
  • Letting the agent declare success without evidence.
  • Giving agents broad credentials "for convenience".
  • Evaluating agents on a handful of demo tasks.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• Place single calls, workflows, routers and agents on the autonomy spectrum
  • Explain the five workflow patterns
  • Draw the agent loop with its stopping conditions
  • Describe planning, reflection and verification
  • Explain short-term, working and long-term memory
  • Compare single- and multi-agent designs
  • Explain compounding errors and list mitigations for eight failure modes

docs.title: Context Engineering
docs.text:
TL;DR

Context engineering is deciding what goes into the model's context window at each step: instructions, tools, retrieved knowledge, memory, history and tool results. The window is a scarce budget: as it fills, quality drops (context rot), cost and latency rise, and irrelevant or conflicting content misleads the model. The goal is the smallest set of high-signal tokens for the current step, achieved with just-in-time retrieval, compaction, structured notes, sub-agents with clean contexts, and a cache-friendly layout.

Where this fits

Before: Prompt Engineering (how to write instructions), RAG (what to retrieve), Agents (long loops that accumulate context), long-context limits. This page: managing everything in the window. Next: Harness Engineering designs the whole system around the model.

docs.title: From prompts to context
docs.text:
Prompt engineering focuses on writing good instructions for a single call. Agents changed the problem: a long-running agent makes dozens or hundreds of calls, and each call's context is assembled from many sources that change as the task proceeds. The term context engineering (popular from mid-2025) names the discipline of curating that assembly.

flowchart TB
    subgraph W["What competes for one context window"]
        direction TB
        SP["System prompt and rules"] ~~~ TD["Tool definitions"]
        TD ~~~ EX["Examples"]
        EX ~~~ MEM["Memory: user and project facts"]
        RET["Retrieved documents"] ~~~ HIS["Conversation and action history"]
        HIS ~~~ TR["Tool results"]
        TR ~~~ CUR["The current request"]
    end
    W --> M["Model call"]
    M --> OUT["Next action or answer"]
    OUT -->|"results append, history grows"| W

docs.title: Why context is scarce
docs.text:
• Attention is spread thin: every token competes for the model's attention, and accuracy on details tends to fall as contexts grow, even well within the advertised window. This decline is often called context rot.
  • Position effects: information in the middle of a long context is used less reliably ("lost in the middle").
  • Distractors: irrelevant but similar-looking text measurably hurts accuracy.
  • Cost and latency: every token is processed on every call; long prompts slow time to first token.
  • Finite size: long agent runs eventually overflow any window.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
1. The smallest high-signal set. Include what this step needs, not everything that might be useful.
  2. System prompts at the right altitude. Specific enough to guide behavior, general enough to let the model use judgment. Avoid both vague platitudes and brittle if-then rule lists. Organize with clear sections.
  3. Curated tools. Few, clearly distinct tools with concise descriptions; overlapping tools confuse selection and every definition costs tokens.
  4. Canonical examples over exhaustive edge cases. A few diverse, representative examples teach behavior better than a long list of rules.
  5. Just-in-time over pre-loading. Keep lightweight references (file paths, document IDs, URLs, queries) and let the agent fetch details when it needs them, the way a person uses a file system instead of memorizing it. Pre-load only what is almost always needed.
  6. Progressive disclosure. Let the agent discover structure (list a directory, read a summary, then open a file) instead of dumping everything at once.

docs.title: Techniques for long-running tasks
docs.text: Technique How Trade-off Compaction When the context nears its limit, summarize the history into a compact state (goal, decisions made, current status, open problems, key file names) and continue from that Summaries can drop details that matter later; preserve decisions and unresolved issues Tool-result clearing Remove or shorten old tool outputs once they've been used Very safe and cheap; keep references to re-fetch if needed Structured note-taking The agent writes progress, plans and findings to files (a to-do list, a notes file) outside the context and reads them back Survives compaction and session restarts; needs discipline in what's written Sub-agents Delegate a focused sub-task to a sub-agent with a clean context; it returns a condensed result (often a few thousand tokens distilled from far more) Clean separation; costs more total tokens; information can be lost in the summary Retrieval on demand Search tools for documents, code and memory instead of preloading Adds steps; needs good search Output truncation Cap tool output sizes, paginate, return summaries plus a handle to the full data The model may miss details beyond the cut; say what was truncated

docs.title: Common ways context goes wrong
docs.text: Problem What happens Fix Poisoning A hallucination or bad tool result enters the context and is treated as fact in later steps Verify important facts against sources; correct the record explicitly; compaction that doesn't preserve errors as truths Distraction So much accumulated history that the model repeats past actions instead of reasoning freshly Compaction, clearing old results, restating the current goal Confusion Too many tools or irrelevant documents lead to wrong choices Fewer tools per step, better retrieval, dynamic tool loading Clash Contradictory information (old vs new versions, conflicting instructions) Remove superseded content, label versions and dates, resolve conflicts before the model sees them

docs.title: Layout and prompt caching
docs.text:
Providers cache the processed prefix of a prompt so identical beginnings aren't recomputed, often charging much less for cached input tokens and cutting time to first token. To benefit:

  • Put stable content first: system prompt, tool definitions, long reference documents, few-shot examples.
  • Put variable content last: retrieved passages for this query, the latest messages, the current question.
  • Avoid inserting timestamps or per-request IDs early in the prompt; they break the shared prefix.
  • In agents, append new turns rather than rewriting earlier ones, so the prefix stays cacheable.

docs.title: Context engineering in practice
docs.text:
• Chat assistants: summarize older turns; keep user preferences in memory; retrieve past conversations only when relevant.
  • RAG: retrieve fewer, better passages; rerank; order by relevance; include source metadata (titles, dates) so the model can judge them.
  • Coding agents: a short project instructions file loaded every session; search tools instead of loading the repository; read files on demand; keep test output short; compact long sessions; notes for multi-session work.
  • Research agents: sub-agents explore sources in parallel and return condensed findings with citations to a lead agent.

docs.title: Measuring it
docs.text: Evaluate tasks at realistic context sizes, not just short prompts: run the same task suite with growing histories, more tools and more retrieved text, and track success, cost and latency. Synthetic "needle in a haystack" tests show whether retrieval of a planted fact works, but say little about reasoning over long, messy contexts.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
What is context engineering, and how is it different from prompt engineering?

Prompt engineering is writing effective instructions and examples for a model call. Context engineering is the broader job of deciding, at every step of an application or agent, which information enters the context window (system prompt, tools, retrieved data, memory, history, tool results) and in what form, under a limited token budget. It matters most for agents, whose context is assembled dynamically over many calls and grows as they work.

What is context rot or 'lost in the middle'?

Model accuracy tends to degrade as the context grows, especially for details buried in long inputs, and information in the middle of a long prompt is used less reliably than information near the start or end. So a large window doesn't mean everything in it will be used well; adding marginally relevant text can lower quality while raising cost. The response is to curate context, position key information well, and retrieve on demand.

How would you manage context for an agent that runs for hours?

Keep a compact, stable base context (system prompt, essential tools, a short project brief). Fetch details just in time through search and file tools. Truncate and clear old tool outputs. Have the agent maintain notes and a to-do file outside the context. Compact the history when nearing the limit, preserving the goal, decisions, current state and open issues. Delegate exploratory sub-tasks to sub-agents that return condensed results. And evaluate the agent on long tasks specifically, since short demos hide these failures.

When do you use sub-agents for context management?

When a sub-task requires reading a lot of material that the main agent doesn't need to keep: searching a large codebase, reading many documents, exploring alternatives. The sub-agent works in a fresh context and returns only a condensed result, keeping the lead agent's context clean. It costs more total tokens and can lose information in the handoff, so use it for genuinely separable, exploration-heavy work, not for tightly coupled edits.

Just-in-time retrieval vs pre-loading context: trade-offs.

Pre-loading puts everything potentially relevant in the prompt up front: simpler, fewer steps, and cache-friendly if stable, but wasteful and distracting when most of it isn't needed. Just-in-time retrieval keeps references and lets the agent fetch what it needs: leaner, scales to huge corpora, but adds tool calls and latency and depends on good search tools. A hybrid is common: pre-load a short, high-value core; fetch the rest on demand.

How do you lay out a prompt to benefit from prompt caching?

Order content from most stable to most variable: system instructions and tool definitions first, then long reference material and examples, then per-session context, and the current user turn last. Avoid placing changing values (timestamps, request IDs, user-specific data) early. In multi-turn agents, append rather than edit earlier messages so the prefix stays identical between calls.

What is context poisoning, and how do you prevent it?

An error, such as a hallucinated fact or a wrong tool result, enters the context and later steps build on it as if it were true, so the mistake compounds. Prevent it by verifying important facts against external sources before relying on them, having tools return clear errors rather than plausible-looking defaults, explicitly correcting the record when an error is found, and making sure compaction summaries don't preserve unverified claims as facts.

Common mistakes

  • Treating a 1M-token window as permission to include everything.
  • Loading every tool from every server into every call.
  • Compaction that drops the original goal or key decisions.
  • Putting per-request data at the top of the prompt and losing caching.
  • Testing only on short conversations.

docs.title: Revision checklist

docs.title: Embeddings & Vector Search
docs.text:
TL;DR

An embedding model maps text (or images) to vectors so that similar meaning means nearby vectors. Models are trained contrastively: pull matching pairs together, push others apart. Bi-encoders embed queries and documents separately (fast, indexable); cross-encoders read them together (accurate, slow), so they rerank a shortlist. Searching millions of vectors needs approximate nearest-neighbor indexes: HNSW (graph, high recall, memory-heavy), IVF (clusters), PQ (compression). Choose models by measuring recall on your own data, and plan for re-embedding when you change models.

Where this fits

Before: word2vec, BERT, contrastive learning, kNN. This page: semantic search, the retrieval half of RAG. Next: RAG.

docs.title: What an embedding is
docs.text:
A fixed-length vector (typically 256–4,096 numbers) summarizing a piece of content. Keyword search fails on "cheap flights" vs "low-cost airfare"; their embeddings sit close together.

How modern text embedders are trained:

  1. Start from a pretrained encoder (or a decoder LLM adapted for embedding).
  2. Contrastive training on pairs that should match: question–answer, query–clicked document, title–body, paraphrases, often hundreds of millions of weakly supervised pairs, then curated high-quality pairs.
  3. InfoNCE loss with in-batch negatives: each query should score its own positive higher than every other document in the batch. Larger batches mean more negatives and better embeddings.
  4. Hard negatives: documents that look relevant but aren't, mined with BM25 or an earlier model, sharpen the boundary.
  5. Instruction-tuned embedders take a task prefix ("query: …", "Represent this question for retrieving answers: …"); using the wrong prefix lowers quality.
  6. Matryoshka representation learning: train so the first \(k\) dimensions are a good embedding on their own, allowing truncation (for example 1,024 → 256) to save memory.
Representation How Strength Weakness Dense (bi-encoder) One vector per text Semantic matching, paraphrase Weak on exact terms, IDs, rare names Sparse lexical (BM25) Term weights over the vocabulary Exact matches, codes, names No semantics Learned sparse (SPLADE) A model predicts weights for vocabulary terms, including expansions Semantics with an inverted index More complex Late interaction (ColBERT) One vector per token; score sums the best token matches Fine-grained relevance Much more storage

docs.title: Similarity measures
docs.text:
Measure Formula Notes Cosine similarity \(\frac{a \cdot b}{\|a\|\|b\|}\) Compares direction only; the usual default Dot product \(a \cdot b\) Same ranking as cosine if vectors are normalized; some models are trained for raw dot product Euclidean (L2) distance \(\|a - b\|\) For unit vectors, \(\|a - b\|^2 = 2 - 2\cos\theta\), so it ranks like cosine

Use the measure the model was trained with, and normalize consistently at indexing and query time.

docs.title: Bi-encoders vs cross-encoders
docs.text:
Bi-encoder Cross-encoder Input Query and document embedded separately Query and document concatenated, read together Output Two vectors; score = similarity One relevance score Precompute documents? Yes: index once No: run for every pair at query time Speed Milliseconds over millions of documents (with ANN) Tens of milliseconds per pair Accuracy Good Better: full attention between query and document Role First-stage retrieval Reranking the top 20–100 candidates

The standard pattern: retrieve broadly with a bi-encoder (plus BM25), then rerank the shortlist with a cross-encoder or an LLM.

docs.title: Choosing an embedding model
docs.text:
1. Shortlist by the MTEB leaderboard's retrieval scores, language coverage, maximum input length, dimension, licence and hosting (API vs open weights).
  2. Evaluate on your own data: build 100–500 real queries with known relevant documents and measure recall@k and MRR. Leaderboard rank often doesn't transfer to your domain.
  3. Weigh cost and latency: embedding the corpus once and every query thereafter; dimension drives storage and search cost.
  4. Consider fine-tuning the embedder on your domain's query–document pairs if recall is the bottleneck.
  5. Plan for change: embeddings from different models aren't comparable, so switching models means re-embedding everything. Version the model alongside the index.

docs.title: Approximate nearest-neighbor search
docs.text:
Exact search compares the query with every vector: \(O(nd)\) per query. Fine for thousands of vectors, too slow for hundreds of millions. ANN indexes trade a little recall for orders of magnitude in speed.

Index Idea Key parameters Trade-offs Flat (exact) Brute force — Perfect recall; slow at scale; a good baseline IVF (inverted file) Cluster vectors with k-means; search only the nprobe nearest clusters nlist, nprobe Fast, compact; recall drops for points near cluster edges; needs training HNSW A multi-layer proximity graph; greedy search from sparse top layers down to the dense bottom layer M (links per node), efConstruction, efSearch Excellent recall and latency; high memory; slower inserts; deletions are awkward PQ (product quantization) Split each vector into \(m\) sub-vectors and replace each by the ID of its nearest centroid (1 byte each) \(m\), codebook size Huge memory savings; lower precision (rerank with full vectors) IVF-PQ IVF clusters plus PQ codes All of the above Billion-scale on modest memory DiskANN / ScaNN Disk-resident graphs; anisotropic quantization Library-specific Very large scale, cost-efficient

Tuning: raising efSearch (HNSW) or nprobe (IVF) increases recall and latency. Measure recall@k against exact search on sample queries, then choose the fastest setting meeting your recall target.

Filtering: "documents from this tenant, after 2024" combines metadata filters with vector search. Post-filtering (search, then filter) can return too few results; pre-filtering or filter-aware indexes keep recall. Multi-tenant systems often use a namespace or index per tenant.

Memory math for 10 million vectors

At 1,024 dimensions in float32: \(10^7 \times 1{,}024 \times 4\) bytes ≈ 41 GB (plus HNSW graph links, often 10–30% more).

  • float16 or int8: about 20 GB or 10 GB.
  • Matryoshka truncation to 256 dimensions in float32: about 10 GB.
  • PQ with 64 one-byte codes per vector: about 640 MB, with full vectors kept on disk for reranking.
  • Binary quantization (one bit per dimension): 128 bytes per vector, about 1.3 GB, usually followed by rescoring.

docs.title: Vector databases
docs.text:
Option When it fits FAISS, hnswlib (libraries) You manage storage and serving yourself; research and batch jobs pgvector (Postgres) You already run Postgres; up to tens of millions of vectors; transactions and joins with metadata Elasticsearch / OpenSearch You need BM25 and vectors together (hybrid search) with mature operations Dedicated vector databases (Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, Qdrant, Chroma) Large scale, managed scaling, built-in filtering, hybrid search, multi-tenancy

Choose on scale, filtering needs, hybrid search, operations burden, latency, cost and data residency, not on hype. Many systems never need more than Postgres.

docs.title: Other uses of embeddings
docs.text: Clustering and topic discovery, deduplication, classification features (embeddings plus logistic regression is a strong baseline), recommendation (two-tower retrieval), semantic caching of LLM responses, anomaly detection, and multimodal search with CLIP-style image–text embeddings.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder: what's the difference and when do you use each?

A bi-encoder embeds query and document independently, so documents are embedded once and searched with a vector index in milliseconds; it's the first-stage retriever. A cross-encoder feeds query and document together through one model, so every query token attends to every document token, giving more accurate relevance scores but requiring a forward pass per pair; it's used to rerank a shortlist of 20–100 candidates. Together: fast recall, then precise ordering.

How are embedding models trained?

Contrastively: given pairs that should match (query and relevant passage, question and answer, paraphrases), the model learns to give each anchor a higher similarity to its positive than to negatives, using an InfoNCE loss over in-batch negatives plus mined hard negatives. Training usually goes from large, noisy weakly supervised pairs to smaller, high-quality labeled sets; many models also use task instructions as prefixes and Matryoshka objectives so embeddings can be truncated.

Why is cosine similarity the usual choice?

It compares direction and ignores vector length, which often reflects things like text length or term frequency rather than meaning. Most text embedding models are trained with cosine or normalized dot-product similarity. If vectors are normalized to unit length, cosine, dot product and Euclidean distance all produce the same ranking, so you can normalize once and use the fastest operation.

How does HNSW work?

It builds a hierarchy of proximity graphs: the bottom layer contains all vectors, each linked to about M near neighbors, and each higher layer contains an exponentially smaller random subset. A search starts at the top layer, greedily walks toward the query, drops to the next layer from the best node found, and repeats, keeping a candidate list of size efSearch at the bottom. It reaches high recall with roughly logarithmic search cost, but stores many links per vector (memory-heavy) and handles deletions poorly.

IVF vs HNSW: trade-offs.

IVF clusters vectors with k-means and searches the closest few clusters: compact, fast to build, pairs naturally with PQ compression for billion-scale data, but recall suffers for queries near cluster boundaries unless nprobe is raised, and it needs a training step. HNSW gives better recall–latency trade-offs at moderate scale and needs no training, but uses more memory and is slower to build and update. Use HNSW for high-recall, in-memory workloads; IVF-PQ when memory is the constraint.

What is product quantization?

A compression scheme: split each vector into m sub-vectors, run k-means (typically 256 centroids) separately on each sub-space, and store each sub-vector as the one-byte ID of its nearest centroid, so a vector becomes m bytes. Distances are computed approximately with precomputed lookup tables of query-to-centroid distances. It cuts memory by 10–100×; to recover precision, rerank the top candidates with full-precision vectors.

How do you choose an embedding model?

Shortlist by retrieval benchmarks (MTEB), languages, maximum sequence length, dimension, license and hosting, then evaluate on a test set from your own domain: real queries labeled with relevant documents, measuring recall@k and MRR, plus latency and cost. Check that it handles your content (code, tables, jargon, multilingual). If none is good enough, fine-tune one on domain pairs. Version it, because switching models means re-embedding the corpus.

Your dense retrieval misses queries with product codes and names. Why, and what do you do?

Dense embeddings capture meaning but compress away exact surface details, so rare tokens like SKUs, error codes and names often don't match well. Add lexical retrieval (BM25) and merge results (hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion), use metadata filters for structured attributes, or use learned sparse retrieval. A cross-encoder reranker then orders the merged candidates.

How much memory do 100 million 768-dimensional float32 embeddings need, and how would you reduce it?

\(10^8 \times 768 \times 4\) bytes ≈ 307 GB, plus index overhead. Reduce it with float16 or int8 (2–4× smaller), Matryoshka truncation to fewer dimensions, product quantization (for example 64 bytes per vector, about 6.4 GB) with full vectors on disk for reranking, binary quantization with rescoring, or disk-based indexes such as DiskANN. Shard across machines if needed.

Pre-filtering vs post-filtering in vector search.

Post-filtering runs the ANN search and then drops results that fail metadata conditions; if the filter is selective, few or none of the top-k survive. Pre-filtering applies the filter first and searches only matching vectors, which is accurate but can be slow if done by brute force. Modern vector databases implement filter-aware search inside the index. For strict separation (tenants, permissions), partition indexes or namespaces instead.

Why can't you mix embeddings from two different models in one index?

Each model defines its own vector space; dimensions don't mean the same thing across models (even with equal sizes), so similarities between vectors from different models are meaningless. Upgrading the model requires re-embedding the whole corpus, usually by building a new index in parallel, evaluating it, and switching over. Store the model version with each vector.

Common mistakes

  • Picking an embedding model from a leaderboard without testing on your data.
  • Forgetting query/document prefixes for instruction-tuned embedders.
  • Using dense retrieval alone for code, IDs and names.
  • Post-filtering with selective filters and getting empty results.
  • Not planning for re-embedding when the model changes.

docs.title: Evaluating LLM Systems
docs.text:
TL;DR

Open-ended outputs rarely have one right answer, and public benchmarks leak into training data, so evaluate your system on your own tasks. Build an evaluation set from real traffic and failures; grade with programmatic checks wherever possible, LLM-as-judge with rubrics (calibrated against people, watching for position, length and self-preference bias), and human review for what matters most. Evaluate components (retrieval, tool use) and end-to-end outcomes, run every change through the suite, report uncertainty, and confirm with online metrics.

Where this fits

Before: classical metrics and A/B testing, RAG, Agents, Harness Engineering. This page: measuring LLM applications. Next: Guardrails & Security and MLOps & LLMOps for production monitoring.

docs.title: Why it's hard
docs.text:
• Many valid answers; quality has several dimensions (correctness, helpfulness, tone, safety, format).
  • Outputs vary between runs.
  • Benchmarks saturate (top models score near 100%) and get contaminated (test items appear in training data).
  • Small prompt or model changes cause regressions in places nobody looked.
  • Agents act over many steps, so the final message alone doesn't show whether the task was done correctly.

docs.title: Benchmarks: useful, but not your evaluation
docs.text:
Area Examples What they test Knowledge and reasoning MMLU, MMLU-Pro, GPQA, Humanity's Last Exam Multiple-choice and expert-level questions Math GSM8K, MATH, AIME problems Multi-step quantitative reasoning Code HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench, SWE-bench Verified From single functions to resolving real repository issues Instruction following IFEval, MT-Bench Following explicit constraints; multi-turn quality Tool use and agents BFCL, τ-bench, web and computer-use benchmarks Function calling, multi-turn tasks with tools and users Human preference LMArena (Chatbot Arena) Crowd-sourced pairwise votes, Elo-style ratings Truthfulness and safety TruthfulQA, refusal and jailbreak suites Misconceptions, harmful compliance, over-refusal

Use benchmarks to shortlist models. Then decide with an evaluation on your data: your prompts, documents, tools, users and success criteria.

docs.title: Building an evaluation set
docs.text:
1. Sources: real user inputs (sampled and anonymized), support tickets, logged failures, expert-written cases, adversarial inputs, and synthetic cases generated by a model and reviewed by people.
  2. Coverage: common cases, important slices (languages, customer tiers, document types), edge cases, unanswerable questions, and known past failures.
  3. Ground truth: a reference answer, a set of required facts, a checkable end state, or a rubric describing what good looks like.
  4. Size: start with 50–200 well-chosen cases; grow toward several hundred to thousands for important systems. A small, accurate set beats a large, noisy one.
  5. Versioning: store it with the code; keep a held-out portion you don't tune against.
  6. Labeling guidelines with examples, and agreement checks between labelers.

docs.title: Grading methods
docs.text: Method How Strengths Weaknesses Programmatic checks Exact match, regex, JSON schema validation, executing code against tests, checking database state Cheap, fast, objective, reproducible Only for checkable properties Reference-based metrics BLEU, ROUGE, embedding similarity, BERTScore Automatic Weak correlation with quality for open-ended text LLM-as-judge A model scores outputs against a rubric (pointwise) or compares two outputs (pairwise) Scales to subjective criteria Biased; must be validated against people Human evaluation Experts or trained raters with guidelines The gold standard for what matters Slow, expensive, variable between raters User signals Ratings, regenerations, edits, copies, escalations, task completion Real-world relevance Noisy, biased, delayed

docs.title: LLM-as-judge done well
docs.text:
Bias or problem Mitigation Position bias (prefers the first or second answer in a pair) Evaluate both orders; count ties when they disagree Verbosity bias (prefers longer answers) Rubrics that reward concision; length-controlled comparisons Self-preference (prefers its own family's outputs) Use a judge from a different model family, or several judges Leniency and vague scales Specific criteria, binary or 3-point scales, examples of each score Inconsistency Ask for reasoning before the verdict; low temperature; multiple samples Unknown accuracy Measure agreement with human labels on a sample before trusting it

Effective judge prompts check one criterion at a time ("Is every claim supported by the sources? yes/no, with the unsupported claims listed") rather than asking for an overall 1–10 score.

docs.title: What to evaluate, by system type
docs.text: System Key measures Chat assistant Helpfulness, correctness, instruction following, tone, refusal and over-refusal rates RAG Retrieval recall@k and MRR; context precision; faithfulness; answer correctness; citation accuracy (see RAG) Extraction / classification Field-level precision and recall, accuracy, schema validity Tool use Tool selection, argument correctness, end-state correctness (see Tool Calling) Agents Task success on the final state, pass@k and pass^k, steps, cost, safety violations (see Harness Engineering) Safety Harmful compliance on red-team prompts, jailbreak resistance, prompt-injection resistance, over-refusal on benign prompts All Latency (p50, p95), cost per request, robustness to paraphrases and typos, performance by slice

docs.title: Comparing two systems fairly
docs.text:
• Run both on the same items; use paired comparisons.
  • Report confidence intervals (bootstrap over items) rather than a single number. With 100 items, an accuracy of 80% has a 95% interval of roughly ±8 points, so a 3-point difference is noise.
  • Repeat runs for stochastic systems and agents; report variance.
  • Look at per-item changes: which cases got better or worse, and why.
  • Watch for overfitting the eval set: keep a held-out set and refresh with new production samples.

docs.title: Eval-driven development
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    A["Observe failures<br/>(traces, feedback, reviews)"] --> B["Add cases to the eval set"]
    B --> C["Change prompt, retrieval,<br/>tools, model or harness"]
    C --> D["Run the eval suite in CI"]
    D -->|"regressions"| C
    D -->|"better"| E["Ship behind an A/B test<br/>or a gradual rollout"]
    E --> F["Monitor online metrics<br/>and sampled judge scores"]
    F -->|"new failures"| A

docs.title: Online evaluation
docs.text:
• A/B tests on task completion, resolution rate, user ratings, retention and cost per successful task (see Evaluation & Metrics).
  • Implicit signals: regenerate rate, edits to drafts, copy rate, conversation abandonment, escalations to humans.
  • Sampled review: run LLM judges continuously on a sample of production traffic, and route low-scoring or flagged conversations to human review.
  • Monitoring: input drift (new topics, languages), judge-score trends, guardrail trigger rates, latency and cost.

Tooling such as promptfoo, DeepEval, RAGAS, Inspect, OpenAI Evals and observability platforms with evaluation features (LangSmith, Braintrust, Arize Phoenix and others) can help, but the evaluation set and grading criteria are the real asset.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
How would you evaluate a customer-support chatbot?

Define success: correct, policy-compliant resolution without unnecessary escalation, in an appropriate tone. Build an evaluation set from real tickets covering the main intents, hard cases and unanswerable questions, with reference resolutions or rubrics. Grade correctness and policy compliance with programmatic checks where possible (right action taken, right fields), faithfulness to retrieved policies with a calibrated LLM judge, and tone with a rubric; validate the judge against human labels. Online, track resolution rate, escalations, CSAT, regenerations and cost per resolved ticket, with A/B tests for changes and sampled human review.

Pros and cons of LLM-as-judge.

Pros: scales to thousands of outputs, handles subjective criteria such as helpfulness and faithfulness, cheap compared with human review, and fast enough for CI. Cons: position, verbosity and self-preference biases; inconsistency; blind spots on domain correctness; and susceptibility to persuasive but wrong answers. Use specific rubrics with binary or short scales, reasoning before verdicts, both orderings for pairwise comparisons, judges from a different model family, and regular agreement checks against human labels.

What is benchmark contamination, and how do you deal with it?

Test items (or close paraphrases) appearing in a model's training data, which inflates scores without reflecting real ability. Signs include much better performance on older benchmarks than on fresh ones, or memorized answers. Deal with it by using recently created or private held-out sets, decontaminating training data, rewriting items, comparing on tasks drawn from your own domain, and treating public leaderboard numbers as rough signals rather than decisions.

How do you set up regression tests for prompts?

Keep a versioned evaluation set of representative and previously failing cases, each with a programmatic check or a judge rubric. Run it automatically in CI on every change to prompts, tools, retrieval, model versions or parameters, with thresholds per metric and per critical slice; block merges on significant regressions; and show per-case diffs so reviewers see what changed. Refresh the set with new production failures, and keep a held-out portion.

How many evaluation examples do you need?

Enough that the differences you care about exceed the noise. The standard error of an accuracy estimate is about \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\): with 100 items at 80% it's about 4 points, so the 95% interval is roughly ±8; with 1,000 items, about ±2.5. To detect small improvements you need hundreds to thousands of items, or paired comparisons on the same items, which reduce variance. Start small with high-quality cases and grow the set where decisions are close.

How do you evaluate an agent rather than a single response?

By outcomes on realistic tasks: check the final state of the environment (tests pass, the right record changed once, the booking exists) instead of only the final message. Run each task multiple times and report success rate, pass@k and pass^k, plus steps, cost, time, safety violations and human interventions. Review trajectories of failures to see whether problems come from tools, context management or verification, and re-run the suite after each change.

What metrics would you use to evaluate RAG specifically?

For retrieval: recall@k (was the needed evidence retrieved?), MRR or NDCG for ranking quality, context precision. For generation: faithfulness (all claims supported by the retrieved context), answer relevance, correctness against references, citation accuracy, and correct abstention on unanswerable questions. End to end: task success and user feedback. Measure stages separately so you know whether to fix retrieval or generation.

How do you measure whether a judge model can be trusted?

Have people label a representative sample (with clear guidelines and, ideally, two raters per item to measure inter-rater agreement), run the judge on the same items, and compute agreement (accuracy against the human labels, or Cohen's kappa). Check agreement by slice and on hard cases, test for position and length bias with swapped orders and padded answers, and re-validate when the judge model or rubric changes. Use the judge only where its agreement approaches human-to-human agreement.

Offline evaluation improved, but users are less happy. What could be going on?

The evaluation set may not represent current traffic (new topics, languages, harder cases); the judge may reward things users don't value (length, formality); the change may have increased latency or cost-related limits; online behavior may differ (longer conversations, different instructions); or the metric may miss a dimension users care about (tone, conciseness). Compare offline cases with recent production samples, review real conversations, check latency, and add the missing dimensions to the evaluation.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing a model from leaderboards without testing on your tasks.
  • Trusting an LLM judge that was never compared with human labels.
  • Reporting a single score without uncertainty or slice breakdowns.
  • Grading only the final text of an agent, not the end state.
  • Letting the evaluation set go stale while production changes.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• Explain why benchmarks aren't enough, including contamination and saturation
  • Build an evaluation set: sources, coverage, ground truth, size, versioning
  • Compare programmatic checks, reference metrics, LLM judges, human review and user signals
  • List LLM-as-judge biases and mitigations
  • Choose metrics for chat, RAG, extraction, tools, agents and safety
  • Compare systems with paired tests and confidence intervals

docs.title: Harness Engineering
docs.text:
TL;DR

The harness is everything around the model that turns it into a working agent: the loop, the tools, the execution environment, permissions and human checkpoints, context management, verification, state for long-running work, observability, budgets and evaluation. The same model can succeed or fail on a task depending on its harness, so harness design is an engineering discipline of its own, improved the way models are: by measuring end-to-end task success and iterating.

Where this fits

Before: Tool Calling, Agents, MCP, Context Engineering. This page: putting them together into a reliable system. Next: Evaluating LLM Systems and Guardrails & Security.

docs.title: Why the harness matters
docs.text: Coding agents made the point vivid: the same model scored very differently on software-engineering benchmarks depending on the tools it was given, how it could view and edit files, how test results were fed back, and how long it could work. Gains often came from changing the harness rather than the model. In production the harness also decides safety (what the agent may do), cost (how many tokens it burns) and user experience (when it asks, how it reports progress).

docs.title: Components of a harness
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    U["User / trigger"] --> L
    subgraph HAR["Harness"]
        L["Agent loop<br/>budgets, stop conditions"] --> CTX["Context assembly<br/>instructions, memory, compaction"]
        CTX --> MOD["Model call"]
        MOD --> POL{"Permission policy<br/>allow / ask / deny"}
        POL -->|"allow"| EXE["Tool execution<br/>in a sandbox"]
        POL -->|"ask"| HU["Human approval"]
        HU --> EXE
        EXE --> VER["Verification<br/>tests, checks, reviewers"]
        VER --> ST["State<br/>notes, checkpoints, git"]
        ST --> L
        OBS["Tracing, cost and token accounting"] -.-> L
        OBS -.-> EXE
    end
    L --> R["Result + evidence"]
Component Decisions Agent loop Max steps, tokens, time and cost; stop conditions; retry and back-off; when to ask the user Tools Which tools, their granularity and descriptions; how results are shaped and truncated; dynamic loading for large catalogs Execution environment Containers or VMs; file-system scope; network egress allow-lists; secrets kept out of the agent's reach; CPU, memory and time limits Permissions Per-tool and per-resource rules (allow, ask, deny); read vs write; escalation paths; acting with the user's identity Human in the loop Approval points for consequential actions; plan review before execution; clear summaries for reviewers Context management What's loaded every call, what's fetched on demand, compaction, tool-result clearing, notes files Verification Tests, linters, type checks, schema validation, screenshots for UI work, independent reviewer passes, an explicit definition of done State Progress files, checkpoints, version control commits, resumable sessions, idempotent steps Observability A trace per run with every model call, tool call, token count, cost and latency; replay for debugging Evaluation An end-to-end task suite, graded on outcomes, run on every harness or model change

docs.title: The loop, with the harness made explicit
docs.text:
def run_agent(task, budget):
    state = load_or_init_state(task)            # notes, plan, checkpoints
    for step in range(budget.max_steps):
        if budget.exhausted(state):
            return escalate(state, reason="budget")
        context = assemble_context(task, state)  # instructions + memory + compacted history
        reply = model.generate(context, tools=select_tools(task, state))
        if reply.is_final:
            evidence = verify(task, state)       # tests, checks, reviewer
            if evidence.passed:
                return finish(state, evidence)
            state.add_feedback(evidence.report)  # not done yet: feed failures back
            continue
        for call in reply.tool_calls:
            decision = permissions.check(call, task.user)
            if decision == "deny":
                result = {"error": "Not permitted: " + decision.reason}
            elif decision == "ask" and not human_approves(call):
                result = {"error": "The user declined this action."}
            else:
                result = sandbox.execute(call, timeout_s=60)
            state.record(call, truncate(result))
        state.maybe_compact()                    # keep the context within budget
        state.checkpoint()                       # resumable after crashes

Everything outside model.generate is harness, and most reliability problems are fixed there.

docs.title: Execution environment and permissions
docs.text:
• Sandbox by default: run code and commands in a container or VM with only the needed files mounted, limited network access (allow-listed hosts), no production credentials, and resource and time limits. Treat the sandbox as disposable.
  • Least privilege: the agent acts with the user's permissions or narrower; separate read and write tools; scope tokens to the task.
  • Policy as code: rules such as "edits inside the repository are allowed, deleting branches needs approval, pushing to the default branch is denied" are enforced by the harness, not left to the prompt.
  • Approvals that are easy to review: show the exact command or diff, its effect and why the agent wants it.
  • The dangerous combination: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally. Break the combination or require human approval. See Guardrails & Security.

docs.title: Verification and feedback
docs.text:
Agents improve dramatically when the harness gives them fast, objective feedback:

  • For code: run the relevant tests, linters and type checkers after edits and feed concise results back; for UI work, render and screenshot.
  • For data tasks: re-query to confirm writes; validate against schemas and invariants.
  • For writing and analysis: a separate reviewer prompt with a rubric, and citation checks against sources.
  • A definition of done the harness checks before accepting "finished", so the agent can't declare success without evidence.

docs.title: Long-running work
docs.text:
Tasks that span many context windows or sessions need state outside the model:

  • Progress files and plans: a feature or task list with status, and notes on what was tried and decided, read at the start of each session.
  • Checkpoints: commit work in small, working increments (version control is an excellent checkpoint system) so failures can be rolled back and sessions resumed.
  • An initializer step: set up the environment, write the plan and success criteria, and create helper scripts once; later sessions make incremental progress against that plan.
  • Idempotent, resumable steps: after a crash, the harness should continue rather than redo or double-apply work.
  • Compaction that preserves goals, decisions and open issues. See Context Engineering.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Record a structured trace for every run: each model call (inputs, outputs, tokens, latency, model version), each tool call (arguments, results, errors), permission decisions, and costs. Traces make it possible to debug failures, find expensive steps, replay runs after a fix, and build evaluation cases from real failures.

docs.title: Evaluating and improving a harness
docs.text:
• End-to-end task suites with checkable outcomes: the tests pass, the ticket is resolved correctly, the report contains the right figures with citations. SWE-bench-style suites are the public model for this.
  • Grade outcomes, not transcripts: check the final state, plus rubric-based grading by people or calibrated model judges for subjective parts.
  • Run each task several times: agents are stochastic. pass@k (at least one of k attempts succeeds) measures capability; pass^k (all k succeed) measures reliability, which is what users experience.
  • Track efficiency and safety: steps, tokens, wall-clock time, cost per task, permission violations, human interventions.
  • Change one thing at a time (a tool description, the compaction policy, the verification step) and compare on the suite.
  • Harness–model fit: a harness tuned for one model may need changes for another; re-run the suite whenever the model changes.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
What is an agent harness, and what does it contain?

The software around the model that makes it a working agent: the loop that calls the model and executes tool calls with budgets and stop conditions; the tool set and how results are shaped; the execution environment (sandbox); permission rules and human approval points; context assembly and compaction; verification steps; persistent state for long tasks; tracing and cost accounting; and the evaluation suite used to improve it. The model decides; the harness determines what it can see, what it can do, and how its work is checked.

Why can the same model perform very differently in different harnesses?

Because the harness controls the information and feedback the model works with: which tools it has and how clear they are, how much irrelevant output floods its context, whether it can run tests and see results, how errors are reported, how long it can work, and whether its plans and notes persist. A well-designed harness turns a capable model's occasional success into reliable success; a poor one wastes capability on confusion, loops and unverified answers.

How do you let an agent run code safely?

Execute in an isolated sandbox (container or VM) with only the needed files, no production secrets, network access limited to allow-listed hosts, and CPU, memory and time limits. Enforce permission policies in the harness (for example, deny pushes to protected branches, require approval for deletions), log every command, and make the environment disposable. Combine with least-privilege credentials so even a successful escape or injection has little reach.

Where should a human approve the agent's actions?

Before consequential, irreversible or external effects: payments, sending messages, deleting or overwriting data, changing permissions, deploying, or acting on behalf of others. Also at plan level for large tasks (review the plan before execution), and whenever the agent is uncertain or the policy is unclear. Make approvals specific and easy to review, and loosen them gradually as evaluation shows reliability, rather than starting fully autonomous.

How do you evaluate an agent end to end?

Assemble realistic tasks with objective success checks on the final state, run each several times, and measure success (pass@k for capability, pass^k for reliability), cost, time, steps, safety violations and human interventions. Use rubric-based grading for subjective outputs, calibrated against people. Review failing transcripts to classify causes (tool confusion, context loss, missing verification), fix the harness, and re-run the suite. Keep a held-out set to avoid tuning to the test.

pass@k vs pass^k: what's the difference and why does it matter?

pass@k is the probability that at least one of k attempts succeeds; it rises with k and measures what the agent can do. pass^k is the probability that all k attempts succeed; it falls with k and measures consistency. A user running a task once cares about per-attempt reliability, and a deployment running it thousands of times cares about pass^k-like consistency, so reporting only pass@k overstates how dependable an agent is.

How would you design a harness for a coding agent?

Tools to search the repository, read files, edit with diffs, and run commands; a sandboxed workspace with the project's dependencies; a project instructions file loaded each session; permission rules (edits allowed, destructive git operations need approval, network limited); automatic test, lint and type-check runs after edits with concise results fed back; small commits as checkpoints; a progress file for multi-session work; compaction for long sessions; sub-agents for broad codebase exploration; full tracing; and an evaluation suite of real issues with hidden tests.

How do you make long-running agent work resumable?

Keep the source of truth outside the context: a plan or task list with statuses, notes of decisions and findings, and frequent checkpoints such as version-control commits of working increments. Make steps idempotent so re-running is safe, record which steps completed in persistent state, and start each new session by reading that state and verifying the environment. Compaction should preserve goals, decisions and open issues.

Common mistakes

  • Putting safety rules only in the prompt instead of enforcing them in the harness.
  • Accepting "done" without a verification step.
  • Running agents with production credentials.
  • Evaluating with one attempt per task and calling the result reliability.
  • Changing several harness components at once and not knowing what helped.
