docs.title: Recommender Systems
docs.text:
TL;DR

Recommenders predict what each user will want from millions of items. Collaborative filtering learns from interaction patterns; matrix factorization represents users and items as vectors whose dot product predicts affinity. Production systems use stages: fast candidate retrieval (two-tower models plus approximate nearest-neighbor search) narrows millions of items to hundreds, a heavier ranking model scores them, and re-ranking adds diversity and business rules. The hard parts are cold start, implicit feedback, position bias and feedback loops.

Where this fits

Before: kNN (neighbors), SVD and PCA (low rank), ranking metrics. This page: the most common ML system design topic. Next: two-tower retrieval is the same machinery as dense retrieval for RAG; full designs are on ML System Design.

docs.title: Feedback: explicit vs implicit
docs.text:
Explicit Implicit Examples Star ratings, thumbs up or down Clicks, views, watch time, purchases, skips Volume Sparse Abundant Meaning Clear preference, positive or negative Noisy; a non-click may mean "didn't see it", not "dislike" Typical loss Regression on ratings (RMSE) Ranking or classification losses with negative sampling

Most real systems run on implicit feedback, which is why negative sampling and bias correction matter so much.

docs.title: Content-based filtering
docs.text: Recommend items similar to what a user liked, using item features (text, category, embeddings of images or descriptions). Works for new items and niche users, but tends to over-specialize (more of the same) and needs good item features.

docs.title: Collaborative filtering
docs.text:
Use the interaction matrix alone: users who behaved similarly will like similar things.

  • User–user: find users similar to you (cosine or Pearson similarity on their interaction vectors) and recommend what they liked.
  • Item–item: recommend items similar to the ones you interacted with, where similarity is computed from co-interaction patterns. Item–item is more stable (items change less than users) and was popularized by Amazon's "customers who bought this also bought".

docs.title: Matrix factorization
docs.text:
Approximate the sparse user–item matrix \(R\) (\(m\) users × \(n\) items) as a product of low-rank factors:

\[ R \approx U V^\top \qquad \hat r_{ui} = u_u^\top v_i + b_u + b_i + \mu \]

with user vectors \(u_u\) and item vectors \(v_i\) of dimension \(k \ll \min(m, n)\), plus user, item and global biases. Train on observed entries only, with L2 regularization:

\[ \min \sum_{(u,i)\ \text{observed}} \left(r_{ui} - \hat r_{ui}\right)^2 + \lambda\left(\|u_u\|^2 + \|v_i\|^2\right) \]
  • SGD or alternating least squares (ALS): fix item vectors and solve for users in closed form, then swap; parallel and suited to implicit feedback with confidence weights.
  • The Netflix Prize (2006–2009) made matrix factorization the standard approach.
  • Plain SVD needs a full matrix, so in practice we use regularized factorization on observed entries.

docs.title: Neural recommenders
docs.text: Model Idea Two-tower (dual encoder) A user tower and an item tower each produce an embedding; score = dot product. Item embeddings are precomputed and indexed for fast retrieval. Wide & Deep (2016) A linear "wide" part memorizes feature crosses; a deep part generalizes through embeddings. DeepFM, DCN Learn feature interactions automatically (factorization machines, cross networks). DLRM Embedding tables for sparse IDs plus MLPs for dense features, with pairwise interactions. Sequential models Transformers or RNNs over a user's recent history (for example SASRec, BERT4Rec) to capture short-term intent.

docs.title: The multi-stage architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    A["Millions of items"] --> B["Candidate generation<br/>two-tower + ANN, co-visitation,<br/>popular, fresh"]
    B -->|"~1,000"| C["Filtering<br/>seen, blocked, unavailable"]
    C --> D["Ranking<br/>GBDT or deep model, rich features"]
    D -->|"~100"| E["Re-ranking<br/>diversity, freshness, business rules"]
    E -->|"~10–50"| F["Shown to the user"]
    F -.->|"logged interactions"| G["Training data"]
    G -.-> B
    G -.-> D
  • Why stages? Scoring millions of items with a heavy model per request is impossible within a latency budget of roughly 100–200 ms. Cheap, high-recall retrieval narrows the set; expensive, high-precision ranking orders it.
  • Retrieval is optimized for recall@k; it often merges several sources (embedding similarity, co-visitation, trending, followed creators).
  • Ranking predicts engagement (click, watch time, purchase, often several objectives combined) with many features: user history, item stats, context (time, device), and cross features.
  • Re-ranking enforces diversity (for example maximal marginal relevance), freshness, fairness to creators, and policy.

docs.title: Training a two-tower retriever
docs.text: Positives are observed interactions. Negatives are usually in-batch negatives (other users' positives in the same batch), trained with a softmax or contrastive loss. Because popular items appear as in-batch negatives more often, apply a log-frequency correction so popular items aren't over-penalized. Add hard negatives (items the user saw and skipped) for sharper ranking.

docs.title: The hard problems
docs.text: Problem What happens Mitigations Cold start: new users No history Onboarding questions, popular and trending items, context (location, device, referrer), fast session-based updates Cold start: new items No interactions Content features and embeddings, exploration slots, creator priors Position bias Top slots get clicked more regardless of quality Log positions, model position as a feature at training and fix it at serving, randomization, inverse propensity weighting Popularity bias Popular items get more exposure and more data Frequency correction, calibrated diversity, exposure caps Feedback loops The model trains on data its own choices produced Exploration (bandits), random holdout traffic, counterfactual evaluation Implicit negatives Non-interaction isn't dislike Negative sampling, impressions as negatives, confidence weighting Short-term vs long-term Clickbait raises clicks, lowers satisfaction Multi-objective ranking, long-term holdouts, satisfaction surveys

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
• Offline: recall@k and hit rate for retrieval; NDCG, MAP and AUC for ranking; coverage, diversity and novelty; always on a time-based split (train on the past, evaluate on the next period).
  • Online: click-through rate, watch time, conversion, retention, session length; guardrails like latency and complaint rates.
  • Offline metrics computed on logs from the old model are biased by its choices; counterfactual methods (inverse propensity scoring) and interleaving help.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Collaborative filtering vs content-based filtering.

Collaborative filtering uses only interaction patterns (users who liked X also liked Y); it discovers non-obvious relationships and needs no item features, but fails on new users and items (cold start) and favors popular items. Content-based filtering uses item and user features; it works for new items and niche interests but needs good features and tends to recommend more of the same. Production systems are hybrids, for example two-tower models that include both IDs and content features.

Explain matrix factorization for recommendations.

Represent each user and item by a \(k\)-dimensional vector so that their dot product (plus biases) predicts the interaction. Learn the vectors by minimizing squared error on observed entries with L2 regularization, using SGD or alternating least squares. The low rank forces the model to find latent factors (genre, style, price level) shared across users and items, which generalizes to unobserved pairs.

How do you handle cold start?

New users: popular or trending items, items popular in their context (location, device, traffic source), a short onboarding to collect preferences, and quick adaptation from the first few interactions in the session. New items: content-based embeddings (text, image, metadata) so the item tower can embed them without history, creator or category priors, and exploration slots (bandits) to gather interactions. Measure cold-start segments separately.

Why use candidate generation and ranking as separate stages?

Latency and cost. A rich ranking model with hundreds of features can score a few hundred items per request, not millions. Candidate generation uses cheap methods (precomputed item embeddings with approximate nearest-neighbor search, co-visitation lists) optimized for recall, so the ranker only sees plausible items and can optimize precision. Stages also let teams improve retrieval and ranking independently.

How is a two-tower model trained and served?

Train with positive (user, item) pairs from interactions and negatives from other items in the batch, using a softmax or contrastive loss over dot-product scores, with a correction for item popularity. At serving time, precompute all item embeddings and load them into an approximate nearest-neighbor index; compute the user embedding per request from recent features and retrieve the top items by dot product. Rebuild the index regularly to include new items.

What is position bias and how do you correct for it?

Items shown higher get more clicks regardless of relevance, so naive training on click logs learns "position" rather than quality and reinforces the existing ranking. Corrections: include position as a feature during training and set it to a constant at serving; inverse propensity weighting using click-propensity estimates per position (from randomized experiments); and occasional randomized ordering to measure propensities.

How do you evaluate a recommender offline and online?

Offline, on a time-based split: recall@k and hit rate for retrieval, NDCG or MAP for ranking, plus coverage, diversity and novelty, broken down by user segment (new vs heavy users). Online, with an A/B test: the primary engagement or business metric (watch time, purchases, retention), guardrails (latency, complaints, creator exposure), and long-term holdouts to catch short-term gains that hurt satisfaction.

What are feedback loops in recommendation, and why are they dangerous?

The model decides what users see, users can only interact with what they see, and the next model trains on those interactions. Items the model ignores never get data, popular items get more popular, and errors compound. Use exploration (a share of traffic for bandit-style exploration or random items), log impressions and propensities, keep a small random holdout to measure true preferences, and diversify.

How do you handle implicit feedback with no explicit negatives?

Treat interactions as positives with confidence weights (watch time, repeat purchases), and sample negatives: random items, in-batch negatives, or impressions the user saw but skipped (the most informative). Use ranking losses (BPR, sampled softmax) instead of rating regression. Account for exposure: an item never shown is unknown, not disliked.

Design a 'people you may know' or 'similar items' feature.

Candidates from graph signals (friends of friends, shared groups or contacts) or from co-interaction and embedding similarity for items; rank with features such as mutual connections, interaction recency, embedding similarity and context, trained on accept or click labels; re-rank for diversity and privacy rules; evaluate offline with recall@k and AUC on a time split, online with acceptance rate and downstream engagement; guard against privacy harms (don't surface sensitive connections) and feedback loops.

Common mistakes

  • Random splits instead of time-based splits.
  • Treating unclicked items as disliked without considering exposure.
  • Optimizing click-through alone and getting clickbait.
  • Ignoring cold-start segments in evaluation.
  • Forgetting latency budgets when proposing a heavy ranking model.

docs.title: Trees & Ensembles
docs.text:
TL;DR

A decision tree splits the feature space greedily to make leaves pure; it's readable and non-linear but has high variance. Bagging and random forests average many de-correlated trees to cut variance. Boosting adds shallow trees one at a time, each fitting the previous ensemble's errors, which cuts bias. XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost add second-order optimization, regularization and engineering that make gradient boosting the default for tabular data.

Where this fits

Before: Linear models need hand-made interactions; SVMs don't scale. This page: trees and their ensembles, still the strongest models for structured data. Next: Unsupervised Learning, then neural networks for raw perception data.

  • Decision tree 1984Readable and non-linear, but high variance.
  • Bagging 1996Average trees trained on bootstrap samples: lower variance.
  • Random forest 2001Random feature subsets de-correlate trees further. Bias unchanged.
  • AdaBoost 1995Sequential: reweight mistakes. Lower bias, sensitive to label noise.
  • Gradient boosting 2001Each tree fits the gradient of any differentiable loss.
  • XGBoost · LightGBM · CatBoost 2014–2017Second-order, regularized, fast, native missing values and categories.

docs.title: Decision trees
docs.text:
The problem it solved: non-linear, interpretable models that handle mixed feature types and missing values with no scaling.

Core idea: recursively split the data on the feature and threshold that make the resulting groups as pure as possible.

docs.title: How a tree is grown
docs.text:
1. At a node, for every feature and candidate threshold, measure how much the split reduces impurity.
  2. Choose the best split, create two children, and recurse.
  3. Stop when a node is pure, too small, or the tree reaches a depth limit.
  4. A leaf predicts the majority class (classification) or the mean target (regression).

For a continuous feature, sort its values and try thresholds between consecutive distinct values: \(O(n \log n)\) per feature per node. Histogram methods (LightGBM) bin values to make this much faster.

docs.title: Split criteria
docs.text:
Criterion Formula Used by Gini impurity \(1 - \sum_k p_k^2\) CART (scikit-learn default) Entropy / information gain \(-\sum_k p_k \log_2 p_k\); gain = parent − weighted children ID3, C4.5 Gain ratio Information gain ÷ split entropy C4.5; reduces the bias toward many-valued features Variance reduction Parent variance − weighted child variance Regression trees

Gini and entropy almost always choose the same splits; Gini is slightly cheaper because it avoids logarithms.

Worked example: choosing a split by Gini

A node has 10 samples: 6 positive and 4 negative. Gini \(= 1 - (0.6^2 + 0.4^2) = 0.48\).

A candidate split sends 4 samples (all positive) left and 6 samples (2 positive, 4 negative) right. Left Gini \(= 0\). Right Gini \(= 1 - \left((\tfrac{2}{6})^2 + (\tfrac{4}{6})^2\right) = 0.444\). Weighted child impurity \(= 0.4 \times 0 + 0.6 \times 0.444 = 0.267\), so the gain is \(0.48 - 0.267 = 0.213\). The split with the largest gain wins.

docs.title: Controlling overfitting
docs.text:
• Pre-pruning: max_depth, min_samples_split, min_samples_leaf, max_leaf_nodes, minimum impurity decrease.
  • Post-pruning: grow a full tree, then remove branches that don't help on validation data. Cost-complexity pruning trades tree size against error with a parameter α.

docs.title: Strengths and weaknesses
docs.text:
Strengths Weaknesses Interpretable; can be drawn and explained High variance: small data changes give a different tree No scaling needed; mixed feature types Deep trees overfit badly Captures interactions and non-linearity Axis-aligned, piecewise-constant boundaries; diagonal boundaries need many splits Fast prediction Greedy splitting isn't globally optimal Handles missing values (surrogate splits, default directions) Can't extrapolate beyond the training range

What came next: reduce the variance by averaging many trees, or reduce the bias by adding trees sequentially.

docs.title: Ensembles: three ways to combine models
docs.text: Bagging Boosting Stacking How Train models independently on bootstrap samples; average or vote Train models sequentially; each fixes the previous ones' errors Train a meta-model on base models' out-of-fold predictions Reduces Variance Bias (and some variance) Both, by combining different model types Base learners Deep, low-bias trees Shallow, high-bias trees ("weak learners") Diverse models Parallel Yes No (sequential) Partly Example Random forest AdaBoost, gradient boosting, XGBoost Kaggle blends

docs.title: Bagging and random forests
docs.text:
Bagging (bootstrap aggregating) trains each tree on a bootstrap sample (drawn with replacement, same size as the data), then averages. Averaging \(B\) models, each with variance \(\sigma^2\) and pairwise correlation \(\rho\), gives:

\[ \operatorname{Var}(\bar f) = \rho\,\sigma^2 + \frac{1 - \rho}{B}\,\sigma^2 \]

More trees shrink the second term; the first term only shrinks if the trees are less correlated. That's why a random forest also samples a random subset of features at each split (often \(\sqrt{d}\) for classification, \(d/3\) for regression): strong features can't dominate every tree, so trees disagree more and the average improves.

  • Out-of-bag (OOB) error: each bootstrap sample leaves out about \((1 - 1/n)^n \approx e^{-1} \approx 37\%\) of rows. Predicting each row with only the trees that didn't see it gives a free validation estimate.
  • Adding trees doesn't overfit; error plateaus. It costs only compute and memory.
  • Extra Trees (extremely randomized trees) also randomize thresholds, adding even more diversity.
  • Feature importance: impurity-based importance (mean decrease in impurity) is biased toward high-cardinality and continuous features; permutation importance on validation data, or SHAP, is more reliable.
Strengths Weaknesses Robust default with little tuning Usually less accurate than tuned boosting Parallel training; OOB validation for free Large models; slower prediction than one tree Hard to overfit by adding trees Less interpretable than a single tree

docs.title: AdaBoost
docs.text: Train a weak learner (often a one-split "stump"), then increase the weight of misclassified points so the next learner focuses on them. Each learner gets a vote \(\alpha_t = \tfrac12\ln\frac{1 - \epsilon_t}{\epsilon_t}\) based on its weighted error \(\epsilon_t\), and point weights update as \(w_i \leftarrow w_i\, e^{-\alpha_t y_i h_t(x_i)}\), then renormalize. It's equivalent to minimizing exponential loss, which makes it sensitive to label noise and outliers (they keep getting heavier).

docs.title: Gradient boosting
docs.text:
The problem it solved: AdaBoost is tied to one loss. Gradient boosting works with any differentiable loss.

Core idea: gradient descent in function space. Each new tree approximates the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions.

  1. Start with a constant prediction \(F_0\) (the mean, or the log-odds of the base rate).

  2. For \(m = 1 \dots M\): compute pseudo-residuals \(r_i = -\frac{\partial L(y_i, F(x_i))}{\partial F(x_i)}\) (for squared error, just \(y_i - F(x_i)\)); fit a shallow tree \(h_m\) to them; update \(F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + \eta\, h_m(x)\).

  3. Learning rate (shrinkage) η: smaller steps generalize better but need more trees. Typical 0.01–0.1.

  4. Shallow trees (depth 3–8): each tree is a weak learner capturing low-order interactions.
  5. Row and column subsampling (stochastic gradient boosting) adds randomness that reduces overfitting.
  6. Early stopping on a validation set picks the number of trees.

docs.title: XGBoost (2014; paper 2016)
docs.text:
XGBoost uses a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss and an explicit regularizer on tree complexity. With per-example gradients \(g_i\) and Hessians \(h_i\), a tree with \(T\) leaves and leaf weights \(w_j\):

\[ \text{Obj} \approx \sum_i \left[g_i f(x_i) + \tfrac12 h_i f(x_i)^2\right] + \gamma T + \tfrac12\lambda\sum_j w_j^2 \]

Summing \(g\) and \(h\) over the examples in leaf \(j\) as \(G_j\) and \(H_j\), the optimal leaf weight and the gain of a split are:

\[ w_j^* = -\frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda} \qquad \text{Gain} = \frac12\left[\frac{G_L^2}{H_L + \lambda} + \frac{G_R^2}{H_R + \lambda} - \frac{(G_L + G_R)^2}{H_L + H_R + \lambda}\right] - \gamma \]

A split is kept only if its gain beats \(\gamma\), which prunes the tree. Engineering: sparsity-aware splits learn a default direction for missing values, a weighted quantile sketch proposes candidate thresholds, column blocks enable parallel split finding, and cache-aware access speeds it up.

docs.title: LightGBM (2017)
docs.text:
• Histogram-based splits: bucket each feature into (by default) up to 255 bins; split finding becomes much cheaper.
  • Leaf-wise growth: expand the leaf with the largest gain anywhere in the tree, instead of level by level. Lower loss for the same number of leaves; can overfit small data, so limit num_leaves and min_data_in_leaf.
  • GOSS: keep all large-gradient examples and sample the small-gradient ones.
  • Exclusive feature bundling: merge sparse features that rarely overlap.

docs.title: CatBoost (2017)
docs.text:
• Ordered target statistics for categorical features: encode each row's category using only the rows before it in a random order, which prevents target leakage.
  • Ordered boosting reduces the prediction shift that comes from computing residuals on the same data the trees were fit to.
  • Symmetric (oblivious) trees: the same split at every node of a level; fast inference and a regularizing effect. Strong defaults with little tuning.
XGBoost LightGBM CatBoost Tree growth Level-wise (default) Leaf-wise Symmetric Speed on large data Fast Fastest Fast; slower to train on some data Categorical features Native support in recent versions Native support Best native handling Tuning effort Medium Medium; watch overfitting Low Missing values Learned default direction Learned Handled

docs.title: The hyperparameters that matter
docs.text: Parameter Effect Typical start learning_rate (eta) Step size; lower needs more trees 0.03–0.1 n_estimators Number of trees Large, with early stopping max_depth / num_leaves Tree complexity, interaction order Depth 4–8, or 31–127 leaves min_child_weight / min_data_in_leaf Minimum Hessian or rows per leaf Raise to reduce overfitting subsample, colsample_bytree Row and column sampling 0.7–0.9 reg_lambda, reg_alpha L2 and L1 on leaf weights 1 and 0 to start scale_pos_weight Class imbalance Negatives ÷ positives

docs.title: Stacking and blending
docs.text: Stacking trains a meta-model (often logistic regression) on the out-of-fold predictions of several base models, so the meta-model learns how much to trust each. Using in-fold predictions would leak. Blending is the same idea with a single held-out set. It wins competitions; in production, weigh the gain against the extra complexity and latency.

docs.title: Trees vs neural networks on tabular data
docs.text: Boosted trees usually win on tabular data because columns are heterogeneous and already meaningful, important patterns are often sharp thresholds, datasets are small to medium, and trees ignore uninformative features and handle missing values natively. Neural networks win when the inputs are raw (text, images), when you need to learn embeddings of very high-cardinality IDs, or when combining tabular data with other modalities. Strong production systems often feed neural embeddings into a GBDT, or GBDT outputs into a neural network.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Gini impurity vs entropy: what's the difference, and does it matter?

Both measure how mixed the classes in a node are and are maximal when classes are evenly split. Gini is \(1 - \sum p_k^2\); entropy is \(-\sum p_k\log p_k\). They choose the same split in the vast majority of cases. Gini is slightly faster (no logarithm) and is scikit-learn's default; entropy is a bit more sensitive to changes in small class probabilities. In practice it rarely matters; depth and minimum leaf size matter far more.

How does a tree choose a split on a continuous feature?

It sorts the feature's values and evaluates candidate thresholds between consecutive distinct values (or bin boundaries in histogram methods), computing the impurity reduction for each, and keeps the best across all features. Sorting costs \(O(n \log n)\) per feature, but sorted orders can be reused, and histogram binning reduces it to roughly \(O(\text{bins})\) per feature.

Why do decision trees overfit, and how do you prevent it?

A tree can keep splitting until each leaf holds one sample, memorizing noise: low bias, very high variance. Prevent it with depth limits, minimum samples per leaf or split, minimum impurity decrease, cost-complexity pruning, or by averaging many trees (random forest) or using shallow trees in boosting.

Why don't tree models need feature scaling?

A split only asks whether a value is above or below a threshold, so any monotonic transformation of a feature (scaling, log) leaves the ordering of values, and therefore the possible splits, unchanged. Distance- and gradient-based models need scaling; trees don't.

Bagging vs boosting.

Bagging trains models independently on bootstrap samples and averages them; it reduces variance, works best with deep, low-bias trees, and is parallel (random forest). Boosting trains models sequentially, each correcting the errors of the ensemble so far; it reduces bias, uses shallow weak learners, and is sequential (AdaBoost, gradient boosting, XGBoost). Boosting is usually more accurate when tuned; bagging is more robust and harder to overfit.

Why does a random forest sample features at each split?

Averaging reduces variance only to the extent the trees are uncorrelated: \(\operatorname{Var} = \rho\sigma^2 + (1-\rho)\sigma^2/B\). Without feature sampling, every tree would split on the same strong features near the top and look alike. Sampling about \(\sqrt{d}\) features per split forces trees to use different features, lowering \(\rho\) and making the average much better.

What is out-of-bag error?

Each tree's bootstrap sample omits about 37% of the rows (\(e^{-1}\)). For each row, predict using only the trees that didn't train on it, and compute the error over all rows. It's an almost unbiased estimate of test error without a separate validation set, useful for tuning random forests cheaply.

Does adding more trees overfit a random forest? What about boosting?

Adding trees to a random forest doesn't overfit; error decreases and then plateaus, because each tree is an independent average term. In boosting, adding trees keeps reducing training loss, so after some point validation error rises: boosting can overfit with too many trees, especially with a high learning rate. Use early stopping on a validation set.

Explain gradient boosting as gradient descent in function space.

Treat the vector of predictions \(F(x_i)\) as the parameters. The gradient of the loss with respect to each prediction tells you how to change it to reduce the loss. A new tree is fit to the negative gradients (pseudo-residuals), which approximates a gradient step that generalizes to new points, and is added with a small learning rate. For squared error the pseudo-residuals are the ordinary residuals; for log loss they're \(y - p\).

Why use shallow trees in boosting but deep trees in random forests?

Boosting reduces bias by adding many small corrections; each learner should be weak (high bias, low variance) so the sequence doesn't overfit quickly, and depth controls the interaction order captured per tree. Random forests reduce variance by averaging; each tree should be strong and low-bias (deep), because averaging can't fix bias but does cancel variance.

What makes XGBoost better than vanilla gradient boosting?

A second-order (gradient and Hessian) approximation that gives closed-form optimal leaf weights and a principled split gain; explicit regularization on leaf count (\(\gamma\)) and leaf weights (\(\lambda\), \(\alpha\)); sparsity-aware split finding that learns where missing values go; row and column subsampling; and systems work (parallel split finding, weighted quantile sketch, cache-aware blocks, out-of-core training) that makes it fast on large data.

Write the optimal leaf weight and split gain in XGBoost.

With \(G\) and \(H\) the sums of gradients and Hessians in a leaf, the optimal weight is \(w^* = -G/(H + \lambda)\), and the leaf's contribution to the objective is \(-\frac12 G^2/(H + \lambda)\). A split's gain is \(\frac12\left[\frac{G_L^2}{H_L+\lambda} + \frac{G_R^2}{H_R+\lambda} - \frac{(G_L+G_R)^2}{H_L+H_R+\lambda}\right] - \gamma\). The split is made only if the gain is positive, so \(\gamma\) acts as a minimum-gain pruning threshold.

LightGBM leaf-wise growth vs level-wise growth.

Level-wise growth (XGBoost's default) expands all nodes at one depth before going deeper: balanced trees, more conservative. Leaf-wise growth (LightGBM) always expands the single leaf with the largest loss reduction: lower loss for the same number of leaves and faster convergence, but deeper, unbalanced trees that can overfit small datasets. Control it with num_leaves, max_depth and min_data_in_leaf.

How do XGBoost and LightGBM handle missing values?

During split finding they try sending all missing values left and then right, and keep the direction with the higher gain. That "default direction" is stored per split and used at prediction time. Missingness can therefore be informative without imputation. CatBoost treats missing values as a separate value by default.

How does CatBoost handle categorical features without leakage?

Plain target encoding uses each row's own label to compute its category's average, which leaks the target. CatBoost uses ordered target statistics: it shuffles the rows and encodes each row's category using only the target values of rows earlier in that order (with a prior for smoothing), and uses several permutations. Combined with ordered boosting, this removes the prediction shift that causes overfitting.

Why is impurity-based feature importance misleading?

Mean decrease in impurity is computed on training data and favors features with many possible split points (continuous or high-cardinality features, even random IDs), and it splits credit arbitrarily between correlated features. Use permutation importance on validation data (shuffle one feature and measure the performance drop) or SHAP values, and remember that importance is not causality.

When would you choose a GBDT over a neural network?

For tabular, structured data of small to medium size with heterogeneous features, when you need strong accuracy with modest tuning, fast CPU inference, native handling of missing values, and good explainability (TreeSHAP). Choose neural networks for raw text, images and audio, very large datasets with high-cardinality IDs that benefit from learned embeddings, multimodal inputs, or when you need to train end to end with other neural components.

What is stacking, and how do you avoid leakage when stacking?

Stacking trains a meta-model on the predictions of several base models. To avoid leakage, the meta-model's training features must be out-of-fold predictions: for each fold, base models are trained on the other folds and predict this one, so no base model predicts a row it trained on. At test time, base models retrained on all data (or the average of fold models) produce the meta-features.

Common mistakes

  • Trusting impurity-based importance for feature selection.
  • Tuning the number of boosting rounds without early stopping.
  • Using a high learning rate with many trees.
  • Target encoding categories on the full dataset before splitting.
  • Expecting trees to extrapolate a trend beyond the training range.

docs.title: Unsupervised Learning
docs.text:
TL;DR

Without labels, we look for structure. k-means finds round clusters fast but needs \(k\) and is sensitive to initialization. Gaussian mixtures give soft, elliptical clusters, fit with EM. DBSCAN finds clusters of any shape and labels noise. PCA projects onto directions of maximum variance; t-SNE and UMAP make 2-D maps of neighborhoods for visualization. Isolation Forest and friends flag anomalies by how easy points are to isolate.

Where this fits

Before: supervised models in Linear Models and Trees & Ensembles. This page: structure without labels. Next: Recommender Systems use the same low-rank and nearest-neighbor ideas; autoencoders learn non-linear compressions.

docs.title: k-means
docs.text:
The problem it solved: split unlabeled data into groups, such as customer segments, quickly.

Core idea: alternate between assigning each point to its nearest centroid and moving each centroid to the mean of its points.

  1. Initialize \(k\) centroids (use k-means++: pick each new centroid with probability proportional to its squared distance from the existing ones, which spreads them out).
  2. Assign each point to the nearest centroid.
  3. Update each centroid to the mean of its assigned points.
  4. Repeat until assignments stop changing.

It minimizes the within-cluster sum of squares, \(\sum_k \sum_{x \in C_k}\|x - \mu_k\|^2\). Each step can only lower it, so it converges, but to a local minimum; run several initializations and keep the best. Cost is \(O(nkd)\) per iteration; mini-batch k-means scales to very large data.

Choosing k: the elbow in within-cluster error against \(k\); the silhouette score; the gap statistic; or, best, the number that's useful for the downstream decision.

Strengths Weaknesses Simple, fast, scales to millions of points Must choose \(k\) Easy to explain Assumes round, similar-sized, similar-density clusters Good initializer for other methods Sensitive to initialization, outliers and feature scaling

k-medoids uses actual data points as centers and any distance, which makes it more robust to outliers but slower.

docs.title: Gaussian mixture models and EM
docs.text:
The problem it solved: k-means gives hard assignments and only round clusters.

Core idea: model the data as a mixture of \(K\) Gaussians, each with its own mean, covariance and weight, and fit it with expectation–maximization (EM).

  • E-step: compute each point's responsibility for each component, \(\gamma_{ik} = \frac{\pi_k\,\mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k)}{\sum_j \pi_j\,\mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_j, \Sigma_j)}\).
  • M-step: re-estimate \(\pi_k\), \(\mu_k\), \(\Sigma_k\) as responsibility-weighted averages.

EM never decreases the likelihood but can stop at local optima. Choose \(K\) with BIC or AIC. Covariance options (full, diagonal, tied, spherical) trade flexibility against parameters. k-means is the limit of a GMM with equal spherical covariances and hard assignments.

EM is the general recipe for latent-variable models: hidden Markov models use it, and VAEs inherit its idea of inferring hidden variables.

docs.title: Hierarchical clustering
docs.text:
Agglomerative: start with every point as its own cluster and repeatedly merge the closest pair, producing a dendrogram you can cut at any level.

Linkage Distance between clusters Behavior Single Closest pair of points Long chains; finds elongated shapes Complete Farthest pair Compact clusters Average Average over pairs In between Ward Increase in within-cluster variance Similar-sized, round clusters

No \(k\) needed in advance and the hierarchy itself is informative (taxonomies, gene expression), but it needs \(O(n^2)\) memory and at least \(O(n^2)\) time, so it suits thousands of points, not millions.

docs.title: DBSCAN and HDBSCAN
docs.text:
The problem it solved: clusters of arbitrary shape, without fixing \(k\), with outliers identified explicitly.

Core idea: a cluster is a dense region. A core point has at least minPts neighbors within radius ε; clusters grow by connecting core points that are within ε of each other; border points are near a core point; everything else is noise.

  • Finds non-convex shapes (rings, moons) and labels outliers.
  • Struggles when clusters have different densities (one ε doesn't fit all) and in high dimensions.
  • HDBSCAN builds a hierarchy over all densities and extracts stable clusters, removing the need to pick ε.

docs.title: Comparing clustering methods
docs.text: k-means GMM Hierarchical DBSCAN Needs \(k\) Yes Yes No (cut the tree) No Cluster shape Round Elliptical Depends on linkage Arbitrary Assignments Hard Soft (probabilities) Hard Hard, plus noise Outliers Pull centroids Hurt fit Depends on linkage Labeled as noise Scale Very large Medium Small Medium to large (with indexes)

docs.title: Evaluating clusters
docs.text:
• Without labels: silhouette score \(s = \frac{b - a}{\max(a, b)}\), where \(a\) is the mean distance to the point's own cluster and \(b\) the mean distance to the nearest other cluster (range −1 to 1); Davies–Bouldin index (lower is better); Calinski–Harabasz index.
  • With reference labels: adjusted Rand index (ARI) and normalized mutual information (NMI).
  • Best of all: whether the clusters are stable across runs and useful for the decision they serve.

docs.title: PCA
docs.text:
The problem it solved: high-dimensional data is redundant, noisy, slow to process, and impossible to visualize.

Core idea: find orthogonal directions of maximum variance and project onto the first few.

  1. Standardize the features (PCA is driven by variance, so units matter).
  2. Compute the covariance matrix \(\frac{1}{n}X^\top X\) of the centered data, or, more stably, the SVD \(X = U\Sigma V^\top\).
  3. The principal components are the eigenvectors (columns of \(V\)); the variance along component \(j\) is its eigenvalue, \(\sigma_j^2 / n\).
  4. Keep the top \(k\) components covering, say, 90–95% of the variance, and project: \(Z = XV_k\).

Uses: compression, de-correlating features for linear models, denoising, visualization, speeding up downstream models. Kernel PCA finds non-linear structure with the kernel trick. Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) is the supervised cousin: it maximizes separation between classes rather than total variance.

Strengths Weaknesses Fast, deterministic, well understood Captures only linear structure Removes correlated, redundant directions Components mix features and are hard to interpret Optimal linear compression (Eckart–Young) High variance isn't the same as useful for the label

docs.title: t-SNE and UMAP
docs.text:
The problem they solved: PCA can't unfold curved manifolds, and we want to see clusters in embedding spaces.

  • t-SNE (2008) converts distances into neighbor probabilities in high-dimensional space (Gaussian) and in 2-D (Student-t, whose heavy tails prevent crowding), then minimizes the KL divergence between them. Perplexity (roughly the effective number of neighbors, typically 5–50) sets the scale.
  • UMAP (2018) builds a fuzzy nearest-neighbor graph and optimizes a low-dimensional layout with cross-entropy. Faster, scales better, and keeps more global structure.

How to read these plots

Cluster sizes and the distances between clusters in a t-SNE plot carry little meaning; results change with perplexity and random seed. Use these methods to explore and visualize, not as features for a model or as proof that clusters exist.

docs.title: Anomaly detection
docs.text:
The problem: fraud, intrusions and defects are rare, varied and often unlabeled.

Core idea: model what normal looks like and flag what doesn't fit.

Method Idea Good for Statistical rules z-scores, interquartile range, seasonal baselines Single metrics, monitoring Isolation Forest Random splits isolate anomalies in fewer steps; score is the average path length Tabular data, fast, few assumptions Local Outlier Factor Compares a point's local density to its neighbors' Clusters with different densities One-Class SVM Learns a boundary around normal data Small, clean training sets Autoencoders High reconstruction error means unusual Images, sequences, high-dimensional signals

Evaluating is hard without labels: use precision@k on cases reviewed by experts, inject synthetic anomalies, and track how investigators rate flagged cases. In production, combine unsupervised scores with supervised models as labels accumulate, and expect drift.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Explain the k-means algorithm and its objective.

k-means minimizes the within-cluster sum of squared distances to centroids. Initialize \(k\) centroids (k-means++), assign each point to its nearest centroid, recompute each centroid as the mean of its points, and repeat until assignments stop changing. Each step lowers the objective, so it converges, but to a local optimum, so run multiple initializations. Cost is \(O(nkd)\) per iteration.

How do you choose k in k-means?

Look for an elbow in the within-cluster sum of squares as \(k\) increases; maximize the average silhouette score; use the gap statistic (compare with a reference uniform distribution); or use BIC with a GMM. Most importantly, check stability across random seeds and whether the segments are useful and actionable for the business decision. There's often no single "true" \(k\).

Why k-means++ initialization?

Random initialization can place several centroids in one cluster and none in another, giving poor local optima and slow convergence. k-means++ picks the first centroid at random and each next one with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest chosen centroid, spreading them out. It comes with an \(O(\log k)\) approximation guarantee in expectation and usually converges faster to better solutions.

When does k-means fail?

With non-spherical shapes (rings, elongated clusters), clusters of very different sizes or densities, outliers (they drag centroids), unscaled features (large-scale features dominate the distance), categorical data (means don't make sense; use k-modes), and high dimensions where distances concentrate. Alternatives: GMMs for elliptical clusters, DBSCAN or HDBSCAN for arbitrary shapes and noise, spectral clustering for graph-like structure.

Explain the EM algorithm.

EM fits models with hidden variables by alternating two steps. The E-step computes the posterior over the hidden variables given current parameters (for a GMM, each point's responsibility for each component). The M-step re-estimates parameters to maximize the expected complete-data log-likelihood under those posteriors (responsibility-weighted means, covariances and weights). Each iteration never decreases the likelihood, but EM can converge to a local optimum, so initialize carefully (often with k-means).

GMM vs k-means.

Both need \(K\). k-means makes hard assignments and assumes spherical, equal-variance clusters; it's faster. A GMM makes soft probabilistic assignments, learns a covariance per component (elliptical clusters of different sizes and orientations), gives a density model you can use for likelihoods and anomaly scores, and supports model selection with BIC. k-means is a special case of a GMM.

DBSCAN vs k-means: when would you use each?

Use k-means for large data with roughly round, similar-sized clusters when you know or can choose \(k\). Use DBSCAN when clusters have irregular shapes, you don't know how many there are, and you need outliers labeled as noise (geospatial points, anomaly-rich data). DBSCAN struggles with clusters of different densities (use HDBSCAN) and in high dimensions, and requires choosing ε and minPts.

What do ε and minPts mean in DBSCAN, and how do you choose them?

ε is the neighborhood radius; minPts is the minimum number of points within ε for a point to be a core point. A common heuristic sets minPts to about twice the number of dimensions, then plots each point's distance to its minPts-th nearest neighbor in sorted order and picks ε at the knee of that curve. Too small an ε labels most points as noise; too large merges clusters.

Derive PCA as variance maximization.

Project centered data onto a unit vector \(u\): the variance of the projection is \(u^\top S u\), where \(S\) is the covariance matrix. Maximize it subject to \(u^\top u = 1\) with a Lagrange multiplier: \(S u = \lambda u\). So \(u\) must be an eigenvector of \(S\), and the variance equals its eigenvalue \(\lambda\); the best direction is the top eigenvector. Each next component is the top eigenvector orthogonal to the previous ones.

How are PCA and SVD related?

For centered data \(X = U\Sigma V^\top\), the covariance is \(\frac{1}{n}X^\top X = V\frac{\Sigma^2}{n}V^\top\). So the right singular vectors \(V\) are the principal components, the eigenvalues are \(\sigma_j^2/n\), and the projected data is \(XV = U\Sigma\). Computing PCA via SVD is more numerically stable than forming the covariance matrix explicitly, and truncated or randomized SVD scales to large data.

Why standardize before PCA? How many components do you keep?

PCA finds directions of maximum variance, so a feature measured in large units (income in dollars) would dominate one in small units (age in years) purely because of scale. Standardizing puts features on equal footing (unless they share units and their variance is meaningful). Keep enough components to explain about 90–95% of the variance, look for an elbow in the scree plot, or pick the number that maximizes downstream validation performance.

Can you trust distances in a t-SNE plot?

Not really. t-SNE preserves local neighborhoods, not global geometry: the size of a cluster and the distance between clusters carry little meaning, apparent clusters can appear in structureless data at low perplexity, and the layout changes with perplexity and seed. Use it to explore; validate any claimed clusters with other methods. UMAP preserves somewhat more global structure but has the same caveats.

How does Isolation Forest detect anomalies?

It builds many random trees, each splitting on a random feature at a random threshold. Anomalies are few and different, so random splits isolate them in few steps (short paths from the root), while normal points sit in dense regions and need many splits. The anomaly score is based on the average path length across trees, normalized by the expected path length for a dataset of that size. It's fast, scales linearly, and needs no distance metric.

How do you evaluate an unsupervised model in practice?

Use internal metrics (silhouette, Davies–Bouldin) to compare settings; check stability across seeds and subsamples; compare with any available labels (ARI, NMI) or with human review of samples from each cluster; and most importantly measure the downstream effect: whether segments behave differently, whether flagged anomalies are confirmed by investigators (precision@k), or whether features derived from clusters improve a supervised model.

Common mistakes

  • Running k-means or PCA on unscaled features.
  • Reading global structure into a t-SNE plot.
  • Using one run of k-means instead of several initializations.
  • Treating a high silhouette score as proof the clusters are meaningful.
  • Reporting anomaly-detection "accuracy" when anomalies are a tiny fraction of the data.

docs.title: CNNs & Computer Vision
docs.text:
TL;DR

Convolutions slide small shared filters over an image, giving translation equivariance with few parameters. AlexNet (2012) proved deep CNNs on GPUs beat hand-made features; ResNet (2015) made very deep networks trainable with skip connections. Detection (Faster R-CNN, YOLO) and segmentation (U-Net, Mask R-CNN) build on CNN backbones. The Vision Transformer treats image patches as tokens and scales better with data. Contrastive learning (SimCLR, CLIP) learns from unlabeled images or image–caption pairs, and CLIP-style encoders now feed multimodal LLMs.

Where this fits

Before: MLPs and backprop, training techniques. This page: the first domain where deep learning won decisively. Next: Sequence Models for text and time; the Transformer later unifies vision and language.

docs.title: Convolutions
docs.text:
The problem: an MLP on a 224×224×3 image needs about 150,000 weights per hidden unit and has no idea that a cat in the top-left corner is the same as a cat in the bottom-right.

Core idea: use small filters (for example 3×3) whose weights are shared across all positions. Each filter detects one pattern wherever it appears.

Concept Meaning Kernel / filter A \(k \times k \times C_{in}\) weight tensor; a layer has \(C_{out}\) of them Stride Step between filter positions; stride 2 halves the resolution Padding Zeros around the border; "same" padding keeps the size Output size \(\left\lfloor \frac{W - k + 2p}{s} \right\rfloor + 1\) Parameters \((k \cdot k \cdot C_{in} + 1) \cdot C_{out}\), independent of image size Receptive field The input region that affects one output; grows with depth, stride and pooling Pooling Max or average over small windows; downsamples and adds small translation invariance 1×1 convolution Mixes channels at each position; cheap way to change channel count Depthwise separable A per-channel spatial filter, then a 1×1 to mix channels; about \(k^2\) times cheaper (MobileNet) Dilated (atrous) Gaps between kernel taps; bigger receptive field without more parameters (DeepLab) Transposed convolution Learned upsampling (decoders, segmentation) Worked example: shapes and parameters

A 3×3 convolution from 64 to 128 channels, stride 1, padding 1, on a 56×56 input: output is 56×56×128 and parameters are \(3\cdot3\cdot64\cdot128 + 128 = 73{,}856\). With stride 2 the output becomes 28×28×128 and the parameter count doesn't change.

Two stacked 3×3 layers see a 5×5 region with \(2 \cdot 9C^2 = 18C^2\) weights instead of \(25C^2\) for one 5×5 layer, plus an extra non-linearity. That's why VGG used only 3×3 filters.

Inductive biases: locality (nearby pixels matter together), weight sharing (the same pattern can appear anywhere) and a hierarchy of features. Convolution is translation-equivariant (shift the input, the feature map shifts the same way); pooling and global averaging add approximate invariance. These biases make CNNs data-efficient, and they're exactly what ViTs give up in exchange for flexibility.

docs.title: The architecture line
docs.text:
• LeNet-5 1998Convolution, pooling, then dense layers for digits. Small images, little compute.
  • AlexNet 20128 layers, ReLU, dropout, data augmentation, two GPUs. ImageNet top-5 error 15.3% vs about 26% for the runner-up.
  • VGG 2014Uniform stacks of 3×3 convolutions, 16–19 layers. Simple but heavy (about 138M parameters).
  • GoogLeNet / Inception 2014Parallel 1×1, 3×3, 5×5 branches with 1×1 bottlenecks: wide and efficient.
  • ResNet 2015Residual blocks \(y = F(x) + x\); 152 layers; 3.57% top-5 error. Deeper finally meant better.
  • DenseNet 2016Each layer receives all previous feature maps; strong reuse of features.
  • MobileNet · EfficientNet 2017–2019Depthwise separable convolutions; compound scaling of depth, width and resolution.
  • ConvNeXt 2022A CNN modernized with Transformer-era choices (large kernels, LayerNorm, GELU) that matches ViTs.

docs.title: Why ResNet works
docs.text:
The degradation problem: adding layers to a plain deep network made training error worse, not just test error. That isn't overfitting; it's an optimization failure. A deeper network could in principle copy the shallower one and set the extra layers to identity, but plain layers find identity hard to learn.

A residual block learns only the change: \(y = F(x) + x\). If identity is best, the block pushes \(F\) toward zero, which is easy. The skip connection also gives gradients a direct path: \(\frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = I + \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}\), so signals reach early layers even when \(F\)'s gradient is small. Bottleneck blocks (1×1 reduce → 3×3 → 1×1 expand) keep very deep ResNets affordable. Every Transformer block uses the same residual idea.

docs.title: Transfer learning in vision
docs.text:
Use a backbone pretrained on a large dataset (ImageNet, or a self-supervised or CLIP model), then:

  • Small data, similar domain: freeze the backbone, train a new head (linear probing).
  • More data or a different domain: fine-tune the whole network with a lower learning rate for early layers.
  • Match the pretraining preprocessing (resolution, normalization) and use augmentation.

docs.title: Object detection
docs.text:
The problem: classification says what; detection also says where, as boxes with classes, often many per image.

Family Examples Idea Trade-off Two-stage R-CNN (2014) → Fast R-CNN → Faster R-CNN (2015) Propose regions (a region proposal network), then classify and refine each Accurate, slower One-stage YOLO (2015 onward), SSD, RetinaNet (2017) Predict classes and boxes densely in one pass Real-time; RetinaNet's focal loss closed the accuracy gap Anchor-free FCOS, CenterNet Predict box centers or distances directly, no predefined anchor boxes Simpler, fewer hyperparameters Transformer-based DETR (2020) Learned object queries plus set matching (Hungarian) to ground truth; no NMS Elegant; slower to train originally

Key pieces:

  • IoU (intersection over union) measures box overlap: \(\frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}\).
  • Non-max suppression removes duplicate boxes: keep the highest-scoring box, drop others overlapping it above an IoU threshold, repeat.
  • mAP: average precision per class from the precision–recall curve at an IoU threshold (for example 0.5, or averaged over 0.5–0.95 in COCO), then averaged over classes.
  • Feature Pyramid Networks combine coarse, semantic features with fine, high-resolution ones to detect objects at many scales.
  • Focal loss: \(FL(p_t) = -(1 - p_t)^\gamma \log p_t\) down-weights the flood of easy background examples so training focuses on hard ones.

docs.title: Segmentation
docs.text:
Task Output Examples Semantic A class per pixel FCN, U-Net (2015), DeepLab Instance A mask per object instance Mask R-CNN (2017) Panoptic Both: every pixel gets a class and, for objects, an instance Panoptic FPN, Mask2Former Promptable A mask for whatever you point at or describe Segment Anything (2023)

U-Net uses an encoder–decoder with skip connections from each encoder level to the matching decoder level, so fine spatial detail lost during downsampling is restored when upsampling. It's still the standard in medical imaging and is the backbone of many diffusion models. Metrics: mean IoU per class and the Dice coefficient \(\frac{2|A \cap B|}{|A| + |B|}\).

docs.title: The Vision Transformer
docs.text:
The problem: CNNs' locality is helpful with limited data, but it limits global context and seemed to scale less well than Transformers did in language.

Core idea: split the image into patches (for example 16×16 pixels, so a 224×224 image becomes 196 tokens), linearly embed each patch, add position embeddings and a [CLS] token, and run a standard Transformer encoder.

  • Weak built-in assumptions, so ViT needs lots of data: it beat CNNs only when pretrained on very large datasets (JFT-300M). DeiT showed strong augmentation and distillation make it competitive on ImageNet alone.
  • Attention cost grows with the square of the number of patches, a problem at high resolution. Swin Transformer uses shifted local windows and a hierarchy, like a CNN, to fix this.
  • One architecture for text and images made multimodal models natural.
CNN ViT Built-in assumptions Locality, translation equivariance, hierarchy Almost none; learns them from data Data efficiency High Low without huge pretraining or heavy augmentation Global context Grows slowly with depth From the first layer Scaling with data and compute Good Better at large scale High-resolution cost Linear in pixels Quadratic in patches (unless windowed)

docs.title: Self-supervised and contrastive learning
docs.text:
The problem: labels are expensive, but unlabeled images and image–caption pairs are abundant.

Method Year Idea SimCLR 2020 Two augmentations of the same image are positives; other images in the batch are negatives; InfoNCE loss. Needs large batches. MoCo 2019 A momentum-updated encoder and a queue of negatives, so batches can be small BYOL, DINO 2020, 2021 No negatives: a student matches a slowly updated teacher's output on another view MAE 2021 Mask 75% of patches and reconstruct them; very efficient for ViTs CLIP 2021 Image and text encoders trained contrastively on 400M image–caption pairs

The InfoNCE loss for a positive pair \((q, k^+)\) among negatives \(k_j\): \(L = -\log\frac{\exp(q \cdot k^+/\tau)}{\sum_j \exp(q \cdot k_j/\tau)}\), with temperature \(\tau\). It's a softmax classification of "which of these is my partner", which is why more negatives (bigger batches) help.

CLIP trains with a symmetric version of that loss over a batch of N image–caption pairs: the N matching pairs should score highest among all N² combinations. Zero-shot classification: embed prompts like "a photo of a {label}" for every class and pick the class whose text embedding is closest to the image embedding. CLIP's zero-shot ImageNet accuracy matched a fully supervised ResNet-50. Its text encoder conditions text-to-image diffusion models, and CLIP or SigLIP vision encoders feed most multimodal LLMs.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Compute the output size and parameter count of a convolutional layer.

Output width \(= \lfloor (W - k + 2p)/s \rfloor + 1\) (same for height); output depth is the number of filters \(C_{out}\). Parameters \(= (k \cdot k \cdot C_{in} + 1)\cdot C_{out}\) with biases. Example: 224×224×3 input, 64 filters of 7×7, stride 2, padding 3 → 112×112×64 output with \(7\cdot7\cdot3\cdot64 + 64 = 9{,}472\) parameters. The count doesn't depend on image size; the compute does.

Why share weights in a CNN?

It encodes the assumption that a useful pattern (an edge, an eye) can appear anywhere, so the same detector should be applied everywhere. That cuts parameters by orders of magnitude, improves data efficiency because every position provides training signal for the same filter, and makes the layer translation-equivariant.

What does a 1×1 convolution do?

At each spatial position it computes a linear combination of the input channels, like a dense layer applied per pixel. It changes the number of channels cheaply (bottlenecks in Inception and ResNet), mixes information across channels, and adds a non-linearity when followed by an activation. In depthwise separable convolutions it's the "pointwise" step.

Equivariance vs invariance.

A function is equivariant to translation if shifting the input shifts the output the same way: convolution feature maps move with the object. It's invariant if shifting the input leaves the output unchanged: a classifier's "cat" score. CNNs are equivariant through convolutions and become approximately invariant through pooling, striding and global average pooling at the end.

What is a receptive field and how do you grow it?

The region of the input that can influence a given output unit. It grows with depth (each 3×3 layer adds 2 pixels), with stride and pooling (which multiply the growth of later layers), and with dilated convolutions. Large receptive fields are needed for context, such as recognizing large objects or segmenting with scene context. The effective receptive field is usually smaller than the theoretical one and concentrated near the center.

Why did AlexNet matter so much?

In 2012 it cut ImageNet top-5 error from about 26% to 15.3%, a far larger jump than incremental improvements to hand-crafted features. It combined a deep CNN, ReLU (much faster training than tanh), dropout, data augmentation, and training on GPUs with a large labeled dataset. It convinced the field that learned features beat engineered ones given enough data and compute, which started the deep-learning era.

Explain the degradation problem and how ResNet solves it.

Plain networks deeper than about 20 layers had higher training error than shallower ones, an optimization problem, not overfitting. ResNet adds identity skip connections so each block learns a residual \(F(x)\) and outputs \(F(x) + x\). Learning identity becomes trivial (drive \(F\) toward zero), and gradients flow directly through the skip paths (\(\partial y/\partial x = I + \partial F/\partial x\)). This made 100- to 1000-layer networks trainable.

Why use two 3×3 convolutions instead of one 5×5?

Same receptive field (5×5), fewer parameters (\(18C^2\) vs \(25C^2\)), and an extra non-linearity between them, which makes the function more expressive. Three 3×3 layers similarly replace a 7×7 (\(27C^2\) vs \(49C^2\)).

How much does a depthwise separable convolution save?

A standard convolution costs about \(k^2 C_{in} C_{out}\) multiply-adds per position. Depthwise separable splits it into a per-channel \(k \times k\) filter (\(k^2 C_{in}\)) plus a 1×1 pointwise convolution (\(C_{in} C_{out}\)). The ratio is \(\frac{1}{C_{out}} + \frac{1}{k^2}\), so about 8–9 times cheaper for 3×3 kernels, with a small accuracy cost. It's the core of MobileNet and EfficientNet.

One-stage vs two-stage object detectors.

Two-stage detectors (Faster R-CNN) first propose candidate regions, then classify and refine each one: more accurate, especially on small objects, but slower. One-stage detectors (YOLO, SSD, RetinaNet) predict boxes and classes densely over the image in a single pass: fast enough for real time. RetinaNet's focal loss addressed the extreme foreground–background imbalance that had held one-stage accuracy back.

Explain IoU, non-max suppression and mAP.

IoU is the overlap between two boxes divided by their union; a detection usually counts as correct if its IoU with a ground-truth box exceeds 0.5. Non-max suppression keeps the highest-scoring box and removes boxes that overlap it above an IoU threshold, repeating until none remain. mAP computes average precision (the area under the precision–recall curve) per class and averages over classes; COCO averages it over IoU thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95 too.

Why does U-Net use skip connections?

The encoder downsamples to capture context but loses fine spatial detail. Skip connections pass high-resolution feature maps from each encoder level directly to the matching decoder level, where they're concatenated with the upsampled features. The decoder can then produce precise boundaries using both "what" (deep features) and "where" (shallow features). It works well even with small datasets, which is why it's standard in medical imaging.

Why does focal loss help RetinaNet?

Dense detectors evaluate tens of thousands of candidate locations, nearly all easy background. With cross-entropy, these easy negatives dominate the total loss and gradients. Focal loss multiplies cross-entropy by \((1 - p_t)^\gamma\) (often \(\gamma = 2\)), shrinking the loss for well-classified examples so training concentrates on hard, misclassified ones. Combined with class-balancing weights, it let one-stage detectors match two-stage accuracy.

How does ViT turn an image into tokens, and why does it need so much data?

It cuts the image into fixed-size patches (for example 16×16), flattens each and projects it linearly to the model dimension, adds learned position embeddings, prepends a [CLS] token, and feeds the sequence to a Transformer encoder. Unlike a CNN, it has no built-in locality or translation equivariance, so it must learn those regularities from data. With limited data CNNs win; with very large pretraining datasets (or strong augmentation and distillation) ViT matches or beats them.

ViT vs CNN: which would you choose?

For small or medium datasets, edge devices or high-resolution dense prediction with tight compute, a CNN (or a hybrid) is often the better choice. With large pretraining data or a strong pretrained checkpoint, ViTs scale better and integrate naturally with language models. In practice you usually fine-tune a pretrained backbone, and modern CNNs (ConvNeXt) and ViTs perform similarly; choose based on available checkpoints, latency and deployment tooling.

Explain the contrastive loss used by SimCLR and CLIP.

InfoNCE treats each example as a classification problem: among one positive and many negatives, pick the positive. \(L = -\log\frac{\exp(\text{sim}(q, k^+)/\tau)}{\sum_j \exp(\text{sim}(q, k_j)/\tau)}\) with cosine similarity and temperature \(\tau\). SimCLR's positives are two augmented views of one image; CLIP's are an image and its caption, with the loss applied symmetrically in both directions. More negatives give a tighter bound and better representations, hence large batches.

How does CLIP do zero-shot classification?

Embed each class name in a prompt such as "a photo of a {class}" with the text encoder, embed the image with the image encoder, and predict the class whose text embedding has the highest cosine similarity with the image embedding. No task-specific training is needed, and prompt wording and ensembling prompts change accuracy. Limits: it inherits web-data biases and struggles with counting, fine-grained distinctions and spatial relations.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting that the parameter count of a convolution doesn't depend on input size.
  • Saying ResNet solved overfitting (it solved an optimization problem).
  • Confusing semantic and instance segmentation.
  • Claiming ViTs are always better than CNNs.
  • Mismatching preprocessing between pretraining and fine-tuning.
