docs.title: Math for ML
docs.text:
TL;DR

Four tools appear everywhere later on. Linear algebra: models are matrix multiplications; dot products measure similarity; SVD and low rank explain PCA and LoRA. Probability: training is usually maximum likelihood; priors are regularizers. Calculus: gradient descent and the chain rule (backprop). Information theory: cross-entropy is the classification and LLM loss; KL divergence measures how far two distributions are apart. You need intuition and a handful of derivations, not proofs.

Where this fits

Before: nothing; this is the toolkit. Next: ML Fundamentals uses these tools to define learning, generalization and regularization.

docs.title: Vectors, dot products and similarity
docs.text:
A data point, a word, an image patch or a user is a vector. The dot product measures alignment:

\[ a \cdot b = \sum_i a_i b_i = \|a\|\,\|b\|\cos\theta \]
  • Cosine similarity \(\frac{a \cdot b}{\|a\|\|b\|}\) ignores length and compares direction. It's the standard for comparing embeddings, because an embedding's length often reflects frequency or confidence rather than meaning.
  • If vectors are normalized to length 1, cosine similarity equals the dot product, and ranking by either gives the same order. That's why vector databases often normalize first.
  • Attention scores are dot products between a query and keys: \(QK^\top\).

docs.title: Matrices as transformations, and shapes
docs.text:
A matrix \(W\) of shape \((m, n)\) maps an \(n\)-dimensional vector to an \(m\)-dimensional one: rotate, scale, project. A neural network layer is \(h = \sigma(Wx + b)\).

Shapes are half of every ML coding round

\(X\) is usually \((n, d)\): \(n\) samples, \(d\) features. Weights \(w\) are \((d,)\) for one output or \((d, k)\) for \(k\) outputs. \(XW\) has shape \((n, k)\). Say shapes out loud while you code; most bugs are shape bugs.

Useful identities:

Identity Where it shows up \((AB)^\top = B^\top A^\top\) Deriving gradients, normal equation \(\nabla_w \|Xw - y\|^2 = 2X^\top(Xw - y)\) Linear regression gradient \(\nabla_x\, x^\top A x = (A + A^\top)x\) Quadratic forms, Gaussian log-likelihood \(\operatorname{tr}(AB) = \operatorname{tr}(BA)\) Matrix calculus tricks

docs.title: Rank, eigenvectors and SVD
docs.text:
• Rank is the number of independent directions in a matrix. A rank-\(r\) matrix of shape \((d, d)\) can be written as \(BA\) with \(B\) of shape \((d, r)\) and \(A\) of shape \((r, d)\): \(2dr\) numbers instead of \(d^2\). That is the whole idea behind LoRA.
  • Eigenvectors of a square matrix \(A\) satisfy \(Av = \lambda v\): directions that are only stretched, by factor \(\lambda\).
  • For a covariance matrix (symmetric, positive semi-definite), eigenvectors are orthogonal directions of variance and eigenvalues are the variance along each. Those eigenvectors are the principal components in PCA.
  • SVD works for any matrix: \(X = U\Sigma V^\top\), with orthogonal \(U\), \(V\) and non-negative singular values in \(\Sigma\). Keeping the top \(k\) singular values gives the best rank-\(k\) approximation (Eckart–Young theorem). Used in PCA, recommender matrix factorization, compression and LoRA initialization variants.

docs.title: Norms
docs.text: Norm Formula Use L1 \(\sum_i \lvert x_i\rvert\) Lasso regularization (sparsity), MAE, Manhattan distance L2 \(\sqrt{\sum_i x_i^2}\) Ridge regularization, Euclidean distance, gradient clipping L∞ \(\max_i \lvert x_i\rvert\) Adversarial robustness bounds Frobenius \(\sqrt{\sum_{ij} A_{ij}^2}\) Matrix approximation error, weight decay on matrices

docs.title: The distributions that matter
docs.text: Distribution Models Where in ML Bernoulli(\(p\)) One yes/no outcome Binary labels → log loss Binomial(\(n, p\)) Number of successes in \(n\) trials Conversion counts in A/B tests Categorical One of \(k\) classes Multiclass labels, next-token prediction → softmax + cross-entropy Gaussian(\(\mu, \sigma^2\)) Continuous values with noise Regression noise → MSE; VAEs; weight initialization Poisson(\(\lambda\)) Counts per interval Event counts, arrivals, Poisson regression Exponential(\(\lambda\)) Waiting times Survival and time-to-event models Beta(\(\alpha, \beta\)) A probability itself Prior for click-through rates; Thompson sampling Uniform Equal chance Random initialization, random search

docs.title: Bayes' theorem
docs.text:
\[ P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)} \] The classic interview puzzle

A test is 99% sensitive (positive when you have the disease) and 99% specific (negative when you don't). The disease affects 1% of people. You test positive. What's the probability you have it?

Out of 10,000 people: 100 have it, and 99 of them test positive. 9,900 don't, and 1% of them, 99, also test positive. So \(P(\text{disease} \mid +) = 99 / (99 + 99) = 50\%\). The low base rate drags it down. Same logic explains why a fraud model with a 1% false-positive rate can still produce mostly false alarms when fraud is rare.

docs.title: Expectation, variance, covariance
docs.text:
• \(\mathbb{E}[aX + b] = a\,\mathbb{E}[X] + b\), and expectation is linear even for dependent variables.
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mathbb{E}[X]^2\); \(\operatorname{Var}(aX) = a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\).
  • For independent variables, \(\operatorname{Var}(X + Y) = \operatorname{Var}(X) + \operatorname{Var}(Y)\). Averaging \(n\) independent estimates divides variance by \(n\): the reason bagging and ensembles work.
  • Correlation is covariance scaled to \([-1, 1]\). It measures linear association only, and correlation is not causation.

docs.title: Maximum likelihood and MAP
docs.text:
Most training objectives are maximum likelihood estimation (MLE): choose parameters \(\theta\) that make the observed data most probable, \(\hat\theta = \arg\max_\theta \sum_i \log p(y_i \mid x_i; \theta)\). Working with the log turns products into sums and avoids underflow.

MAP adds a prior: \(\hat\theta = \arg\max_\theta \left[\sum_i \log p(y_i \mid x_i;\theta) + \log p(\theta)\right]\).

Assumption What MLE or MAP becomes Gaussian noise on \(y\) Mean squared error Bernoulli label Binary cross-entropy (log loss) Categorical label Softmax cross-entropy Gaussian prior on weights L2 regularization (ridge, weight decay) Laplace prior on weights L1 regularization (lasso) Derivation: MSE from Gaussian noise

Assume \(y_i = f(x_i) + \epsilon_i\) with \(\epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\). Then \(\log p(y_i \mid x_i) = -\frac{(y_i - f(x_i))^2}{2\sigma^2} - \frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2)\). Summing over the data and dropping constants, maximizing the log-likelihood equals minimizing \(\sum_i (y_i - f(x_i))^2\): the squared error. The same steps with a Bernoulli likelihood \(p^{y}(1-p)^{1-y}\) give log loss.

docs.title: Statistics for experiments
docs.text:
Concept Meaning Null hypothesis The default claim, usually "no difference between A and B" p-value Probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null were true. Not the probability the null is true. Type I error (α) False positive: declaring an effect that isn't there. Usually capped at 5%. Type II error (β) False negative: missing a real effect. Power = \(1 - \beta\), usually targeted at 80%. Confidence interval A range built so that 95% of such intervals (over repeated experiments) contain the true value Central Limit Theorem Means of many independent samples are approximately normal, which justifies z- and t-tests on averages and conversion rates Multiple testing Testing many metrics or variants inflates false positives; correct with Bonferroni or control the false discovery rate

Which test: z-test for proportions with large samples, t-test for means with unknown variance, chi-square for categorical counts, Mann–Whitney when normality is doubtful. A/B testing in practice is on Evaluation & Metrics.

docs.title: Gradients and the chain rule
docs.text:
The gradient \(\nabla_\theta L\) points in the direction of steepest increase, so we step against it:

\[ \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\, \nabla_\theta L(\theta) \]

The chain rule composes derivatives: if \(L = f(g(x))\) then \(\frac{dL}{dx} = f'(g(x))\,g'(x)\). Backpropagation is the chain rule applied layer by layer from the loss backwards, reusing intermediate results. See Neural Network Fundamentals.

Derivatives you should know by heart:

Function Derivative Why it matters Sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\) \(\sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z))\) At most 0.25, so stacked sigmoids shrink gradients \(\tanh(z)\) \(1 - \tanh^2(z)\) At most 1, still saturates ReLU \(\max(0, z)\) 1 if \(z > 0\), else 0 No saturation for positive inputs Softmax + cross-entropy \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial z} = p - y\) The cleanest gradient in ML; same form as logistic regression MSE \(\frac{1}{2}(\hat y - y)^2\) \(\hat y - y\) Linear regression gradient

docs.title: Convexity
docs.text: A function is convex if every line segment between two points on its graph lies above the graph. Convex losses (linear regression, logistic regression, SVM) have a single global minimum, so gradient descent finds it. Neural network losses are non-convex, with many minima and saddle points; in high dimensions most critical points are saddle points rather than bad local minima, and SGD's noise helps escape them.

docs.title: Gradient descent variants
docs.text:
Variant Gradient computed on Trade-off Batch The whole dataset Stable, exact, but one step per full pass Stochastic One example Very noisy, cheap steps, noise can help generalization Mini-batch 32 to thousands of examples The practical default; matches GPU parallelism

Second-order methods (Newton's method) use the Hessian of second derivatives, which costs \(O(d^2)\) memory and \(O(d^3)\) to invert, so they're impractical for models with millions of parameters. Adam approximates per-parameter curvature cheaply instead. See Training Deep Networks.

docs.title: Constrained optimization
docs.text: Lagrange multipliers turn a constrained problem into an unconstrained one by adding the constraint to the objective with a multiplier. You'll see this in the SVM dual form, where only points with non-zero multipliers (the support vectors) affect the solution.

docs.title: Information theory
docs.text:
Quantity Formula Intuition and use Entropy \(H(p) = -\sum_x p(x)\log p(x)\) Average surprise; uncertainty of a distribution. Decision-tree splits reduce it. Cross-entropy \(H(p, q) = -\sum_x p(x)\log q(x)\) Surprise when the truth is \(p\) but you predicted \(q\). The classification and LLM training loss. KL divergence \(D_{KL}(p\|q) = \sum_x p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)} = H(p,q) - H(p)\) Extra surprise from using \(q\) instead of \(p\). Always \(\ge 0\), zero only when equal, not symmetric. Mutual information \(I(X;Y) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y)\) How much knowing \(Y\) reduces uncertainty about \(X\). Feature selection; contrastive learning. Perplexity \(\exp(\text{cross-entropy per token})\) Effective number of choices a language model is unsure between. Lower is better.

Because the true label distribution \(p\) is fixed, minimizing cross-entropy \(H(p, q)\) is the same as minimizing \(D_{KL}(p\|q)\), and the same as maximizing likelihood.

Forward vs reverse KL. Minimizing \(D_{KL}(p\|q)\) (forward) forces \(q\) to put mass wherever \(p\) has mass, so it covers all modes and may be blurry. Minimizing \(D_{KL}(q\|p)\) (reverse) punishes \(q\) for putting mass where \(p\) has none, so it seeks one mode. VAEs and variational inference use the reverse form; RLHF's KL penalty keeps the policy close to the reference model.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
What does a dot product measure, and why use cosine similarity for embeddings?

The dot product \(a \cdot b = \|a\|\|b\|\cos\theta\) grows with both alignment and length. Cosine similarity divides out the lengths, so it compares only direction. For embeddings, direction carries meaning while length often reflects frequency or confidence, so cosine is more robust. If all vectors are normalized to unit length, dot product and cosine give identical rankings, which is why many vector stores normalize once and then use the faster dot product.

Explain SVD and give two ML uses.

Any matrix factors as \(X = U\Sigma V^\top\): orthogonal input directions \(V\), scaling by singular values \(\Sigma\), orthogonal output directions \(U\). Truncating to the top \(k\) singular values gives the best rank-\(k\) approximation. Uses: PCA (principal components are the right singular vectors of the centered data matrix), recommender systems (low-rank factorization of the user–item matrix), compression of weight matrices, latent semantic analysis, and the low-rank view behind LoRA.

Derive the MSE loss from maximum likelihood.

Assume targets are the model output plus Gaussian noise: \(y = f(x) + \epsilon\), \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\). The log-likelihood of one point is \(-\frac{(y - f(x))^2}{2\sigma^2}\) plus a constant. Summing over data and maximizing is equivalent to minimizing \(\sum (y_i - f(x_i))^2\). So MSE is the right loss when errors are roughly Gaussian; heavy-tailed errors call for MAE or Huber loss instead.

How is a prior related to regularization?

MAP estimation maximizes log-likelihood plus \(\log p(\theta)\). A zero-mean Gaussian prior gives \(\log p(\theta) = -\lambda\|\theta\|_2^2\) + const, which is L2 regularization. A Laplace prior gives \(-\lambda\|\theta\|_1\), which is L1. The regularization strength \(\lambda\) corresponds to how tight the prior is: a stronger prior belief that weights are small means more regularization.

A disease affects 1% of people; a test is 99% sensitive and 99% specific. You test positive. What's the chance you're sick?

About 50%. Per 10,000 people: 100 are sick and 99 test positive; 9,900 are healthy and 99 of them falsely test positive. So 99 of 198 positives are real. The point interviewers want: when the base rate is low, even an accurate test yields many false positives. The same applies to fraud and rare-event detection, which is why precision matters so much there.

What is a p-value? What are type I and type II errors?

A p-value is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as yours assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null is true. A type I error is rejecting a true null (a false positive), controlled by the significance level α. A type II error is failing to reject a false null (a false negative); power is \(1 - \beta\). Lowering α reduces false positives but increases false negatives unless you collect more data.

What does the Central Limit Theorem say, and why does it matter in ML?

The mean of many independent, identically distributed samples is approximately normally distributed, with variance \(\sigma^2/n\), whatever the original distribution (given finite variance). It justifies confidence intervals and z/t-tests on averages and conversion rates in A/B tests, and explains why mini-batch gradients are noisy estimates whose noise shrinks as batch size grows.

Why is the gradient of softmax plus cross-entropy so simple?

With logits \(z\), probabilities \(p = \text{softmax}(z)\) and one-hot label \(y\), the loss is \(L = -\sum_k y_k \log p_k\). Differentiating through the softmax, the terms cancel to \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial z} = p - y\): predicted minus true. It's well-behaved (no saturation when the model is confidently wrong), which is one reason cross-entropy trains classifiers better than MSE on probabilities. Logistic regression's gradient \((p - y)x\) is the two-class case.

Why don't we use Newton's method to train neural networks?

Newton's method needs the Hessian, a \(d \times d\) matrix of second derivatives. For a model with \(d = 10^9\) parameters that's \(10^{18}\) entries to store, and inverting it costs \(O(d^3)\). It also behaves badly on non-convex losses, where it can move toward saddle points. Instead we use first-order methods with cheap curvature approximations, such as Adam's per-parameter scaling.

Why cross-entropy instead of MSE for classification?

Three reasons. It is the maximum-likelihood loss for categorical labels, so it's statistically correct. Its gradient with softmax or sigmoid is \(p - y\), which stays large when the model is confidently wrong, while MSE through a sigmoid has a gradient scaled by \(\sigma'(z)\) that vanishes in saturated regions. And combined with sigmoid it is convex in the logistic regression weights, while MSE through a sigmoid is not.

Forward vs reverse KL divergence: which is mode-seeking?

Reverse KL, \(D_{KL}(q\|p)\), is mode-seeking: \(q\) is heavily penalized for placing mass where \(p\) is near zero, so it locks onto one mode. Forward KL, \(D_{KL}(p\|q)\), is mode-covering: \(q\) is penalized for missing any region where \(p\) has mass, so it spreads out. Maximum likelihood training minimizes forward KL from data to model; variational inference typically minimizes reverse KL.

What is perplexity?

The exponential of the average per-token cross-entropy: \(\text{PPL} = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{N}\sum_t \log p(x_t \mid x_{<t})\right)\). It can be read as the number of equally likely choices the model is effectively choosing between at each step. A perplexity of 10 means the model is as uncertain as a uniform choice over 10 tokens. It's only comparable between models with the same tokenizer and test set.

Eigenvalues of a covariance matrix: what do they tell you?

Each eigenvalue is the variance of the data along its eigenvector. Large eigenvalues mark directions where the data spreads out; tiny ones mark nearly redundant directions. Their ratio to the total shows the share of variance each principal component explains, which is how you choose how many components to keep in PCA. A near-zero eigenvalue also signals multicollinearity, which makes linear regression unstable.

Common mistakes

  • Saying a p-value is the probability the null hypothesis is true.
  • Confusing correlation with causation, or saying zero correlation means independence.
  • Forgetting that KL divergence is asymmetric.
  • Mixing up rows and columns: always state the shape of \(X\).
  • Quoting sigmoid's derivative maximum as 1 (it's 0.25).

docs.text:

  • State what rank, eigenvalues and SVD mean and connect them to PCA and LoRA

  • Derive MSE and log loss from maximum likelihood; map priors to L1/L2
  • Define p-value, type I/II errors, power and the CLT
  • Write the softmax + cross-entropy gradient
  • Define entropy, cross-entropy, KL and perplexity; say which KL is mode-seeking

docs.title: ML Fundamentals
docs.text:
TL;DR

ML learns a function from examples by minimizing a loss on training data, hoping it generalizes to unseen data. Generalization error splits into bias (too simple), variance (too sensitive to the sample) and noise. Regularization controls variance. Validation measures generalization honestly, and leakage is the most common way it lies to you. On tabular data, features and careful handling of imbalance matter as much as the model.

Where this fits

Before: Math for ML supplies MLE, gradients and loss functions. Next: Evaluation & Metrics chooses what to measure, then Classical ML applies all of this to real algorithms.

docs.title: The learning problem
docs.text:
The problem before it: hand-written rules break on messy inputs such as spam, images and speech. The idea: learn the rules from examples.

Every supervised algorithm has the same four parts:

  1. Data \(\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\), assumed to be drawn independently from one distribution (the i.i.d. assumption).
  2. A model family (hypothesis class): linear functions, trees, neural networks.
  3. A loss \(L(y, \hat y)\) that scores mistakes.
  4. An optimizer that searches the family for the lowest average training loss. This is empirical risk minimization.
Paradigm Signal Examples Supervised Labeled pairs \((x, y)\) Classification, regression, ranking Unsupervised Only \(x\) Clustering, dimensionality reduction, density estimation Self-supervised Labels created from the data itself Next-token prediction (GPT), masked tokens (BERT), contrastive learning (CLIP) Semi-supervised A few labels plus lots of unlabeled data Pseudo-labeling, consistency training Reinforcement Rewards for actions Games, robotics, RLHF, reasoning models

Two distinctions interviewers like:

  • Parametric vs non-parametric. Parametric models have a fixed number of parameters regardless of data size (linear regression, neural networks). Non-parametric models grow with the data (kNN stores it all; trees can grow a leaf per point).
  • Discriminative vs generative. Discriminative models learn \(P(y \mid x)\) or a decision boundary directly (logistic regression, SVM). Generative models learn \(P(x, y)\) or \(P(x)\) and can sample data (Naive Bayes, GMMs, GPT, diffusion models). Discriminative models usually win on prediction accuracy given enough data; generative ones handle missing data, small data and generation.

docs.title: Bias, variance and overfitting
docs.text:
The problem: a model can fit the training data perfectly and still fail on new data.

For squared error, the expected test error at a point decomposes as:

\[ \mathbb{E}\left[(y - \hat f(x))^2\right] = \underbrace{\left(\mathbb{E}[\hat f(x)] - f(x)\right)^2}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{\operatorname{Var}\left[\hat f(x)\right]}_{\text{variance}} + \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{irreducible noise}} \]
  • Bias: error from wrong assumptions; the model is too simple to capture the pattern (underfitting).
  • Variance: error from sensitivity to the particular training sample; the model fits noise (overfitting).

Symptom Diagnosis Fixes High training error, validation error close to it High bias Bigger or more flexible model, better features, less regularization, train longer Low training error, much higher validation error High variance More data, regularization, simpler model, early stopping, augmentation, ensembling (bagging) Both low, but production is bad Distribution shift or leakage Check splits, training–serving skew, drift

Learning curves plot error against training-set size. If validation error is still falling as data grows, more data will help (variance). If both curves have flattened at a high error, more data won't help (bias).

Double descent. For very over-parameterized models (large neural networks), test error can rise near the point where the model can just fit the training data, then fall again as the model keeps growing. The classical U-curve still describes most classical models; double descent explains why huge networks generalize despite being able to memorize.

docs.title: Regularization
docs.text:
The problem: models with many parameters assign large weights to noise. The idea: penalize complexity so the model prefers simpler explanations.

Method Penalty added to the loss Effect Bayesian view L2 / ridge \(\lambda\|w\|_2^2\) Shrinks all weights smoothly; stabilizes correlated features Gaussian prior L1 / lasso \(\lambda\|w\|_1\) Drives some weights exactly to zero: feature selection Laplace prior Elastic Net \(\lambda_1\|w\|_1 + \lambda_2\|w\|_2^2\) Sparse, but keeps groups of correlated features together Mixed prior

Why L1 gives zeros. Picture minimizing the loss subject to \(\|w\|_1 \le t\). The L1 constraint region is a diamond with corners on the axes, and the loss contours usually touch it first at a corner, where some coordinates are exactly zero. The L2 region is a circle with no corners, so the solution shrinks weights without zeroing them. Algebraically, L1's gradient has constant magnitude \(\lambda\) however small the weight, which pushes it all the way to zero; L2's gradient \(2\lambda w\) fades as \(w\) shrinks.

Other regularizers: early stopping (stop when validation loss stops improving), dropout, data augmentation, weight decay in neural networks, pruning and depth limits in trees, and ensembling.

Scale before you regularize

L1 and L2 penalize weights equally, but a weight's size depends on its feature's units. Standardize features first, or the penalty is unfair across features.

docs.title: Validation, cross-validation and leakage
docs.text:
The problem: tuning on the test set gives optimistic, fake accuracy.

  • Train / validation / test. Fit on train, tune hyperparameters and select models on validation, report once on test. Touching the test set repeatedly turns it into a validation set.
  • k-fold cross-validation. Split into \(k\) folds, train on \(k-1\), validate on the remaining one, rotate and average. Uses data efficiently and gives a variance estimate; costs \(k\) times the compute.
  • Stratified k-fold keeps class proportions in every fold (important under imbalance).
  • Group k-fold keeps all rows from one entity (user, patient, device) in the same fold, so the model can't memorize the entity.
  • Time-series splits always train on the past and validate on the future (rolling or expanding windows). Random splits on time-ordered data leak the future.
  • Nested cross-validation uses an inner loop for tuning and an outer loop for an unbiased performance estimate.

docs.title: Data leakage
docs.text:
Leakage means information that won't be available at prediction time reaches the model during training or evaluation. Offline scores look great; production fails.

Leak Example Prevention Target leakage A "refund issued" feature in a fraud model; the refund happens because of the fraud Ask of every feature: would I know this at prediction time? Preprocessing on all data Fitting the scaler, imputer or target encoder before splitting Fit transformations inside each training fold (use pipelines) Temporal leakage Random split on time-ordered data; features computed with future data Time-based splits; point-in-time feature joins Group leakage The same patient or user in train and test Group k-fold Duplicates Near-identical rows across splits Deduplicate before splitting Test-set tuning Picking the model with the best test score Keep a held-out test set you touch once

docs.title: Hyperparameter tuning
docs.text:
Method How When Grid search Try every combination Few hyperparameters with known ranges Random search Sample combinations at random Usually better than grid per trial: when only a few hyperparameters matter, random search tries more distinct values of each Bayesian optimization Fit a surrogate model of score vs hyperparameters, pick promising points Expensive training runs Successive halving / Hyperband Start many configurations cheaply, keep the best, give them more budget Large search spaces with early signal

Tune on validation data or with cross-validation, never on test. Search learning rates and regularization strengths on a log scale.

docs.title: Feature engineering and preprocessing
docs.text:
The problem: classical models only see what you give them, and raw data has missing values, categories and wildly different scales.

Scaling. Standardize (z-score) or min-max scale for models that use distances or gradients: linear and logistic regression with regularization, SVM, kNN, k-means, PCA, neural networks. Tree models don't need scaling, because splits depend only on the order of values.

Categorical features.

Cardinality Encoding Caveat Low (< ~20) One-hot Dimensionality grows with categories High (IDs, ZIP codes) Target / mean encoding Must be computed out-of-fold with smoothing, or it leaks the label High Hashing trick Collisions; no inverse mapping Very high, with lots of data Learned embeddings Needs a neural model or embedding pretraining Ordered (low, medium, high) Ordinal integers Only if the order is real

Missing values. Impute (median, mode, a model), and add an is_missing indicator, since missingness itself can be informative. XGBoost and LightGBM learn a default direction for missing values natively.

Skew and outliers. Log-transform heavy-tailed values such as income or counts; clip extreme values; use robust scalers or losses (MAE, Huber).

Feature selection. Filter methods (correlation, mutual information), wrapper methods (recursive feature elimination), and embedded methods (L1, tree importance).

Curse of dimensionality. As dimensions grow, data becomes sparse and distances concentrate: the nearest and farthest neighbors end up almost equally far, so distance-based methods such as kNN and k-means degrade. Remedies: dimensionality reduction, feature selection, or models that learn representations.

docs.title: Imbalanced data
docs.text:
The problem: with 1% fraud, a model that always predicts "not fraud" is 99% accurate and useless.

  1. Use the right metric: precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC, or recall at a fixed false-positive rate. Not accuracy. See Evaluation & Metrics.
  2. Reweight the loss: class weights inversely proportional to frequency, or focal loss, which down-weights easy examples so training focuses on hard ones.
  3. Resample the training fold only: undersample the majority (fast; discards data), oversample the minority (risk of overfitting duplicates), or SMOTE (create synthetic minority points by interpolating between neighbors; can create unrealistic points near the boundary).
  4. Tune the decision threshold on validation data to match the business cost of each error type. The default 0.5 is rarely right.
  5. Recalibrate probabilities if you resampled or reweighted, because the model's scores no longer reflect real base rates.
  6. Reframe extremely rare positives as anomaly detection.

docs.title: No free lunch
docs.text:
No single algorithm is best for every problem. Good defaults by data type:

Data Strong first choice Tabular, structured Gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost), with logistic regression as a baseline Images Pretrained CNN or ViT, fine-tuned Text Pretrained Transformer (embeddings plus a classifier, or an LLM) Time series Strong baselines (seasonal naive), then GBDT with lag features, then deep models Very little data Simple, regularized models; transfer learning; strong priors

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Explain the bias–variance trade-off with an example.

Bias is error from a model being too simple for the pattern; variance is error from being too sensitive to the particular training sample. Example: fitting house prices with a straight line (high bias, it misses the curve) versus a degree-15 polynomial (low training error, but it swings wildly between points, high variance). Increasing complexity lowers bias and raises variance, so validation error is U-shaped. You diagnose by comparing training and validation error, and you trade them off with model size, regularization, more data and ensembling.

How do you detect and fix overfitting?

Detect it with a large gap between training and validation performance, or validation loss rising while training loss keeps falling. Fixes: more or augmented data; regularization (L1/L2, dropout, weight decay); a simpler model or fewer features; early stopping; ensembling such as bagging; cross-validation for model selection so you don't overfit the validation set itself.

Does adding more data reduce bias or variance?

Mainly variance. More data makes it harder for a flexible model to fit noise, so the training–validation gap shrinks. It does little for bias: if a linear model can't represent a curved relationship, more data won't fix that. Learning curves tell you which case you're in.

L1 vs L2 regularization: why does L1 produce sparse weights?

Geometrically, the L1 constraint region is a diamond whose corners lie on the axes; loss contours usually first touch it at a corner, where some weights are exactly zero. L2's region is a circle, so it shrinks weights without zeroing them. Analytically, L1's penalty gradient has constant size \(\lambda\) regardless of the weight's magnitude, so it can push small weights all the way to zero, while L2's gradient \(2\lambda w\) vanishes as \(w\) shrinks. Use L1 for feature selection and L2 for stability with correlated features; Elastic Net combines both.

What is data leakage? Give three examples.

Information unavailable at prediction time that reaches training or evaluation. Examples: (1) fitting a scaler or target encoder on the full dataset before splitting; (2) a random train/test split on time-ordered data, so the model trains on the future; (3) a feature that is a consequence of the label, like "chargeback filed" in a fraud model; (4) the same user appearing in both train and test. Symptoms: suspiciously high offline metrics and a big drop in production. Prevent with time-based or grouped splits, pipelines that fit preprocessing inside folds, and asking of each feature whether it exists at prediction time.

How do you cross-validate a time-series model?

Never shuffle. Use forward-chaining splits: train on periods 1..k and validate on period k+1, then expand (or roll) the window and repeat. Leave a gap between train and validation if features use look-back windows or labels arrive late. Compute features point-in-time so nothing from the future leaks in. Report the average and the spread across folds, and check performance on the most recent fold, since that's closest to production.

Why is random search often better than grid search?

Usually only a few hyperparameters matter much. With a 3×3 grid over two hyperparameters you test only three distinct values of each; nine random points test nine distinct values of each. So for the same budget, random search explores the important dimensions more finely. Bayesian optimization goes further by using past results to choose the next trial.

Which models need feature scaling, and which don't?

Models based on distances or gradient-based optimization with penalties need scaling: kNN, k-means, SVM (especially RBF), PCA, linear and logistic regression with regularization, and neural networks (for stable training). Tree-based models (decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting) don't, because a split only depends on the ordering of values within a feature.

How do you encode a categorical feature with 10,000 values?

One-hot is too wide and sparse for most models. Options: target encoding (replace each category by the smoothed mean of the target, computed out-of-fold to avoid leakage); frequency encoding; the hashing trick into a fixed number of buckets; learned embeddings in a neural model; or native categorical handling in CatBoost or LightGBM. Group rare categories into "other". Mention leakage and smoothing for target encoding; that's what interviewers listen for.

How do you handle missing data?

First ask why it's missing: completely at random, related to other features, or related to the value itself (for example, high earners skipping an income question). Options: drop rows or columns if missingness is rare or a column is mostly empty; impute with median or mode; model-based imputation (kNN, iterative); add an is_missing flag because missingness can carry signal; or use models that handle missing values natively, such as XGBoost. Always fit the imputer on training data only.

Explain the curse of dimensionality.

As the number of dimensions grows, the volume of the space grows exponentially, so a fixed amount of data becomes sparse. Distances concentrate: the ratio between the nearest and farthest neighbor distances approaches 1, so "nearest" stops meaning much. kNN, k-means and kernel methods degrade, and you need far more data to cover the space. Remedies: feature selection, dimensionality reduction (PCA, autoencoders), regularization, or models that learn compact representations.

Your fraud dataset is 0.5% positive. How do you build a model?

Use PR-AUC and recall at a fixed false-positive rate (set by review capacity) rather than accuracy. Split by time and group by customer to avoid leakage. Start with a GBDT using class weights or scale_pos_weight; try undersampling the majority within the training fold only. Tune the threshold to the business cost of a missed fraud versus a false alarm. Recalibrate probabilities if you resampled. Add anomaly-detection signals for new fraud patterns, and monitor drift, since fraudsters adapt.

Class weights vs resampling: when would you use each?

Class weights change the loss without changing the data: no information is thrown away and nothing is duplicated, and most libraries support them. Undersampling speeds up training on huge datasets but discards majority data. Oversampling or SMOTE can help models that can't take weights, but risks overfitting duplicated or synthetic points. Both distort predicted probabilities, so recalibrate. In practice: class weights first, undersampling when data is huge, and always threshold tuning.

Generative vs discriminative models: give examples and trade-offs.

Discriminative models learn \(P(y \mid x)\) or the boundary directly: logistic regression, SVM, most neural classifiers. Generative models learn how the data is produced, \(P(x \mid y)P(y)\) or \(P(x)\): Naive Bayes, GMMs, HMMs, VAEs, GPT, diffusion. Discriminative models usually give better accuracy with enough data. Generative models can work with less data (Naive Bayes on tiny text sets), handle missing features, detect outliers by low likelihood, and generate new samples.

What is the i.i.d. assumption and when does it break?

That training and test examples are drawn independently from the same distribution. It breaks with time (seasonality, trends, drift), groups (many rows per user, so rows aren't independent), feedback loops (the model influences future data, as in recommendations), selection bias (you only observe labels for approved loans), and adversaries (fraudsters adapt). When it breaks, random splits overestimate performance, so use time-based or grouped splits and monitor drift.

What is double descent?

As model capacity grows, test error first follows the classical U-curve, peaks near the interpolation threshold (where the model can just fit the training data exactly), then decreases again as capacity keeps growing. It has been observed with model size, training time and data size. It helps explain why very large neural networks generalize well despite being able to memorize: among the many solutions that fit the data, gradient descent tends to find smooth, low-norm ones.

Common mistakes

  • Reporting accuracy on imbalanced data.
  • Fitting scalers, imputers or encoders on the full dataset before splitting.
  • Random splits on time series or on data with repeated users.
  • Tuning hyperparameters against the test set.
  • Using SMOTE before the train/test split, so synthetic points leak into evaluation.
  • Forgetting to recalibrate after resampling.

docs.text:

  • Explain why L1 is sparse, geometrically and through its gradient
  • Name five kinds of leakage and how to prevent each
  • Choose a CV scheme for i.i.d., grouped and time-series data
  • Encode a high-cardinality categorical safely
  • Walk through an imbalanced-data strategy from metric to threshold

docs.title: Efficient Attention & MoE
docs.text:
TL;DR

Attention's cost grows with the square of sequence length, and generation is limited by memory, not arithmetic. The KV cache avoids recomputing past tokens but grows with context; MQA, GQA and MLA shrink it by sharing or compressing keys and values. FlashAttention computes exact attention in on-chip tiles, so the \(n \times n\) matrix never hits GPU memory. Sparse, linear and state-space alternatives trade some quality for sub-quadratic cost. Mixture of experts grows parameters without growing compute per token.

Where this fits

Before: The Transformer and its \(O(n^2)\) attention. This page: making it fast and long. Next: Pretraining & LLMs scales it; Inference & Serving applies these ideas in production.

  • Full multi-head attention 2017Quadratic in length; every head stores its own keys and values.
  • KV cache 2017+Reuse past keys and values when generating. Memory grows with context.
  • Multi-query attention 2019All heads share one key/value head: tiny cache, some quality loss.
  • Sparse · sliding-window attention 2019–2020Attend locally plus a few global tokens.
  • FlashAttention 2022Exact attention in on-chip tiles; linear memory, much faster.
  • Grouped-query attention 2023Groups of heads share K/V: near-full quality, small cache.
  • State-space models (Mamba) 2023Linear-time sequence layers, often mixed with attention.
  • Multi-head latent attention 2024Compress K/V into a small latent vector per token.

docs.title: Where the time and memory go
docs.text:
Generation has two phases:

  • Prefill: process the whole prompt in parallel. Large matrix multiplications; compute-bound.
  • Decode: produce one token at a time. Each step reads all model weights and the whole KV cache from GPU memory to do relatively little arithmetic; memory-bandwidth-bound.

So the levers differ: prefill benefits from faster matrix math, decode from moving fewer bytes (smaller weights via quantization, smaller KV caches, batching many requests so each weight read serves many tokens).

docs.title: The KV cache
docs.text:
The problem: at decode step \(t\), attention needs keys and values for all \(t\) previous tokens. Recomputing them every step would make generating \(n\) tokens cost \(O(n^2)\) projections.

Core idea: store each token's keys and values per layer the first time they're computed; each new token computes only its own and attends over the cache.

\[ \text{KV cache bytes} = 2 \times \text{layers} \times \text{KV heads} \times d_{head} \times \text{sequence length} \times \text{batch} \times \text{bytes per value} \] Worked example: how big is the cache?

A 7B model with 32 layers, 32 heads of dimension 128, in FP16 (2 bytes): per token \(2 \times 32 \times 32 \times 128 \times 2 = 524{,}288\) bytes, about 0.5 MB per token. A 4,096-token context is about 2 GB per sequence; a batch of 16 such sequences needs 32 GB, more than the model's own 14 GB of weights.

A 70B model with grouped-query attention (80 layers, 8 KV heads of 128): \(2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 \approx 0.33\) MB per token. GQA keeps a model ten times larger at a smaller per-token cache.

The cache, not the weights, often limits batch size and context length in serving. Hence the methods below, plus KV-cache quantization (8-bit or 4-bit), paging (vLLM's PagedAttention) and prefix sharing.

docs.title: Sharing keys and values: MQA, GQA and MLA
docs.text:
Method Keys/values per layer Cache size vs MHA Quality Used in Multi-head (MHA) One K/V per query head 1× Baseline Original Transformer, GPT-3 Multi-query (MQA) One K/V shared by all heads \(1/h\) Some degradation, less stable training PaLM, Falcon Grouped-query (GQA) One K/V per group of query heads (for example 8 groups) \(g/h\) Close to MHA LLaMA 2 70B, LLaMA 3, Mistral, most open LLMs Multi-head latent (MLA) A low-rank latent vector per token, projected up to K/V per head Much smaller than GQA Comparable to MHA DeepSeek-V2, V3

GQA can also be created from an existing MHA checkpoint by mean-pooling key and value heads into groups and briefly continuing training ("uptraining").

docs.title: FlashAttention
docs.text:
The problem: standard attention computes the \(n \times n\) score matrix, writes it to GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM), reads it back for the softmax, writes the probabilities, and reads them again to multiply by \(V\). Those memory transfers, not the arithmetic, dominate the time, and the matrix needs \(O(n^2)\) memory.

Core idea: be IO-aware. Split \(Q\), \(K\) and \(V\) into blocks that fit in fast on-chip SRAM, compute attention block by block, and never write the full matrix to HBM.

  • Online softmax: keep a running maximum and running sum for each query row, so partial results from each key block can be combined exactly, rescaling as the maximum changes.
  • Backward pass: recompute attention blocks from \(Q\), \(K\), \(V\) instead of storing the matrix. More arithmetic, much less memory traffic, and faster overall.
  • Exact: the output is the same as standard attention (up to floating-point rounding); it's not an approximation.
  • Results: memory becomes linear in sequence length, and attention runs several times faster, enabling longer contexts. FlashAttention-2 improved parallelism and work partitioning; FlashAttention-3 targets newer GPU features such as asynchronous execution and FP8.

docs.title: Sparse and linear attention
docs.text: Approach Idea Cost Trade-off Sliding-window Each token attends to the previous \(w\) tokens; stacked layers widen the reach \(O(nw)\) Distant tokens interact only through many layers (Mistral 7B used a 4,096-token window) Sparse patterns (Longformer, BigBird) Local windows plus a few global tokens plus random links \(O(n)\) Fixed patterns can miss needed interactions Low-rank (Linformer) Project keys and values to a fixed length \(O(nk)\) Assumes the attention matrix is low-rank Kernel / linear attention (Performer, linear Transformers) Replace softmax with a feature map so \((QK^\top)V\) becomes \(Q(K^\top V)\) \(O(n d^2)\) Usually lower quality than softmax attention Attention sinks (StreamingLLM) Keep the first few tokens plus a recent window in the cache Constant memory For streaming, not for recalling details from the middle

docs.title: State-space models and hybrids
docs.text:
The problem: a fixed-size recurrent state makes inference cost per token constant, but classic RNNs train slowly and forget.

Core idea: structured state-space models (S4, 2021) and Mamba (2023) use a linear recurrence that can be trained in parallel (with convolutions or a parallel scan) and run as a recurrence at inference: constant memory per token and linear time in sequence length. Mamba makes the state-space parameters depend on the input ("selective"), so the model can choose what to remember.

  • Strengths: linear scaling, fast long-sequence inference, no KV cache growth.
  • Weaknesses: weaker at precise recall from long contexts (copying, looking up a specific fact) than attention.
  • Hybrids interleave a few attention layers with many SSM layers to get most of both.

docs.title: Long context
docs.text:
• Position scaling: RoPE models extended beyond their training length with position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling or YaRN, plus a short fine-tune on long documents.
  • Training long: context (sequence) parallelism and ring attention split one long sequence across GPUs.
  • Using long context well: accuracy tends to drop for information in the middle of very long prompts ("lost in the middle"), and quality can decline as irrelevant context accumulates. Long windows don't remove the need for retrieval or careful context engineering.
  • Cost: prefill grows with prompt length, and the KV cache grows linearly; prompt caching of stable prefixes cuts repeated cost.

docs.title: Mixture of experts
docs.text:
The problem: in a dense model every parameter is used for every token, so more capacity always means more compute per token.

Core idea: replace each FFN with \(E\) expert FFNs and a router that sends each token to its top-\(k\) experts (often \(k = 1\) or 2). Total parameters grow with \(E\); compute per token grows only with \(k\).

flowchart TB
    T["token hidden state"] --> R["router: softmax(W·h)"]
    R -->|"top-2"| E1["expert 3"]
    R -->|"top-2"| E2["expert 7"]
    R -.->|"not chosen"| E3["other experts"]
    E1 --> M["weighted sum"]
    E2 --> M
    M --> O["output"]
  • Load balancing: without help, the router sends most tokens to a few experts, which then dominate and the rest never train. An auxiliary loss encourages even usage, for example Switch Transformer's \(\alpha N \sum_i f_i P_i\) (fraction of tokens routed to expert \(i\) times its average router probability). DeepSeek-V3 instead adjusts per-expert bias terms to balance load without an auxiliary loss.
  • Capacity factor: cap tokens per expert per batch; overflow tokens skip the layer through the residual connection.
  • Expert parallelism: experts live on different GPUs and tokens are exchanged with all-to-all communication, which becomes a bottleneck.
  • Fine-grained and shared experts: many small experts plus one or more always-on shared experts (DeepSeekMoE) improve specialization.
Model Total parameters Active per token Routing Switch Transformer (2021) Up to 1.6T Small fraction Top-1 Mixtral 8×7B (2023) About 47B About 13B Top-2 of 8 per layer DeepSeek-V3 (2024) 671B 37B Top-8 of 256 routed experts plus 1 shared

Trade-offs: much better quality per FLOP, but all experts must be in memory (serving memory follows total parameters while speed follows active parameters), routing can be unstable, batches must be large to keep experts busy, and fine-tuning is trickier.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
What is the KV cache and why does it help?

During autoregressive generation, each new token attends to all previous tokens' keys and values, which don't change once computed. Caching them per layer means each step only computes the new token's query, key and value and attends over the cache, turning per-token work from re-processing the whole prefix into a single step. The cost is memory that grows linearly with context length and batch size, which often limits how many requests a GPU can serve.

Compute the KV-cache size for a model.

Multiply 2 (keys and values) × layers × KV heads × head dimension × tokens × batch × bytes per value. For 32 layers, 32 KV heads of size 128 in FP16: \(2 \cdot 32 \cdot 32 \cdot 128 \cdot 2 = 524{,}288\) bytes, about 0.5 MB per token, so 8,192 tokens × batch 8 ≈ 34 GB. With 8 KV heads (GQA) it's a quarter of that.

MHA vs MQA vs GQA.

Multi-head attention gives every query head its own key and value projections: best quality, largest cache. Multi-query attention shares a single key/value head across all query heads: the cache shrinks by the number of heads, decode gets much faster, but quality and training stability can suffer. Grouped-query attention is the middle ground: query heads are split into groups that share K/V (for example 64 query heads, 8 KV heads), giving most of MQA's savings with near-MHA quality. Most current open models use GQA.

How does FlashAttention speed up attention without approximating it?

Standard attention is limited by memory traffic: it writes and reads the full \(n \times n\) score and probability matrices to and from GPU HBM. FlashAttention tiles \(Q\), \(K\) and \(V\) into blocks that fit in on-chip SRAM, computes each block's contribution, and combines blocks exactly using an online softmax (running max and sum per row). The full matrix is never materialized, memory becomes \(O(n)\), and the backward pass recomputes blocks instead of storing them. Same result, far fewer memory transfers, several times faster.

Prefill vs decode: which is compute-bound and which is memory-bound?

Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel with large matrix multiplications, so it's compute-bound and drives time-to-first-token. Decode generates one token per step per sequence, reading every weight and the KV cache for a small amount of arithmetic, so it's memory-bandwidth-bound and drives time per output token. Batching helps decode because one weight read serves many sequences; quantization and smaller caches help because fewer bytes move.

What is sliding-window attention, and what does it give up?

Each token attends only to the previous \(w\) tokens, so cost and KV memory scale with \(nw\) instead of \(n^2\). Information can still travel farther than \(w\) through stacked layers (the receptive field grows by about \(w\) per layer), but distant interactions are indirect and weaker. Some models alternate windowed and full-attention layers to keep exact long-range access.

What's the idea behind linear attention, and why isn't it standard?

Softmax attention computes \(\text{softmax}(QK^\top)V\), which needs the \(n \times n\) matrix. Linear attention replaces the softmax similarity with a kernel feature map \(\phi\), so \((\phi(Q)\phi(K)^\top)V = \phi(Q)(\phi(K)^\top V)\) can be computed right to left in \(O(n)\), and it can even run as a recurrence. In practice these approximations lose quality, especially on precise retrieval from context, so softmax attention with FlashAttention remains the default, with linear-time layers used in hybrids.

What is Mamba, and how does it differ from a Transformer?

Mamba is a selective state-space model: a linear recurrence whose parameters depend on the input, so it can decide what to keep in its fixed-size state. It trains in parallel with a hardware-aware scan and runs as a recurrence at inference, giving linear time and constant memory per token with no KV cache. Transformers keep every past token's keys and values and can look any of them up exactly, which makes them better at copying and precise recall; hybrids combine a few attention layers with many Mamba layers.

How do models extend their context length?

Architecturally, with RoPE scaling (position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, YaRN) so positions beyond the trained range map onto rotations the model has seen, followed by fine-tuning on long sequences. Systems-wise, with FlashAttention, context parallelism for training, and KV-cache paging, quantization or eviction for serving. And practically by evaluating long-context use, since models often under-use information in the middle of long prompts.

How does mixture-of-experts routing work?

A router (a linear layer plus softmax) scores all experts for each token, the top-\(k\) experts process it, and their outputs are combined with the router weights. Only those \(k\) experts' FFN weights are used for that token. An auxiliary load-balancing loss or bias adjustment keeps tokens spread across experts, and a capacity limit caps tokens per expert per batch.

Why does MoE need a load-balancing mechanism?

Routing is learned, and early on some experts happen to perform slightly better, receive more tokens, improve further, and attract even more: a rich-get-richer collapse where a few experts do everything and the rest stay untrained. Imbalance also overloads some GPUs while others idle. A balancing loss (penalizing uneven token fractions and router probabilities) or per-expert bias adjustments keep utilization even.

Total vs active parameters in MoE: which determines memory and which determines speed?

Memory is set by total parameters: every expert must be loaded somewhere, so a 47B-total MoE needs memory like a 47B dense model. Compute per token is set by active parameters: each token uses only its top-\(k\) experts plus shared layers, so it runs roughly like a 13B dense model. Serving MoEs therefore needs large memory but gives high throughput per FLOP, especially at large batch sizes.

What is the 'lost in the middle' problem?

When relevant information is placed in the middle of a long prompt, models retrieve and use it less reliably than when it's near the beginning or end. It shows that a large context window isn't the same as using all of it well. Mitigations: put the most important content at the start or end, retrieve less but better, summarize, and evaluate long-context tasks directly.

Common mistakes

  • Calling FlashAttention an approximation.
  • Forgetting that the KV cache, not the weights, often limits batch size.
  • Saying MoE reduces memory (it reduces compute per token).
  • Assuming a long context window means the model uses all of it well.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• Explain prefill vs decode and which resource limits each
  • Compute KV-cache size for MHA and GQA models
  • Compare MHA, MQA, GQA and MLA
  • Explain FlashAttention's tiling and online softmax
  • Describe sliding-window, sparse, linear attention and SSMs, with their trade-offs
  • Explain MoE routing, load balancing, and total vs active parameters

docs.title: Fine-Tuning & Efficiency
docs.text:
TL;DR

Fine-tune to change behavior, format, style or domain language; use RAG to add knowledge. PEFT freezes the base model and trains a few new parameters; LoRA learns a low-rank update \(\Delta W = BA\) that merges back with no added latency, and QLoRA does it on a 4-bit base model. Quantization stores weights in 8 or 4 bits for cheaper serving; distillation trains a small student from a large teacher. Memory math matters: full fine-tuning with Adam needs about 16 bytes per parameter. Distributed training splits data, optimizer state, layers or matrices across GPUs.

Where this fits

Before: Pretraining & LLMs produces a base model. This page: adapting and compressing it. Next: Inference & Serving runs it efficiently; Post-Training uses these techniques for SFT and preference tuning.

  • Train from scratch classicLots of labeled data per task.
  • Feature extraction 2014+Freeze a pretrained network; train a small head.
  • Full fine-tuning 2018Best quality, but a full copy of the weights per task.
  • Adapters · prefix/prompt tuning 2019–2021Train few new parameters; adapters add latency.
  • LoRA 2021Low-rank updates merged into the weights: no added latency.
  • QLoRA 2023LoRA on a 4-bit frozen base: 65B fine-tuned on one 48 GB GPU.

docs.title: When to fine-tune
docs.text:
Goal Best tool Teach the model facts that change or are private RAG, not fine-tuning Consistent output format, tone or style Fine-tuning (SFT) Domain language (legal, medical, code base conventions) Fine-tuning, often plus RAG A cheaper or faster model for a narrow task Fine-tune or distill a small model New behaviors (tool use, refusals, following a policy) SFT plus preference tuning Very different domain or language Continued pretraining, then fine-tuning

Start with prompting and measure; fine-tune when prompting plateaus and you have a few hundred to a few thousand high-quality examples. Full decision guide: Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning.

docs.title: Full fine-tuning vs parameter-efficient fine-tuning
docs.text: Method What trains Added inference cost Notes Full fine-tuning All weights None Best quality on big shifts; huge memory; risk of catastrophic forgetting; one full copy per task Adapters (2019) Small bottleneck layers inserted in each block Extra layers at inference Modular; adds latency Prefix / prompt tuning (2021) Learned "virtual token" vectors prepended to inputs or each layer Slightly longer sequence Tiny; weaker on smaller models BitFit Only bias terms None Surprisingly decent, limited LoRA (2021) Low-rank matrices added to chosen weights None after merging The default PEFT method QLoRA (2023) LoRA on a 4-bit quantized frozen base None after merging (or serve adapters on the 4-bit base) Fits large models on one GPU

docs.title: LoRA
docs.text:
The problem it solved: full fine-tuning is too expensive in memory and storage, and adapters slow inference.

Core idea: the weight change needed for adaptation has low intrinsic rank, so learn it as a product of two thin matrices and keep the pretrained weight frozen:

\[ h = W_0 x + \Delta W x = W_0 x + \frac{\alpha}{r}\, B A\, x, \qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r},\; A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k},\; r \ll \min(d, k) \]
  • Initialization: \(A\) random, \(B = 0\), so \(\Delta W = 0\) at the start and training begins exactly from the pretrained model.
  • Parameters: \(r(d + k)\) instead of \(dk\). For a 4096×4096 matrix with \(r = 16\): 131,072 instead of 16.8 million (about 0.8%).
  • Scaling: \(\alpha/r\) keeps the update's magnitude stable when you change the rank.
  • Merging: after training, add \(\frac{\alpha}{r}BA\) to \(W_0\); inference has zero added latency. Or keep adapters separate and swap them per customer or task on one shared base model.
  • Where: originally the query and value projections; now commonly all attention and MLP linear layers, which usually helps.
  • Choosing r: 8–64 is typical; higher rank adds capacity for bigger shifts. Tune rank, alpha and learning rate together (LoRA typically uses a higher learning rate than full fine-tuning).
  • Variants: DoRA (separates magnitude and direction), rsLoRA (rank-stabilized scaling), LoRA+ (different learning rates for A and B).

docs.title: QLoRA
docs.text:
The problem it solved: even with LoRA, the frozen base model in 16-bit must fit in GPU memory.

Core idea: keep the frozen base in 4-bit and train LoRA adapters in 16-bit through it.

  • NF4 (4-bit NormalFloat): a 4-bit data type whose levels are spaced for normally distributed weights.
  • Double quantization: quantize the quantization constants too, saving about 0.4 bits per parameter.
  • Paged optimizers: move optimizer state to CPU memory during memory spikes.
  • Weights are dequantized to BF16 on the fly for each matrix multiplication; gradients flow through them to the adapters, never updating the 4-bit weights.
  • Result: a 65B model fine-tuned on a single 48 GB GPU, with quality close to 16-bit LoRA.

docs.title: Quantization
docs.text:
The problem: a 70B model in FP16 needs about 140 GB just for weights, and decoding is limited by how fast weights stream from memory.

Core idea: represent weights (and sometimes activations and the KV cache) with fewer bits, accepting a small accuracy loss.

Precision Bytes per parameter 7B model 70B model FP32 4 28 GB 280 GB FP16 / BF16 2 14 GB 140 GB INT8 / FP8 1 7 GB 70 GB INT4 / NF4 0.5 3.5 GB 35 GB

Plus overhead for scales and zero-points, and memory for the KV cache and activations.

Approach Idea Post-training quantization (PTQ) Quantize a trained model with a small calibration set. No retraining. Quantization-aware training (QAT) Simulate quantization during training so the model adapts. Best quality at low bits, costly. Weight-only Quantize weights; compute in 16-bit. Speeds memory-bound decoding. Weight + activation (W8A8, FP8) Also quantize activations, so matrix multiplications run in low precision. Speeds compute-bound prefill too.

Methods to know:

  • Absmax / zero-point scaling: map a block of values to integers with a per-block (or per-channel, per-group) scale. Smaller groups are more accurate but add more scale parameters.
  • LLM.int8() (2022): a few activation dimensions have huge outlier values that wreck naive INT8; it keeps those outlier features in FP16 and the rest in INT8.
  • GPTQ (2022): quantize weights layer by layer, using approximate second-order information to adjust the remaining weights and compensate for each rounding error.
  • AWQ (2023): protect the weights that matter most for activations by scaling salient channels before quantizing.
  • SmoothQuant: move quantization difficulty from activations to weights so both can be 8-bit.
  • GGUF / llama.cpp: quantized formats for running models on CPUs and laptops.
  • KV-cache quantization: 8-bit or 4-bit caches allow longer contexts and bigger batches.

Quality usually holds well at 8 bits and reasonably at 4 bits; below that it degrades, with math, code and long reasoning chains most sensitive. Always evaluate on your own tasks.

docs.title: Distillation and pruning
docs.text:
Knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015): train a small student to match a large teacher's output distribution. With temperature \(T\):

\[ \mathcal{L} = \alpha\, \text{CE}(y, p_s) + (1 - \alpha)\, T^2\, \text{KL}\!\left(p_t^{(T)} \,\|\, p_s^{(T)}\right) \]
  • Softened teacher probabilities carry "dark knowledge" (that a 7 looks more like a 1 than an 8), a richer signal than hard labels. The \(T^2\) factor keeps gradient sizes comparable.
  • For LLMs: sequence-level distillation, fine-tuning a student on teacher-generated answers and reasoning traces; or logit distillation when the teacher's probabilities are available.
  • Examples: DistilBERT; small reasoning models distilled from large ones.
  • Check the teacher model's license: some forbid training competing models on their outputs.

Pruning: remove weights that matter little. Unstructured (individual weights, for example by magnitude) gives sparse matrices that need special kernels to speed up; structured (whole heads, channels, layers) speeds up any hardware but costs more accuracy. Usually followed by brief retraining or distillation.

docs.title: Mixed precision and memory math
docs.text:
• FP16 has a small range, so gradients can underflow: use loss scaling (multiply the loss, then unscale gradients).
  • BF16 keeps FP32's exponent range with less precision; no loss scaling needed. The standard for LLM training.
  • Keep an FP32 master copy of weights and optimizer states for accurate updates; compute in BF16.
  • FP8 training and inference on recent GPUs, with per-tensor or per-block scaling.

Memory per parameter for full training with Adam in mixed precision:

Item Bytes BF16 weights 2 BF16 gradients 2 FP32 master weights 4 Adam first moment (FP32) 4 Adam second moment (FP32) 4 Total 16

So a 7B model needs about 112 GB before activations, which grow with batch size, sequence length and depth (reduced by gradient checkpointing). LoRA on a frozen BF16 base needs roughly 2 bytes per base parameter plus small adapter states; QLoRA about 0.5–0.6 bytes per base parameter.

docs.title: Distributed training
docs.text:
Strategy What's split Communication When Data parallel (DDP) The batch; each GPU holds a full model copy All-reduce gradients every step The model fits on one GPU ZeRO / FSDP Optimizer states (stage 1), + gradients (stage 2), + parameters (stage 3) across data-parallel GPUs Gather parameters per layer as needed The model doesn't fit with full optimizer state Tensor parallel (Megatron) Individual weight matrices within a layer Every layer, so needs fast links (NVLink) Very large layers; within a node Pipeline parallel Groups of layers (stages) on different GPUs; micro-batches flow through Activations between stages Very deep models, across nodes Sequence / context parallel The sequence dimension Attention needs keys and values from other chunks Long contexts Expert parallel MoE experts on different GPUs All-to-all token routing Mixture-of-experts models

Large runs combine them ("3D parallelism": data × tensor × pipeline). Pipeline bubbles are idle time while the pipeline fills and drains; more micro-batches and interleaved schedules shrink them. Gradient accumulation emulates large batches with small memory. Checkpointing to disk regularly matters, because at thousands of GPUs hardware failures are routine.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
When would you fine-tune instead of using RAG or prompting?

Fine-tune when you need to change how the model behaves: a consistent output format, tone or persona, domain-specific language, following a complex policy, reliable tool use, or a smaller, cheaper model for a narrow task. Use RAG when the problem is what the model knows: private, large or frequently changing information that needs citations and access control. Try prompting first, measure on an evaluation set, and combine approaches (a fine-tuned model that also uses RAG) when needed.

Explain LoRA and why B is initialized to zero.

LoRA freezes a pretrained weight \(W_0\) and learns a low-rank update \(\Delta W = \frac{\alpha}{r}BA\), with \(B\) of shape \((d, r)\) and \(A\) of shape \((r, k)\) and \(r\) small, so only \(r(d + k)\) parameters train. \(A\) starts random and \(B\) starts at zero so that \(\Delta W = 0\) initially: the model starts exactly at the pretrained behavior and the adapter learns only the change. If both were random, training would start from a randomly perturbed model.

Why does LoRA add no inference latency?

After training, \(\frac{\alpha}{r}BA\) is a matrix of the same shape as \(W_0\), so you can add it once: \(W = W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA\). The deployed model has exactly the original architecture and cost. Adapters, by contrast, insert extra layers that run on every forward pass. You can also keep LoRA weights separate to swap them per request, which adds a small cost but lets many tasks share one base model.

What does QLoRA quantize, and what stays in higher precision?

The frozen base model's weights are stored in 4-bit NF4 (with double-quantized scales). The LoRA adapter weights, their gradients and optimizer states stay in 16-bit (BF16), and computation happens in BF16 by dequantizing each weight block on the fly. Gradients flow through the frozen 4-bit weights into the adapters, but the 4-bit weights are never updated.

How do you choose the LoRA rank?

Start around 8–16 for style and format changes and 32–64 or more for larger domain shifts or harder tasks; apply LoRA to all linear layers rather than only attention, which often matters more than rank. Tune rank, alpha (often set to 2× rank or equal to rank) and learning rate together, and compare against full fine-tuning on a validation set if the shift is large. Too high a rank on little data can overfit.

How much memory do you need to fully fine-tune a 7B model?

About 16 bytes per parameter with Adam in mixed precision (2 for BF16 weights, 2 for gradients, 4 for FP32 master weights, 8 for Adam's two moments), so roughly 112 GB, plus activations that depend on batch size and sequence length. That needs several GPUs with ZeRO/FSDP sharding, or tricks like 8-bit optimizers and gradient checkpointing. LoRA cuts it to roughly the 14 GB BF16 base plus small extras; QLoRA to around 4–6 GB for the base.

How much memory does a 70B model need in FP16 vs INT4?

Weights alone: 70B × 2 bytes ≈ 140 GB in FP16, about 70 GB in 8-bit, and about 35 GB in 4-bit (plus a few percent for quantization scales). On top of that you need KV-cache memory, which grows with context length and batch size, and some activation workspace. So FP16 needs at least two 80 GB GPUs, while a 4-bit version can fit on one 48 GB or 80 GB GPU with room for the cache.

Post-training quantization vs quantization-aware training.

PTQ quantizes an already-trained model using a small calibration set, with no retraining: fast and cheap, and good at 8 bits and usually acceptable at 4 bits with methods like GPTQ or AWQ. QAT simulates quantization during training (with straight-through gradient estimates) so the weights adapt to the rounding: better quality at very low bit widths, but it needs a training pipeline and compute. Most LLM deployments use PTQ.

Why do activation outliers make LLM quantization hard?

In large Transformers, a few hidden dimensions take on values far larger than the rest. With one scale per tensor or per row, those outliers force a huge scale, so all the normal values collapse into a handful of integer levels and lose precision. Solutions: keep outlier dimensions in higher precision (LLM.int8), use finer-grained scales (per-channel or per-group), or move the difficulty into the weights by rescaling (SmoothQuant, AWQ).

Weight-only vs weight-and-activation quantization.

Weight-only quantization (for example 4-bit weights with 16-bit compute) shrinks memory and speeds up memory-bound decoding, because fewer bytes stream from memory, but matrix multiplications still run in 16-bit after dequantization. Weight-and-activation quantization (W8A8 or FP8) also runs the matrix multiplications in low precision on hardware that supports it, speeding up compute-bound phases such as prefill and large-batch serving, but activations are harder to quantize accurately.

Why use a temperature in knowledge distillation?

A confident teacher assigns nearly all probability to the top class, so its outputs carry little more information than hard labels. Dividing logits by \(T > 1\) softens the distribution and reveals relative similarities among the wrong classes ("dark knowledge"), which is a richer training signal for the student. The KL term is multiplied by \(T^2\) because softening shrinks gradients by about \(1/T^2\).

Structured vs unstructured pruning.

Unstructured pruning removes individual weights (for example the smallest magnitudes), reaching high sparsity with little accuracy loss, but irregular sparsity only speeds things up with specialized kernels or hardware (such as 2:4 sparsity). Structured pruning removes whole units, heads, channels or layers, so the smaller model is dense and faster everywhere, at a larger accuracy cost that usually needs fine-tuning or distillation to recover.

How would you shrink a model to run on a phone?

Pick a small, capable base model, distill it from a larger teacher on your task, quantize to 8-bit or 4-bit with calibration data (or QAT if quality drops), prune or remove layers if needed, compile it with a mobile runtime, and evaluate accuracy, latency, memory and battery on real devices. Keep a server fallback for hard cases.

BF16 vs FP16.

Both use 16 bits. FP16 has 5 exponent bits and 10 mantissa bits: more precision but a small range, so gradients can underflow and training needs loss scaling. BF16 has 8 exponent bits (the same range as FP32) and 7 mantissa bits: less precision but no overflow or underflow issues in practice, so no loss scaling. BF16 is the standard for training large models on hardware that supports it.

DDP vs FSDP/ZeRO.

DDP replicates the full model, gradients and optimizer state on every GPU and all-reduces gradients each step; it's simple and fast but limited to models whose full training state fits on one GPU. ZeRO and FSDP shard optimizer states, gradients and, at stage 3, parameters across the data-parallel GPUs, gathering each layer's parameters just in time for its computation. Memory per GPU drops roughly in proportion to the number of GPUs, at the cost of more communication.

Tensor vs pipeline parallelism, and what is the pipeline bubble?

Tensor parallelism splits individual matrices across GPUs, so each layer's computation is shared; it communicates inside every layer and needs very fast links, so it's used within a node. Pipeline parallelism puts different layers on different GPUs and passes activations between stages; communication is lighter, so it works across nodes, but GPUs idle while the pipeline fills and drains: that idle time is the bubble. Splitting batches into many micro-batches and interleaving schedules shrinks it.

What is catastrophic forgetting, and how do you limit it when fine-tuning?

Fine-tuning on a narrow dataset can overwrite general capabilities the model had, such as reasoning, other languages or safety behavior. Limit it with PEFT (LoRA keeps base weights frozen), lower learning rates and fewer epochs, mixing some general or original-task data into the fine-tuning set, regularizing toward the original weights, and evaluating general benchmarks alongside the target task.

Common mistakes

  • Proposing fine-tuning to teach a model frequently changing facts.
  • Forgetting optimizer state and gradients in memory estimates.
  • Saying quantization always speeds up compute (weight-only mainly helps memory-bound decoding).
  • Assuming 4-bit is always fine without evaluating math, code and long-context tasks.
  • Using another provider's model outputs for distillation without checking the license.

docs.text:
• Decide between prompting, RAG, fine-tuning and continued pretraining
  • Write the LoRA update, its parameter count, and why B starts at zero
  • Explain QLoRA's NF4, double quantization and paged optimizers
  • Compute weight memory at FP16, INT8 and INT4; explain PTQ, QAT, GPTQ and AWQ
  • Write the distillation loss and explain the temperature
  • Derive the 16 bytes per parameter for Adam training
  • Compare DDP, FSDP/ZeRO, tensor, pipeline and expert parallelism
