docs.title: Generative Models
docs.text:
TL;DR

Generative models learn to produce new data. Autoencoders compress but can't sample well. VAEs shape the latent space into a Gaussian, so sampling works, but outputs are blurry. GANs make sharp images through an adversarial game but are unstable and drop modes. Diffusion models learn to remove noise step by step: stable training, high quality, easy text conditioning, slow sampling. Latent diffusion (Stable Diffusion) runs diffusion in a compressed space; DiTs, flow matching and distillation make it faster and more scalable. Multimodal LLMs connect vision and audio encoders to language models.

Where this fits

Before: CNNs and U-Net, CLIP, the Transformer. This page: generating images, audio and video, and models that see. Next: Alignment & Reasoning returns to language models.

  • Autoencoder 1980s · 2006Compress and reconstruct. The latent space has holes, so random samples look bad.
  • VAE 2013A smooth Gaussian latent space; easy sampling, blurry outputs.
  • GAN 2014Generator vs discriminator: sharp but unstable, with mode collapse.
  • Diffusion (DDPM) 2020Learn to denoise step by step. Stable, diverse, slow to sample.
  • Latent diffusion 2022Diffuse in a compressed latent space with text conditioning.
  • DiT · flow matching · few-step distillation 2023+Transformer denoisers, straighter paths, 1–4 step sampling; images and video.

docs.title: The families at a glance
docs.text: Family Learns Sampling Strengths Weaknesses Autoregressive (GPT, PixelCNN) Exact likelihood, one token at a time Sequential Exact likelihood; best for text Slow for high-dimensional data VAE A lower bound on likelihood One decoder pass Stable; smooth latent space Blurry samples GAN Implicitly, through a discriminator One generator pass Sharp, fast Unstable; mode collapse; no likelihood Normalizing flow Exact likelihood via invertible maps One pass Exact likelihood and sampling Restrictive architectures Diffusion / score-based To denoise (equivalently, the score \(\nabla_x \log p\)) Many denoising steps (fewer with distillation) Quality, diversity, stable training, conditioning Slow sampling, compute-heavy

docs.title: Autoencoders
docs.text:
The problem: learn compact representations without labels.

Core idea: an encoder compresses \(x\) to a small code \(z\), a decoder reconstructs \(\hat x\), and training minimizes reconstruction error.

  • An undercomplete linear autoencoder learns the same subspace as PCA; non-linear ones learn curved manifolds.
  • Denoising autoencoders reconstruct clean inputs from corrupted ones (a precursor of diffusion and of BERT-style masking). Sparse autoencoders keep few units active, and are now used to find interpretable features inside LLMs.
  • Uses: compression, denoising, anomaly detection (high reconstruction error means unusual), pretraining.

Weakness: nothing forces the latent space to be continuous or filled in, so decoding a random \(z\) often gives garbage. It's not a real generative model.

docs.title: Variational autoencoders
docs.text:
The problem it solved: autoencoders can't sample.

Core idea: encode each input to a distribution \(q_\phi(z \mid x) = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\), sample \(z\), decode, and pull every encoding toward a standard normal prior so the whole latent space is usable.

Maximize the evidence lower bound (ELBO) on \(\log p(x)\):

\[ \text{ELBO} = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z\mid x)}\left[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\right]}_{\text{reconstruction}} - \underbrace{D_{KL}\left(q_\phi(z \mid x)\,\|\,\mathcal{N}(0, I)\right)}_{\text{keep codes near the prior}} \]
  • Reparameterization trick: sampling isn't differentiable, so write \(z = \mu + \sigma \odot \epsilon\) with \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\); gradients then flow through \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\).
  • For Gaussians the KL term has a closed form: \(\frac12\sum_j\left(\mu_j^2 + \sigma_j^2 - \log\sigma_j^2 - 1\right)\).
  • Why blurry? A Gaussian (MSE-like) reconstruction loss rewards averaging over plausible outputs, and the KL pressure limits how much detail \(z\) carries.
  • β-VAE weights the KL term to encourage disentangled factors. Posterior collapse: a powerful decoder ignores \(z\) (KL goes to zero). VQ-VAE uses a discrete codebook of latents; such tokenizers turn images and audio into tokens for autoregressive and multimodal models.
  • A VAE is the image compressor inside Stable Diffusion.

docs.title: Generative adversarial networks
docs.text:
The problem it solved: likelihood-based models of the time produced blurry images.

Core idea: a generator \(G\) maps noise \(z\) to samples; a discriminator \(D\) tries to tell real from generated; they play a minimax game:

\[ \min_G \max_D\ \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{data}}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{z}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))] \]
  • For a fixed generator the optimal discriminator is \(D^*(x) = \frac{p_{data}(x)}{p_{data}(x) + p_g(x)}\), and the generator's objective becomes minimizing the Jensen–Shannon divergence between \(p_{data}\) and \(p_g\).
  • Non-saturating loss: in practice \(G\) maximizes \(\log D(G(z))\), because the original term gives vanishing gradients when \(D\) easily rejects early fakes.
Problem What happens Fixes Mode collapse The generator produces only a few kinds of outputs that fool \(D\) Minibatch discrimination, unrolled GANs, WGAN, diversity terms Instability / non-convergence The two players oscillate WGAN with gradient penalty, spectral normalization, two learning rates (TTUR), careful architectures Vanishing gradients A perfect \(D\) gives \(G\) no signal Non-saturating loss, Wasserstein loss Evaluation No likelihood to report FID, Inception Score, precision and recall for generative models

Landmarks: DCGAN (convolutional GANs), conditional GANs, CycleGAN (unpaired image-to-image translation), StyleGAN (high-resolution faces with a style-based generator), and GAN losses inside super-resolution and some diffusion distillation methods. FID compares the mean and covariance of Inception-network features between real and generated images; lower is better.

docs.title: Normalizing flows
docs.text: Transform a simple distribution through a sequence of invertible functions with tractable Jacobian determinants, so the change-of-variables formula gives exact likelihoods: \(\log p(x) = \log p(z) + \log\left|\det \frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right|\). Examples: RealNVP, Glow. Exact likelihood and one-pass sampling, but the invertibility constraint limits architectures. Their continuous-time descendants connect to flow matching below.

docs.title: Diffusion models
docs.text:
The problem it solved: GANs are unstable and drop modes; VAEs are blurry.

Core idea: destroy data gradually with noise, and train a network to reverse one small step at a time.

docs.title: Forward process (fixed)
docs.text:
Add Gaussian noise over \(T\) steps with a schedule \(\beta_t\). With \(\bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s \le t}(1 - \beta_s)\), you can jump straight to any step:

\[ x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\, \epsilon, \qquad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) \]

The cosine schedule keeps more signal through the middle steps, so fewer steps are wasted on nearly pure noise.

docs.title: Reverse process (learned)
docs.text:
Train a network \(\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\) (originally a U-Net) to predict the noise that was added, with a simple regression loss:

\[ \mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{x_0, \epsilon, t}\left[\left\|\epsilon - \epsilon_\theta\!\left(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon,\ t\right)\right\|^2\right] \]
  • Predicting the noise is equivalent to learning the score \(\nabla_x \log p(x_t)\), the direction toward higher data density (the score-matching view). Variants predict \(x_0\) or a "velocity" \(v\) instead.
  • Sampling: start from pure noise \(x_T\) and repeatedly denoise. DDPM used about 1,000 stochastic steps; DDIM and modern ODE solvers produce good samples in about 20–50 deterministic steps.

docs.title: Guidance and conditioning
docs.text:
• Conditioning: feed the condition (class label, text embedding, image) into the denoiser, usually through cross-attention to text-encoder outputs (CLIP or T5).
  • Classifier guidance used a separate noisy-image classifier's gradient to steer samples.
  • Classifier-free guidance (CFG): train one model both with and without the condition (randomly dropping it), then extrapolate at sampling time:
\[ \hat\epsilon = \epsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing) + w\left(\epsilon_\theta(x_t, c) - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, \varnothing)\right) \]

A guidance scale \(w > 1\) follows the prompt more closely at the cost of diversity, and very high values over-saturate images.

docs.title: Latent diffusion and beyond
docs.text:
The problem: diffusion in pixel space at 1024×1024 is very expensive.

Core idea (Stable Diffusion): compress images with a VAE (8× downsampling per side), run diffusion in that latent space, and decode at the end.

flowchart TB
    P["Text prompt"] --> TE["Text encoder<br/>(CLIP / T5)"]
    N["Random latent noise"] --> D["Denoiser (U-Net or DiT)<br/>× N steps"]
    TE -->|"cross-attention"| D
    D --> L["Clean latent"]
    L --> VD["VAE decoder"]
    VD --> I["Image"]
  • ControlNet adds spatial conditions (edges, depth, pose) through a trainable copy of the encoder. DreamBooth, textual inversion and LoRA personalize a model on a few images. Inpainting and image-to-image start from a partially noised real image.
  • DiT (Diffusion Transformer): replace the U-Net with a Transformer over latent patches; it scales with compute like LLMs and underlies many recent image and video models.
  • Flow matching / rectified flow: learn a velocity field that moves samples along (nearly) straight paths from noise to data; simpler training and fewer sampling steps.
  • Few-step generation: consistency models, progressive and adversarial distillation reach good samples in 1–4 steps.
  • Video: spatio-temporal latents and Transformer denoisers generate clips; consistency over time is the hard part.

docs.title: Multimodal LLMs
docs.text:
The problem: text-only LLMs can't read images, charts, documents or screens, or listen.

Core idea: turn other modalities into embeddings or tokens the language model can attend to.

Design How Examples Projector (late fusion) A pretrained vision encoder (CLIP or SigLIP ViT) produces patch features; a small MLP projects them into the LLM's embedding space as "image tokens" LLaVA (2023) and many open models Cross-attention / resampler Insert cross-attention layers so a frozen LLM attends to visual features, often compressed by a resampler Flamingo (2022) Native (early fusion) Train one model on interleaved text, image (and audio) tokens from the start Recent frontier models

Training stages (LLaVA-style): first align by training the projector on image–caption pairs with encoder and LLM frozen; then visual instruction tuning on question–answer and conversation data, often unfreezing the LLM.

Practical notes: high-resolution images are tiled into many patches, and image tokens are expensive; OCR-free document understanding and chart reading are major uses; visual hallucination (describing objects that aren't there), counting and fine spatial reasoning remain weak spots. Speech: Whisper is an encoder–decoder speech recognizer trained on large weakly supervised data; speech-to-speech models handle audio end to end. Computer-use agents rely on multimodal models reading screenshots.

docs.title: Risks to mention
docs.text: Deepfakes and impersonation, non-consensual imagery, copyright and training-data consent, memorization of training images, and bias in generated content. Mitigations include content provenance standards (C2PA), watermarking, safety classifiers on prompts and outputs, and dataset curation.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Autoencoder vs VAE: why can't a plain autoencoder generate good samples?

A plain autoencoder only learns to reconstruct training inputs; nothing constrains where codes land, so the latent space has gaps and irregular regions, and decoding a random point often produces nonsense. A VAE encodes each input as a distribution and adds a KL penalty pulling every encoding toward a standard normal, so the latent space is continuous and covered: sampling \(z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) and decoding gives plausible outputs.

Explain the two terms of the VAE ELBO.

The reconstruction term \(\mathbb{E}_q[\log p(x \mid z)]\) rewards decoding the input accurately from its sampled code. The KL term \(D_{KL}(q(z \mid x)\,\|\,p(z))\) penalizes encodings that stray from the prior, which regularizes the latent space and makes sampling possible. Maximizing their difference maximizes a lower bound on the data log-likelihood; their balance (scaled by β in β-VAE) trades sharpness against latent-space structure.

Why is the reparameterization trick needed?

The ELBO requires sampling \(z\) from \(q(z \mid x)\), and you can't backpropagate through a random sampling step. Writing \(z = \mu + \sigma \odot \epsilon\) with \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) moves the randomness into an input that doesn't depend on the parameters, so \(z\) becomes a deterministic, differentiable function of \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\), and gradients reach the encoder.

Why are VAE samples blurry?

With a Gaussian likelihood, the reconstruction term is effectively MSE, which is minimized by the average of all plausible outputs for a given code, and averages of sharp images are blurry. The KL term also limits how much information each code carries, so fine detail isn't encoded. Remedies: perceptual or adversarial losses (VAE-GAN), discrete latents (VQ-VAE), or using the VAE only as a compressor while another model (diffusion, autoregressive) models the latents.

Explain the GAN objective.

The discriminator maximizes \(\mathbb{E}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))]\), learning to output high probability for real data and low for fakes; the generator minimizes the same expression, learning to produce samples the discriminator accepts. At the optimal discriminator, the generator is minimizing the Jensen–Shannon divergence between data and generated distributions. In practice the generator maximizes \(\log D(G(z))\) to avoid weak gradients early in training.

What is mode collapse, and how is it mitigated?

The generator finds a few outputs that fool the discriminator and produces only those, ignoring the rest of the data distribution: low diversity despite good-looking samples. Mitigations: Wasserstein loss with gradient penalty (smoother, more informative gradients), minibatch discrimination or feature statistics that let the discriminator detect lack of diversity, unrolled GAN training, spectral normalization, and multiple generators. Diffusion models largely avoid it by design.

Why did WGAN help?

The original objective relates to the Jensen–Shannon divergence, which saturates when real and generated distributions don't overlap, giving the generator vanishing gradients. WGAN minimizes an approximation of the Wasserstein (earth-mover) distance, which still changes smoothly when distributions are far apart, using a critic constrained to be 1-Lipschitz (by weight clipping, or better, a gradient penalty). Training is more stable and the critic's loss correlates with sample quality.

What does FID measure?

Fréchet Inception Distance embeds real and generated images with an Inception network, fits a Gaussian (mean and covariance) to each set of features, and computes the Fréchet distance between the two Gaussians. Lower is better; it captures both quality and diversity. Caveats: it depends on the feature network, needs many samples, is biased with small sample sizes, and doesn't measure prompt alignment (use CLIP score or human preference for that).

Explain the forward and reverse processes in diffusion models.

The forward process gradually adds Gaussian noise according to a fixed schedule until the data becomes pure noise; thanks to Gaussian properties, \(x_t\) can be sampled directly from \(x_0\) as \(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\epsilon\). The reverse process is learned: a network predicts the added noise (or the clean image, or a velocity) at each step, and sampling starts from noise and denoises step by step to generate new data.

What does the diffusion network predict, and what is the loss?

Commonly the noise \(\epsilon\) that was added to produce \(x_t\), trained with mean squared error between the true and predicted noise at a randomly sampled timestep. Predicting noise is equivalent to estimating the score (gradient of log density) up to scaling. Alternatives predict the clean image \(x_0\) or the velocity \(v\), which can be more stable at some noise levels; all are interconvertible.

What is classifier-free guidance?

Train one denoiser both with the condition (such as the text prompt) and without it, by randomly dropping the condition during training. At sampling time, compute both predictions and extrapolate: \(\hat\epsilon = \epsilon(x_t, \varnothing) + w(\epsilon(x_t, c) - \epsilon(x_t, \varnothing))\). Guidance scale \(w\) trades diversity for prompt adherence and image quality. It removed the need for a separate classifier and is standard in text-to-image models.

Why is diffusion sampling slow, and how is it sped up?

Each sample needs many sequential denoising steps (hundreds to a thousand originally), each a full network evaluation. Speed-ups: better samplers and ODE solvers (DDIM, DPM-Solver) needing 20–50 steps; latent diffusion so each step is cheaper; flow matching with straighter trajectories; and distillation (progressive, consistency, adversarial) to 1–4 steps. Smaller or quantized denoisers and caching also help.

Why diffuse in latent space?

Pixel space is enormous (a 1024×1024 RGB image has about 3 million values), and most of that detail is perceptually redundant. A VAE compresses images about 8× per side into a latent that keeps the semantic and perceptual content; running diffusion there cuts compute and memory dramatically, enabling high resolution on consumer GPUs, while the VAE decoder restores detail.

How does text conditioning work in Stable Diffusion?

A text encoder (CLIP's, and in newer models also T5) turns the prompt into a sequence of token embeddings. The denoiser attends to them through cross-attention layers: queries from image latent features, keys and values from the text embeddings, so each region of the image can draw on relevant words. Classifier-free guidance strengthens the effect at sampling time.

What is flow matching?

A way to train continuous-time generative models by regressing a neural velocity field onto a target velocity that transports noise to data along a chosen path, often a straight line between a noise sample and a data sample (rectified flow). Sampling integrates that velocity field from noise to data. Training is simple and stable, and straighter paths allow good samples with fewer integration steps; several recent image models use it.

How does a LLaVA-style model connect a vision encoder to an LLM?

A pretrained vision encoder (a CLIP or SigLIP ViT) turns the image into patch features; a small projector (linear layer or MLP) maps each feature into the LLM's embedding space; those vectors are inserted into the token sequence as image tokens alongside the text. Training first aligns the projector on image–caption pairs with the other parts frozen, then instruction-tunes on visual question answering and conversation data.

Early vs late fusion in multimodal models.

Late fusion encodes each modality with its own pretrained encoder and combines them later (projector or cross-attention into an LLM): cheaper, reuses strong unimodal models, modular. Early fusion tokenizes all modalities into one sequence and trains a single model on them jointly from the start: deeper cross-modal interaction and native generation in several modalities, but much more expensive and harder to train.

How would you build question answering over scanned PDFs?

Options: (1) OCR plus layout parsing into text and tables, then a normal RAG pipeline; (2) a vision-language model that reads page images directly (better for charts, forms and complex layouts); or (3) retrieval over page-image embeddings with a VLM answering from the top pages. Production often mixes them: extract text for search, render pages for the VLM, cite page numbers, and evaluate on real documents for extraction accuracy and faithfulness.

Common mistakes

  • Claiming GANs provide likelihoods.
  • Forgetting that diffusion's forward process has no learned parameters.
  • Saying classifier-free guidance needs a separate classifier.
  • Assuming multimodal models "see" fine detail reliably.

docs.title: Inference & Serving
docs.text:
TL;DR

Generating text has two phases: prefill (process the prompt in parallel; compute-bound; sets time to first token) and decode (one token at a time; memory-bandwidth-bound; sets time per token). Serving is about keeping GPUs busy without blowing latency: continuous batching, PagedAttention for the KV cache, prefix caching, quantization, and speculative decoding, which drafts several tokens with a small model and verifies them in one pass without changing the output distribution. Estimate cost from tokens per request, throughput per GPU and GPU price.

Where this fits

Before: Efficient Attention & MoE (KV cache, GQA, FlashAttention) and Fine-Tuning & Efficiency (quantization). This page: running models in production. Next: applications built on top: prompting, RAG, agents.

docs.title: How generation works
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    participant G as GPU
    C->>S: prompt (n tokens)
    S->>G: prefill: all n tokens at once,<br/>fill the KV cache
    G-->>S: logits for token n+1
    S-->>C: first token (TTFT)
    loop until a stop token or max length
        S->>G: decode: 1 new token<br/>reads the KV cache
        G-->>S: logits for the next token
        S-->>C: stream token<br/>(time per token)
    end
  • Prefill runs big matrix multiplications over the whole prompt: compute-bound. Long prompts mean slow first tokens.
  • Decode produces one token per sequence per step. Each step reads every weight and the sequence's KV cache from GPU memory to do a little arithmetic: memory-bandwidth-bound.
Back-of-envelope: the decode speed limit

At batch size 1, each decode step must read all weights once. A 7B model in FP16 is about 14 GB; with about 3 TB/s of memory bandwidth, one step takes at least \(14 / 3000 \approx 4.7\) ms, so about 210 tokens per second at most, whatever the compute. In 4-bit (about 3.5 GB) the limit rises to about 850 tokens per second. Batching 32 sequences reads the weights once for 32 tokens, which is why throughput rises with batch size until compute or KV-cache memory runs out.

docs.title: Metrics that matter
docs.text:
Metric Meaning Driven by Time to first token (TTFT) Delay before the first token appears Queueing, prompt length (prefill), retrieval or tool calls before generation Time per output token / inter-token latency Gap between streamed tokens Decode speed, batch size, model size End-to-end latency TTFT + output tokens × time per token Both, plus output length Throughput Tokens per second across all requests Batching, memory, hardware utilization Goodput Throughput that meets latency targets The trade-off between batching and latency Cost per million tokens Dollars per input and output token Throughput per GPU and GPU price

Measure percentiles (p50, p95, p99), not averages, and separate input and output tokens: output tokens are far more expensive because they're generated sequentially.

docs.title: Batching
docs.text: Strategy How Problem it solves Static batching Wait for a full batch, run it to completion Short requests wait for the longest one; GPUs idle Dynamic batching Group requests that arrive within a time window Better, but still finishes batches together Continuous (in-flight) batching At every decode step, finished sequences leave and new ones join Keeps the GPU full; large throughput gains Chunked prefill Split long prompts into chunks interleaved with decode steps Long prompts no longer stall everyone else's decoding Prefill–decode disaggregation Run prefill and decode on separate GPU pools Each phase gets hardware and batching suited to it

docs.title: Managing KV-cache memory
docs.text:
• PagedAttention (vLLM, 2023): store each sequence's KV cache in fixed-size blocks allocated on demand, like pages of virtual memory, instead of one contiguous region sized for the maximum length. Fragmentation and over-reservation largely disappear, so many more sequences fit, and blocks can be shared.
  • Prefix caching: requests that start with the same tokens (a long system prompt, shared documents, few-shot examples, earlier turns of a conversation) reuse the cached keys and values instead of recomputing prefill. SGLang's RadixAttention organizes cached prefixes as a tree. Hosted APIs expose this as prompt caching, usually priced well below normal input tokens, so put stable content first.
  • KV-cache quantization (8-bit or 4-bit) and offloading to CPU memory extend capacity further.
  • Smaller caches by design: GQA, MLA and sliding-window attention (see Efficient Attention).

docs.title: Speculative decoding
docs.text:
The problem: decode is memory-bound, so the GPU has spare compute while it waits on memory; generating one token per expensive pass wastes it.

Core idea: a small, fast draft model proposes \(k\) tokens; the large target model scores all \(k\) in one parallel pass (like a short prefill); accept the longest prefix that the target agrees with, then continue.

  • Acceptance rule: accept draft token \(x\) with probability \(\min\left(1, \frac{p_{target}(x)}{p_{draft}(x)}\right)\); on rejection, sample a replacement from the normalized difference \(\max(0, p_{target} - p_{draft})\). This makes the output distribution exactly the target model's, so quality is unchanged.
  • Speed-up depends on how often the draft agrees (the acceptance rate); 2–3× is common for well-matched pairs.
  • Variants: Medusa (extra prediction heads on the target model itself), EAGLE (a light draft head using the target's hidden features), lookahead decoding, and prompt-lookup / n-gram drafting, which copies candidate continuations from the prompt and works well for editing and RAG answers that quote their sources.

docs.title: Other speed-ups
docs.text:
• Quantization: weight-only INT4/INT8 for memory-bound decode; FP8 weights and activations on newer GPUs. See Fine-Tuning & Efficiency.
  • Kernels: FlashAttention for prefill, decode-optimized attention kernels, fused operations, CUDA graphs to cut launch overhead.
  • Parallelism for latency: tensor parallelism across GPUs in a node splits each step's work, lowering per-token latency for big models.
  • Structured output: constrained decoding avoids retries for malformed JSON.
  • Shorter outputs: ask for concise answers, set max_tokens, and stop on sentinel sequences. Output tokens dominate latency and cost.

docs.title: Serving engines
docs.text:
Engine Notes vLLM PagedAttention, continuous batching, prefix caching, many quantization formats, multi-LoRA serving SGLang RadixAttention prefix caching, fast structured generation, strong for agent-style workloads TensorRT-LLM NVIDIA-optimized kernels and FP8; high performance, more build effort Hugging Face TGI Production server with continuous batching llama.cpp / Ollama Quantized models on CPUs, laptops and edge devices

Around the engine: an API gateway with authentication and rate limits, request queues, autoscaling on queue depth or GPU utilization, and observability (tokens, latency percentiles, errors, cost per request).

docs.title: Routing, caching and cost control
docs.text:
• Model routing and cascades: send easy requests to a small, cheap model and escalate hard ones (by classifier, confidence or task type) to a large one.
  • Response caching: exact-match caching for repeated requests; semantic caching (embedding similarity) for near-duplicates, with care for freshness and personalization.
  • Prompt hygiene: trim retrieved context, summarize history, keep stable prefixes for prompt caching.
  • Batch APIs for offline workloads at lower prices.
  • Multi-LoRA serving: many fine-tuned adapters share one base model in memory.
Worked example: estimating serving cost

A support assistant handles 1 million requests a day, each with 2,000 input tokens (system prompt plus retrieved context) and 300 output tokens.

Hosted API: with prices of, say, P₁ per million input tokens and P₂ per million output tokens, daily cost is \(2{,}000 \times P_1 + 300 \times P_2\) (because 1M requests × 2,000 tokens = 2,000M input tokens). If the 1,500-token system prompt and instructions are identical across requests, prompt caching bills most of those input tokens at a large discount.

Self-hosted: if one GPU sustains 2,500 output tokens per second at your latency target, 300M output tokens a day need \(300\text{M} / (2{,}500 \times 86{,}400) \approx 1.4\) GPU-days of decode, plus prefill capacity and headroom for peak traffic (often 3–5× the average). Multiply GPUs by hourly price to compare.

“How would you cut LLM serving cost by half?”
  1. Measure first: cost per request split into input and output tokens, by feature and route.
  2. Use fewer tokens: shorter system prompts, retrieve fewer but better chunks, summarize history, cap output length.
  3. Cache: prompt caching for stable prefixes; response or semantic caching for repeats.
  4. Route: a small model for easy requests, escalating only when needed; or distill or fine-tune a small model for the main task.
  5. Serve efficiently (if self-hosting): continuous batching, quantization, prefix caching, speculative decoding, right-sized GPUs, autoscaling.
  6. Batch offline work through batch APIs.
  7. Guard quality with an evaluation set so savings don't silently degrade answers.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Prefill vs decode: what's the difference, and which is the bottleneck?

Prefill processes all prompt tokens at once to build the KV cache and produce the first token; it's dominated by large matrix multiplications, so it's compute-bound and determines time to first token. Decode generates tokens one at a time; each step reads all the weights and the KV cache for a small amount of arithmetic, so it's memory-bandwidth-bound and determines time per token. Long prompts hurt TTFT; long outputs hurt total latency.

What is continuous batching and why does it matter?

Instead of running a fixed batch until every sequence finishes, the scheduler updates the batch at each decode step: finished sequences leave and waiting requests join immediately. GPUs stay full despite very different output lengths, and short requests don't wait for long ones. It's one of the largest throughput wins in LLM serving and is standard in vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM and SGLang.

Explain PagedAttention.

Naive servers reserve a contiguous KV-cache region per sequence sized for the maximum length, wasting most of it through over-reservation and fragmentation. PagedAttention splits the cache into fixed-size blocks allocated on demand and tracked with a block table, like virtual-memory pages, and the attention kernel reads keys and values from non-contiguous blocks. Waste drops to near zero, many more sequences fit in memory (higher batch sizes and throughput), and blocks can be shared across sequences, for example for common prefixes or parallel sampling.

How does speculative decoding keep the output identical in distribution?

A draft model proposes tokens; the target model computes its own probabilities for all of them in one pass. Each draft token \(x\) is accepted with probability \(\min(1, p_{target}(x)/p_{draft}(x))\); at the first rejection, a token is sampled from the normalized residual \(\max(0, p_{target} - p_{draft})\) and the rest of the draft is discarded. This rejection-sampling scheme provably yields samples from exactly the target distribution, so speed improves without changing quality; the speed-up depends on the acceptance rate.

What limits decode speed at batch size 1, and how do you estimate it?

Memory bandwidth. Each token requires reading all model weights (plus the KV cache) from GPU memory, so the minimum time per token is roughly model bytes ÷ bandwidth. A 7B FP16 model (14 GB) on a GPU with about 3 TB/s is limited to about 210 tokens per second; quantizing to 4 bits raises the ceiling about fourfold. Batching amortizes the weight reads across sequences, which is why throughput grows with batch size.

What's the difference between latency and throughput in LLM serving, and how do you trade them off?

Latency is how fast one request completes (TTFT and time per token); throughput is total tokens per second across all users. Larger batches raise throughput and lower cost per token but increase each request's per-token latency and queueing. Set latency targets (p95 TTFT and inter-token latency), then maximize goodput, the throughput that meets those targets, with batching, chunked prefill, and separate pools for latency-sensitive and batch traffic.

What is prefix caching and when does it help?

Reusing the KV cache for a shared beginning of the prompt instead of recomputing prefill. It helps when many requests share long prefixes: system prompts, tool definitions, few-shot examples, the same document in a RAG or agent loop, and multi-turn chats where each turn resends history. It cuts TTFT and cost substantially. Put stable content first and variable content last so prefixes actually match.

What is semantic caching, and what are its risks?

Storing previous responses keyed by an embedding of the request and returning a cached answer when a new request is similar enough. It saves cost and latency for repetitive queries. Risks: returning a wrong answer for a subtly different question (the similarity threshold matters), stale answers when data changes, and leaking personalized or permissioned answers across users. Scope caches by user or tenant, set expiry, and evaluate the false-hit rate.

How would you serve 50 fine-tuned variants of one base model?

Fine-tune them as LoRA adapters and use multi-LoRA serving: one copy of the base model in GPU memory, adapters loaded or swapped per request, and kernels that batch requests for different adapters together (as vLLM and others support). This avoids 50 full model copies. Group heavy-traffic adapters on dedicated replicas and keep a cache of hot adapters on the GPU.

How do you choose between a hosted API and self-hosting an open model?

Hosted APIs give top quality, no infrastructure work, elastic scale and fast iteration, priced per token. Self-hosting gives control over data residency, latency and customization, and can be cheaper at high, steady volume, but needs GPU capacity planning, serving expertise, monitoring and upgrades. Decide on quality for your task (measured on your eval set), data and compliance needs, volume and traffic shape, latency targets and team skills; many teams use both, routing by task.

Why does TTFT increase in RAG and agent applications?

Before generation starts, the application may embed the query, search an index, rerank, call tools, and then send a much longer prompt, which lengthens prefill. Each step adds latency, and agent loops repeat it per step. Mitigations: parallelize retrieval steps, cache embeddings and results, trim context, use prefix caching for stable parts, stream partial results, and run cheap steps on small models.

Common mistakes

  • Reporting average latency instead of percentiles.
  • Treating input and output tokens as equally expensive.
  • Thinking speculative decoding changes output quality.
  • Sizing GPUs on weights alone and forgetting the KV cache.
  • Optimizing cost without an evaluation set to catch quality regressions.

docs.title: Pretraining & LLMs
docs.text:
TL;DR

Pretraining learns from raw text with a self-supervised objective: masked tokens (BERT, for understanding) or the next token (GPT, for generation). Scale turned next-token predictors into general models that learn tasks from the prompt (in-context learning). Scaling laws predict loss from parameters, data and compute; Chinchilla showed about 20 training tokens per parameter is compute-optimal, though models are now trained far longer to make inference cheaper. Data quality matters as much as quantity. Decoding (temperature, top-k, top-p) shapes outputs, and next-token training explains hallucination.

Where this fits

Before: The Transformer and efficient attention. This page: pretraining at scale. Next: adapting models cheaply (Fine-Tuning & Efficiency), serving them (Inference & Serving), and turning them into assistants (Post-Training).

  • ELMo · ULMFiT 2018Pretrain a language model, transfer it. LSTM-based: slow, limited context.
  • GPT-1 · BERT 2018The same recipe with Transformers: generation (GPT) and understanding (BERT).
  • GPT-2 · T5 2019Zero-shot ability at 1.5B parameters; every task as text-to-text.
  • GPT-3 · scaling laws 2020175B parameters; few-shot learning from the prompt; loss follows power laws.
  • Chinchilla 2022Most models were undertrained; scale data with parameters.
  • LLaMA and open models 2023+Smaller models trained on far more tokens; a standard recipe.

docs.title: Transfer learning comes to NLP
docs.text:
The problem: every NLP task was trained from scratch on small labeled datasets, and word2vec gave only one static vector per word.

Core idea: pretrain a language model on lots of unlabeled text, then reuse it.

  • ELMo (2018): a bidirectional LSTM language model whose internal states give contextual embeddings, so "bank" gets different vectors in different sentences.
  • ULMFiT (2018): pretrain an LSTM language model, fine-tune it on the target domain, then on the task, with layer-wise learning rates and gradual unfreezing to avoid catastrophic forgetting.
  • GPT-1 (2018): the same pretrain-then-fine-tune recipe with a Transformer decoder.

docs.title: BERT and the encoder family
docs.text:
The problem: left-to-right language models see only past context, but understanding a word benefits from both sides.

Core idea: pretrain a Transformer encoder to fill in masked tokens using bidirectional context.

  • Masked language modeling (MLM): select 15% of tokens; replace 80% of them with [MASK], 10% with a random token, and leave 10% unchanged (so the model can't rely on [MASK] appearing, which it never does at fine-tuning time). Predict the originals.
  • Next-sentence prediction (NSP): predict whether sentence B follows sentence A. Later work found it unhelpful.
  • Fine-tuning: add a task head (classification on the [CLS] token, token tagging, span extraction for QA) and train the whole model briefly.
  • BERT-base has about 110M parameters and BERT-large about 340M, trained on BooksCorpus and English Wikipedia.
Variant Change Effect RoBERTa (2019) More data, longer training, dynamic masking, no NSP Clearly better than BERT ALBERT Factorized embeddings, parameters shared across layers Far fewer parameters DistilBERT Knowledge distillation from BERT About 40% smaller and 60% faster, keeping most accuracy ELECTRA Detect tokens replaced by a small generator, for every position More sample-efficient pretraining DeBERTa Disentangled content and position attention Strong on understanding benchmarks

Encoders remain the workhorses for classification, extraction, embeddings (Sentence-BERT and its successors) and cross-encoder rerankers in RAG.

docs.title: GPT and decoder-only LLMs
docs.text:
The problem: a separate fine-tuned model per task doesn't scale, and encoders can't generate.

Core idea: train a decoder-only Transformer to predict the next token on internet-scale text. The loss is cross-entropy over every position:

\[ \mathcal{L} = -\sum_{t} \log P_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t}) \] Model Year Size What it showed GPT-1 2018 117M Generative pretraining plus fine-tuning transfers well GPT-2 2019 1.5B Zero-shot task performance from prompting alone GPT-3 2020 175B (about 300B training tokens) Few-shot in-context learning at scale LLaMA 2023 7B–65B (1–1.4T tokens) Smaller models trained longer rival much larger ones; open weights LLaMA 2 / 3 and other open families 2023–2025 1B to 400B+ The recipe standardizes: RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE, GQA, huge token counts

docs.title: T5 and text-to-text
docs.text: T5 (2019) cast every task as text in, text out ("translate English to German: …", "summarize: …") with one encoder–decoder model, trained with span corruption: replace random spans with sentinel tokens and generate the missing spans. Its paper is a systematic study of architectures, objectives and data (the C4 corpus). Flan-T5 added instruction tuning; T5 encoders are still used as text encoders, including in image generators.

docs.title: Pretraining data
docs.text:
Data decides much of a model's quality. A typical pipeline:

flowchart LR
    subgraph COLLECT["Collect and filter"]
        direction TB
        A["Web crawl, code,<br/>books, papers, math"] --> B["Language ID and<br/>heuristic filters"]
        B --> C["Quality filtering<br/>(classifiers, perplexity)"]
        C --> D["Deduplication<br/>exact + near-duplicate"]
    end
    subgraph PREP["Clean, mix, tokenize"]
        direction TB
        E["Safety and PII<br/>filtering"] --> F["Mixture weighting<br/>by source"]
        F --> G["Tokenization"]
    end
    COLLECT --> PREP
  • Filtering: remove boilerplate, spam and very short or symbol-heavy pages; keep text a quality classifier judges reference-like.
  • Deduplication: exact hashing plus near-duplicate detection (MinHash with locality-sensitive hashing). Duplicates waste compute and increase memorization.
  • Mixture: proportions of web, code, math, books, multilingual text; code and math noticeably improve reasoning.
  • Decontamination: remove benchmark test sets from training data, or evaluations are meaningless.
  • Synthetic data: text generated or rewritten by stronger models is increasingly used, especially for reasoning, code and instruction data.
  • Annealing: many recipes end training on a smaller, higher-quality mixture with a decaying learning rate.

docs.title: Scaling laws
docs.text:
The problem: with a fixed compute budget, should you train a bigger model or train on more data?

Core idea: loss falls smoothly and predictably, as a power law, with model size \(N\), data \(D\) and compute \(C\), so small experiments can forecast large ones.

  • Kaplan et al. (2020): loss follows power laws in \(N\), \(D\) and \(C\) over many orders of magnitude; their fits suggested growing models faster than data.
  • Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al., 2022): with training compute \(C \approx 6ND\), the loss-minimizing choice scales \(N\) and \(D\) roughly equally, about 20 tokens per parameter. Chinchilla (70B parameters, 1.4T tokens) beat the 280B-parameter Gopher with the same compute. Many earlier models were badly undertrained.
  • Training past "optimal": compute-optimal minimizes training cost for a given loss. If a model will serve billions of requests, a smaller model trained on far more tokens is cheaper overall. LLaMA 3 8B, for example, was trained on about 15T tokens, roughly 1,900 tokens per parameter.
  • Limits: scaling laws predict loss, not specific abilities; high-quality data is finite (driving synthetic data and multi-epoch training); and a newer axis is test-time compute, spending more computation per answer (see Reasoning Models).

docs.title: Training at scale
docs.text:
• Optimizer: AdamW with warmup and cosine or warmup–stable–decay schedules; batch sizes of millions of tokens.
  • Precision: BF16 compute, sometimes FP8 for matrix multiplications.
  • Parallelism: data, tensor, pipeline, sequence and expert parallelism combined; see Fine-Tuning & Efficiency.
  • Stability: loss spikes are handled with gradient clipping, lower learning rates, restarting from a checkpoint and skipping the bad data, z-loss on the output logits, and normalization of queries and keys.
  • Evaluation during training: held-out loss on each data source plus small benchmark suites, decontaminated.

docs.title: In-context learning
docs.text:
The problem: fine-tuning for every new task needs labeled data and training runs.

Core idea: large models learn a task from instructions and a few examples placed in the prompt, with no weight updates.

  • Zero-shot: only an instruction. Few-shot: a handful of input–output examples, then the new input.
  • Proposed mechanisms: induction heads copy patterns from the context; the model may infer a latent task (a Bayesian view); some analyses show attention can implement steps resembling gradient descent on the examples.
  • Sensitivities: the choice, order and format of examples, label balance, and even whether example labels are correct can shift accuracy.
  • Emergence: some abilities appeared to jump suddenly with scale; later analysis (Schaeffer et al., 2023) showed many jumps come from all-or-nothing metrics and look smooth with continuous ones.

docs.title: Decoding strategies
docs.text:
The model outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary; a decoding strategy picks the token.

Strategy How When Greedy Always take the most likely token Deterministic tasks (extraction, short answers); prone to repetition in long text Beam search Keep the \(B\) best partial sequences Translation, summarization; bland and repetitive for open-ended chat Temperature Sample from \(\text{softmax}(z/T)\); \(T < 1\) sharpens, \(T > 1\) flattens Controls randomness Top-k Sample only from the \(k\) most likely tokens Cuts the long tail of unlikely tokens Top-p (nucleus) Sample from the smallest set whose probability sums to \(p\) Adapts the candidate set to the model's confidence Min-p Keep tokens with probability at least \(p_{min}\) times the top token's Robust at higher temperatures Repetition / frequency penalties Lower the logits of tokens already used Reduce loops Constrained decoding Mask tokens that would violate a grammar or JSON schema Guaranteed parseable structured output

Temperature 0 isn't perfectly deterministic on GPUs: batching and floating-point reduction order can change results slightly.

docs.title: Hallucination and other limits
docs.text:
Why LLMs hallucinate: next-token training rewards plausible continuations, not truth. When the model lacks a fact, the most likely-sounding answer is still produced fluently. Contributing factors: gaps and errors in training data, knowledge frozen at a cutoff, sampling randomness, preference training that rewards confident or agreeable answers (sycophancy), and evaluations that reward guessing over saying "I don't know".

Mitigations: ground answers in retrieved sources with citations (RAG); give the model tools (search, calculators, code); allow and reward abstaining; lower temperature for factual tasks; verification steps (self-checking, a second model, rules); fine-tuning for calibration; and measuring hallucination on a representative evaluation set.

Other limits to mention: finite context and imperfect use of long context, multi-step reasoning errors, sensitivity to prompt wording, prompt injection, bias inherited from data, and cost and latency.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Explain the causal language modeling objective.

Given a sequence \(x_1 \dots x_T\), train the model to maximize \(\sum_t \log P(x_t \mid x_{<t})\): at every position, predict the next token from everything before it. With a causal mask, all positions train in parallel from one forward pass. It's self-supervised, so any text is training data, and it's equivalent to minimizing cross-entropy between the model's next-token distribution and the actual next token.

Explain BERT's masked language modeling and the 80/10/10 rule.

BERT selects 15% of input tokens and trains the encoder to predict them using context from both sides. Of the selected tokens, 80% become [MASK], 10% become a random token and 10% stay unchanged. Because [MASK] never appears during fine-tuning or real use, always masking would create a train–test mismatch; mixing in random and unchanged tokens forces the model to build good representations for every position, not just masked ones.

BERT vs GPT: objectives and uses.

BERT is an encoder trained with masked language modeling: bidirectional context, excellent representations for classification, extraction, embeddings and reranking, but no natural way to generate. GPT is a decoder trained with next-token prediction: causal context, naturally generative, and at scale capable of in-context learning across tasks. Today GPT-style models are the general-purpose LLMs, while BERT-style encoders remain efficient specialists.

Why was next-sentence prediction dropped in RoBERTa?

Ablations showed NSP didn't help and sometimes hurt downstream performance. The task was too easy: negative pairs came from different documents, so the model could solve it from topic differences rather than coherence. RoBERTa instead trained longer, on more data, with larger batches and dynamic masking, on full sentences packed into long sequences, and did better.

What changed architecturally from GPT-2 to LLaMA?

The core decoder-only Transformer stayed the same; the components were modernized: Pre-LN with RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm, SwiGLU feed-forward layers instead of GELU MLPs, rotary position embeddings instead of learned absolute positions, no bias terms, and in later versions grouped-query attention and much larger vocabularies. The bigger change was training: far more tokens per parameter on carefully filtered data.

What did Chinchilla change?

It showed that for a fixed training compute budget (\(C \approx 6ND\)), parameters and training tokens should grow roughly equally, about 20 tokens per parameter, and that models like GPT-3 and Gopher were undertrained. Chinchilla, 70B parameters on 1.4T tokens, outperformed the 280B Gopher with the same compute and was cheaper to serve. It shifted the field toward training smaller models on much more data.

Why train small models on far more tokens than the compute-optimal amount?

Chinchilla-optimal minimizes training compute for a target loss. But total cost includes inference, which scales with model size and with how many tokens are served. A smaller model trained much longer reaches a similar loss with higher training cost but far lower serving cost, latency and memory, and fits on cheaper hardware or devices. For widely deployed models that trade is worth it.

Estimate the training compute for a 7B model on 2 trillion tokens.

Use \(C \approx 6ND = 6 \times 7\times10^9 \times 2\times10^{12} = 8.4\times10^{22}\) FLOPs. If a GPU sustains about \(4\times10^{14}\) FLOP/s (around 40% utilization of a modern accelerator's BF16 peak), that's \(2.1\times10^8\) GPU-seconds, about 58,000 GPU-hours, or roughly 25 days on 100 GPUs.

How is pretraining data cleaned?

Start from web crawls, code, books and papers; identify language; apply heuristic filters (length, symbol and repetition ratios, boilerplate removal); score quality with classifiers or reference-model perplexity; deduplicate exactly and approximately (MinHash/LSH), which reduces memorization and wasted compute; filter unsafe content and personal information; remove benchmark test sets (decontamination); then set mixture weights across sources, often with a final high-quality annealing phase.

What is in-context learning?

The ability of a pretrained model to perform a task described in the prompt, from instructions and a few examples, without changing its weights. Its performance depends on model scale and on the examples' selection, order and format. Proposed explanations include induction heads that copy patterns, implicit inference of the task, and attention implementing learning-like updates over the examples.

Few-shot prompting vs fine-tuning: trade-offs.

Few-shot prompting needs no training, adapts instantly and keeps one model for many tasks, but uses context window space and tokens on every call, is sensitive to example choice, and is capped by what the base model can already do. Fine-tuning bakes the behavior into the weights: shorter prompts, more consistent format, often a smaller and cheaper model, and better results with enough data, at the cost of a training pipeline, data collection and maintenance.

Are emergent abilities real?

Some abilities appear to jump from near-random to good at a certain scale. Later analysis showed many of these jumps come from discontinuous metrics like exact match: measured with continuous metrics such as token-level log-likelihood, improvement is often smooth and predictable. Capabilities still do improve with scale, and some practically useful behaviors only become reliable past certain sizes, but "sudden emergence" is often a measurement artifact.

Top-k vs top-p sampling.

Top-k samples from a fixed number of the most likely tokens, regardless of how confident the model is: too many candidates when the distribution is peaked, too few when it's flat. Top-p (nucleus) sampling takes the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches \(p\), so the candidate set shrinks when the model is confident and grows when it isn't. They're often combined, together with temperature.

What does temperature do mathematically?

It divides the logits before the softmax: \(p_i = \frac{\exp(z_i/T)}{\sum_j \exp(z_j/T)}\). \(T < 1\) exaggerates differences between logits, concentrating probability on the top tokens (as \(T \to 0\) it becomes greedy). \(T > 1\) shrinks differences, flattening the distribution and increasing diversity and the chance of unlikely tokens. \(T = 1\) is the model's own distribution.

Why is beam search a poor fit for chat?

Beam search seeks the highest-probability sequence, and the highest-probability text is often short, generic and repetitive, unlike how people write. It's also slower and reduces diversity. For open-ended generation, sampling with temperature and top-p produces more natural and varied responses; beam search still suits tasks with one correct output, such as translation.

How do you force an LLM to produce valid JSON?

Strongest: constrained decoding, where at each step tokens that would violate the JSON schema or grammar are masked out, so the output is guaranteed parseable (structured-output features in model APIs, or libraries that compile a schema into a grammar). Weaker: clear instructions with a schema and examples, tool or function-calling interfaces, then validating, and retrying with the error message on failure.

Why do LLMs hallucinate?

They're trained to produce likely continuations, not verified facts, so when knowledge is missing or uncertain they still generate fluent, plausible text. Causes include gaps and errors in training data, knowledge cutoffs, sampling randomness, preference training that rewards confident or agreeable answers, and evaluations that reward guessing over abstaining. Hallucination is a property of the objective, so it can be reduced and measured but not eliminated.

How would you reduce hallucinations in a production chatbot?

Ground answers in retrieved documents and require citations; instruct and allow the model to say it doesn't know; use tools for facts and arithmetic; lower temperature; validate outputs (schema checks, entailment checks between answer and sources, a verifier model); fine-tune on examples of abstaining; restrict scope to supported topics; and measure the hallucination rate on a labeled evaluation set drawn from real traffic, tracking it in production with user feedback.

How do you measure hallucination?

Build an evaluation set representative of real questions with known answers or source documents. For grounded tasks, measure faithfulness: whether each claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context, using human labels or an LLM judge calibrated against humans. For open questions, measure factual accuracy against references, and track abstention rates (a model that never answers never hallucinates). Report by category and monitor in production through sampling and user flags.

Common mistakes

  • Saying Chinchilla means every model should use 20 tokens per parameter (it's compute-optimal for training only).
  • Confusing pretraining with fine-tuning or instruction tuning.
  • Claiming temperature 0 guarantees identical outputs.
  • Treating benchmark scores as reliable without asking about contamination.
  • Calling hallucination a bug that more data will fully fix.

  • State Kaplan and Chinchilla, \(C \approx 6ND\) and 20 tokens per parameter, and why models are trained past it
  • Explain in-context learning and the emergence debate
  • Compare greedy, beam, temperature, top-k and top-p decoding
