docs.title: The Transformer
docs.text:
TL;DR

The Transformer (2017) replaced recurrence with self-attention: every token builds its new representation as a weighted mix of all tokens' values, with weights from query–key similarity, \(\text{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V\). Multiple heads capture different relationships; positional encodings (now usually RoPE) supply order; a feed-forward network processes each token; residual connections and normalization keep deep stacks trainable. It trains in parallel and connects distant tokens directly, at \(O(n^2)\) cost in sequence length. Decoder-only Transformers trained on next-token prediction are today's LLMs.

Where this fits

Before: attention on top of RNNs fixed the seq2seq bottleneck but stayed sequential. This page: attention only. Next: Efficient Attention & MoE attacks the quadratic cost; Pretraining & LLMs scales it up.

docs.title: The architecture at a glance
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    T["Input tokens"] --> E["Token embeddings<br/>(+ positions)"]
    E --> B1
    subgraph B1["Transformer block × N"]
        direction TB
        N1["RMSNorm / LayerNorm"] --> A["Multi-head self-attention<br/>(causal mask in decoders)"]
        A --> R1(("+"))
        R1 --> N2["RMSNorm / LayerNorm"] --> F["Feed-forward network<br/>(GELU or SwiGLU)"]
        F --> R2(("+"))
    end
    B1 --> FN["Final norm"] --> H["Linear head to vocabulary"] --> S["Softmax → next-token probabilities"]

Each block has two sublayers, and each sublayer is wrapped in a residual connection: attention lets tokens exchange information; the feed-forward network transforms each token independently. This page shows the Pre-LN arrangement used by modern LLMs: \(x \leftarrow x + \text{Attn}(\text{Norm}(x))\), then \(x \leftarrow x + \text{FFN}(\text{Norm}(x))\).

docs.title: Self-attention
docs.text:
The problem it solved: RNNs process tokens one after another (slow to train) and pass information between distant tokens through many steps (it fades).

Core idea: every token looks at every other token directly, in one step, and takes a weighted average of what they offer.

docs.title: Queries, keys and values
docs.text:
Each token's vector \(x_i\) is projected three ways with learned matrices:

  • Query \(q_i = x_i W_Q\): what this token is looking for.
  • Key \(k_j = x_j W_K\): what each token offers to be matched against.
  • Value \(v_j = x_j W_V\): the information each token passes on if attended to.

Think of a library search: the query is your request, keys are the catalogue entries, values are the books. You take a mix of books weighted by how well each catalogue entry matches your request.

\[ \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V \]

With \(n\) tokens, \(Q\) and \(K\) are \((n, d_k)\) and \(V\) is \((n, d_v)\). \(QK^\top\) is an \((n, n)\) score matrix; softmax over each row turns scores into weights that sum to 1; multiplying by \(V\) gives each token a new \((d_v)\) vector.

docs.title: Why divide by √d_k
docs.text: If query and key components are roughly independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). With \(d_k = 128\), raw scores have a standard deviation around 11, which pushes softmax toward a one-hot output where its gradients are nearly zero, so learning stalls. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) restores unit variance.

docs.title: Masks
docs.text:
• Causal mask (decoders): position \(i\) may only attend to positions \(\le i\). Scores for future positions are set to \(-\infty\) before the softmax so they get exactly zero weight. This is what makes next-token training honest: the model can't peek at the token it's predicting. A large negative number instead of \(-\infty\) is used in practice to avoid NaNs.
  • Padding mask: ignore padding tokens in batches of unequal length.

docs.title: Costs and benefits
docs.text:
RNN Self-attention Sequential operations per layer \(O(n)\) \(O(1)\): all positions at once Path length between two tokens \(O(n)\) \(O(1)\) Compute per layer \(O(n\,d^2)\) \(O(n^2 d)\) for attention, plus \(O(n\,d^2)\) for projections and FFN Memory for attention weights — \(O(n^2)\) per head (avoided by FlashAttention)

For short sequences the \(O(nd^2)\) projections dominate; past a few thousand tokens the \(O(n^2d)\) attention term does, which is why long context needs efficient attention.

docs.title: Multi-head attention
docs.text:
The problem: a single softmax produces one weighted average per token, but tokens relate in several ways at once: syntax, coreference, position, topic.

Core idea: run \(h\) attention operations in parallel on smaller projections, each with \(d_k = d_{model}/h\), then concatenate and project back:

\[ \text{MultiHead}(X) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \dots, \text{head}_h)\,W_O,\qquad \text{head}_i = \text{Attention}(XW_Q^{(i)}, XW_K^{(i)}, XW_V^{(i)}) \]
  • The total cost is about the same as one full-width head, because each head is \(h\) times narrower.
  • Parameters: \(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O\) are each \(d \times d\), so \(4d^2\) per layer (plus biases if used).
  • Heads specialize. Some attend to the previous token, some track syntax; induction heads find an earlier occurrence of the current token and copy what followed it, a mechanism behind in-context learning.
  • Many heads turn out to be redundant and can be pruned; sharing keys and values across heads (MQA, GQA) saves memory at inference. See Efficient Attention.

docs.title: Positional information
docs.text:
The problem: attention is permutation-invariant. Without position information, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look identical.

Method How Strengths Weaknesses Used in Sinusoidal (2017) Add \(\sin(pos/10000^{2i/d})\) and \(\cos(\cdot)\) of different frequencies to embeddings No parameters; any length in principle Poor extrapolation in practice Original Transformer Learned absolute A trainable vector per position Simple, flexible Hard limit at the trained length BERT, GPT-2 Relative bias Add a learned bias to scores based on distance \(i - j\) Generalizes across positions Extra computation T5 RoPE (2021) Rotate query and key vectors by position-dependent angles Relative by construction, no parameters, extendable Extrapolation still needs scaling tricks LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, most open LLMs ALiBi (2021) Subtract a head-specific penalty proportional to distance from scores Extrapolates to longer inputs well Strong recency bias BLOOM, MPT

docs.title: RoPE in one paragraph
docs.text: Split each query and key into pairs of dimensions and treat each pair as a 2-D vector. At position \(m\), rotate pair \(i\) by angle \(m\theta_i\) with \(\theta_i = 10000^{-2i/d}\) (so different pairs rotate at different speeds). Because rotating \(q\) by \(m\theta\) and \(k\) by \(n\theta\) leaves their dot product depending only on the angle difference, \(q_m'^\top k_n' = q_m^\top R_{(n-m)\theta}\, k_n\): attention scores depend on relative position, with no added parameters. To extend context after training, rescale the rotation frequencies: position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling and YaRN.

docs.title: The feed-forward network
docs.text:
Each token passes independently through a two-layer MLP: \(\text{FFN}(x) = W_2\,\phi(W_1 x)\), typically widening from \(d\) to \(4d\) and back, with GELU. LLaMA-style models use SwiGLU, \(W_2(\text{SiLU}(W_1x) \odot W_3x)\), with hidden size about \(\tfrac{8}{3}d\) so the parameter count stays near \(8d^2\).

  • Attention moves information between tokens; the FFN transforms it within each token.
  • FFNs hold about two-thirds of a block's parameters, and research suggests they act like key–value memories that store much of a model's factual knowledge.
  • Mixture-of-experts models replace this FFN with many expert FFNs and a router.

docs.title: Residuals and normalization
docs.text:
• Residual connections (\(x + F(x)\)) give gradients a direct path through dozens of layers, exactly as in ResNet.
  • Normalization: LayerNorm in the original and in BERT/GPT-2; RMSNorm in most recent LLMs (cheaper, equally good).
  • Pre-LN (normalize each sublayer's input) trains deep stacks more stably than the original Post-LN and needs less warmup. A final normalization sits before the output head.

docs.title: Three ways to use the block
docs.text:
Architecture Attention Training objective Examples Best for Encoder-only Bidirectional Masked-token prediction BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa Classification, extraction, embeddings, reranking Decoder-only Causal Next-token prediction GPT series, LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, Claude-style chat models Generation, chat, general-purpose LLMs Encoder–decoder Bidirectional encoder; causal decoder with cross-attention to the encoder Span corruption or seq2seq Original Transformer, T5, BART, Whisper Translation, summarization, speech recognition

Cross-attention: queries come from the decoder; keys and values come from the encoder's outputs. It's how a decoder "reads" the source sentence or the audio.

Why decoder-only won for general LLMs: one simple objective (predict the next token) uses every token of every document as a training signal, scales cleanly, and frames every task as text continuation, so a single model can do translation, summarization, coding and chat. Inference also benefits from caching keys and values. Encoders remain the right tool for cheap, fast embeddings and classifiers.

docs.title: Tokenization
docs.text:
The problem: word-level vocabularies explode and can't represent new words; character-level sequences are too long.

Core idea: split text into subword units: common words become single tokens, rare words are built from pieces.

Byte-pair encoding (BPE): start from characters (or bytes), count adjacent pairs across the corpus, merge the most frequent pair into a new token, and repeat until the vocabulary reaches the target size. Encoding new text applies the learned merges in order.

BPE on a tiny corpus

Corpus: "low" ×5, "lower" ×2, "newest" ×6, "widest" ×3. Starting from characters, the most frequent pairs are "e s" and "s t" (9 times each, from newest and widest). Merging "e s" gives "es", and then "es t" (9) becomes "est"; breaking the tie the other way gives "st" then "e st", reaching the same token. Next come "l o" (7) → "lo" and "lo w" (7) → "low", and so on. Frequent words end up as single tokens, and an unseen word like "lowest" is still encodable as "low" + "est".

Tokenizer How merges are chosen Used by Byte-level BPE Most frequent pair, over bytes, so any text is representable (no unknown token) GPT-2 onward, LLaMA 3 WordPiece The pair that most increases likelihood BERT Unigram LM (SentencePiece) Start large and prune tokens that least reduce likelihood; treats spaces as a symbol T5, earlier LLaMA, many multilingual models

Vocabulary size (typically 32k–256k) is a trade-off: larger vocabularies give shorter sequences (cheaper attention, more text per context window) but a larger embedding matrix and output softmax, and rarer tokens with less training signal.

Quirks tokenization explains: counting letters in a word ("strawberry" may be 2–3 tokens, so the model never sees individual letters), digit-by-digit arithmetic, sensitivity to leading spaces and capitalization, and non-English text costing more tokens per word (higher cost and shorter effective context).

docs.title: Embeddings and the output head
docs.text: Token IDs index an embedding matrix of shape \((V, d)\). The output head maps the final hidden state back to \(V\) logits. Many models tie these two matrices (use the same weights), which saves \(V \times d\) parameters and often helps smaller models; many large models leave them untied.

docs.title: Counting parameters and FLOPs
docs.text:
Per block, ignoring biases and norms: attention \(4d^2\) + FFN \(8d^2\) = \(12d^2\).

Worked example: a 7B-class model

With \(d = 4096\) and \(L = 32\) layers: \(12 \times 4096^2 \times 32 \approx 6.4\) billion parameters in the blocks. A 32,000-token vocabulary adds \(32{,}000 \times 4096 \approx 131\) million for embeddings, doubled if the output head is untied. Total: about 6.7 billion, which is LLaMA-7B's size.

FLOPs per token: a forward pass costs about \(2N\) FLOPs for a model with \(N\) parameters (one multiply and one add per weight), plus attention's \(O(n \cdot d)\) per layer for a context of length \(n\). Training (forward plus backward) costs about \(6N\) per token, so training a 7B model on 2 trillion tokens needs about \(6 \times 7\times10^9 \times 2\times10^{12} \approx 8.4\times10^{22}\) FLOPs.

docs.title: Training and inference
docs.text:
• Training (teacher forcing): feed the whole sequence at once; the causal mask lets every position predict its next token in parallel; the loss is cross-entropy averaged over positions.
  • Inference (autoregressive): generate one token at a time, appending each to the input. Recomputing everything for each new token would be wasteful, so implementations cache past keys and values (the KV cache). See Efficient Attention and Inference & Serving.

docs.title: Code: attention from scratch
docs.text:
import numpy as np

def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    x = x - x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)        # numerical stability
    e = np.exp(x)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

def scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V, causal=False):
    """Q: (..., n, d_k), K: (..., m, d_k), V: (..., m, d_v) -> (..., n, d_v)."""
    d_k = Q.shape[-1]
    scores = Q @ K.swapaxes(-1, -2) / np.sqrt(d_k)  # (..., n, m)
    if causal:
        n, m = scores.shape[-2:]
        future = np.triu(np.ones((n, m), dtype=bool), k=1)
        scores = np.where(future, -1e9, scores)     # large negative instead of -inf avoids NaNs
    weights = softmax(scores, axis=-1)
    return weights @ V

def multi_head_attention(X, W_q, W_k, W_v, W_o, num_heads, causal=True):
    """X: (n, d_model); each W: (d_model, d_model)."""
    n, d_model = X.shape
    d_head = d_model // num_heads

    def split_heads(T):                             # (n, d_model) -> (heads, n, d_head)
        return T.reshape(n, num_heads, d_head).transpose(1, 0, 2)

    Q, K, V = (split_heads(X @ W) for W in (W_q, W_k, W_v))
    heads = scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V, causal)  # (heads, n, d_head)
    concat = heads.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(n, d_model)  # join heads back
    return concat @ W_o

Be ready to explain every shape, why the mask uses a large negative number, and how you'd add a padding mask (combine it with the causal mask before the softmax).

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Explain queries, keys and values intuitively.

Each token produces three vectors from its embedding. The query says what the token is looking for, each key says what a token can be matched on, and each value is the content a token contributes if attended to. The dot product of a query with every key scores relevance; softmax turns scores into weights; the output is the weighted sum of values. Separating keys from values lets what you match on differ from what you pass along.

Why divide by √d_k in attention?

For random vectors with unit-variance components, \(q \cdot k\) has variance \(d_k\), so with large head dimensions the raw scores have large magnitude. Softmax of large scores is nearly one-hot, with gradients close to zero, which stalls training. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) keeps the scores' variance around 1 so softmax stays in a range with useful gradients.

What are the time and memory costs of self-attention?

Computing \(QK^\top\) and multiplying by \(V\) costs \(O(n^2 d)\) time per layer for \(n\) tokens and dimension \(d\), and storing the attention matrix costs \(O(n^2)\) memory per head. Projections and the FFN cost \(O(n d^2)\). So attention dominates for long sequences. In exchange, all positions are processed in parallel and any two tokens interact in one step. FlashAttention removes the \(O(n^2)\) memory without changing the result.

What does the causal mask do, and why use −∞ rather than 0?

It stops each position from attending to later positions, so during training position \(t\) predicts token \(t+1\) without seeing it, and every position can be trained in parallel. The mask is applied to the scores before softmax: setting a score to \(-\infty\) makes its weight \(e^{-\infty} = 0\) after normalization. Setting the weight to 0 after softmax would break normalization; setting the score to 0 would still give the future token a positive weight.

Why use multiple attention heads instead of one big head?

One softmax yields a single distribution of attention per token, which must average over all the kinds of relationships at once. Several narrower heads can each attend to different positions for different reasons (previous token, subject of the sentence, matching brackets) and their outputs are combined. Because each head has dimension \(d/h\), the total compute and parameters match one full-width head.

How many parameters are in a multi-head attention layer, and in a Transformer block?

Attention: \(W_Q\), \(W_K\), \(W_V\) and \(W_O\), each \(d \times d\), so \(4d^2\) (plus \(4d\) for biases if used), independent of the number of heads. FFN with a \(4d\) hidden layer: \(2 \times d \times 4d = 8d^2\). A block is therefore about \(12d^2\), plus small normalization parameters. With grouped-query attention, \(W_K\) and \(W_V\) shrink in proportion to the number of key–value heads.

Why does a Transformer need positional encoding?

Self-attention treats its input as a set: permuting the tokens permutes the outputs identically, so without position information word order is invisible. Positional encodings inject order, either by adding position vectors to the embeddings (sinusoidal, learned) or by making attention scores depend on relative position (relative biases, RoPE, ALiBi).

Explain RoPE intuitively.

RoPE rotates each two-dimensional slice of the query and key vectors by an angle proportional to the token's position, with different slices rotating at different frequencies. A dot product between two rotated vectors depends only on the difference of their angles, so the attention score between positions \(m\) and \(n\) depends on \(m - n\): relative position, encoded without extra parameters and inside the attention computation itself. Context can be extended later by rescaling the frequencies (position interpolation, NTK scaling, YaRN).

Compare sinusoidal, learned, RoPE and ALiBi positional encodings.

Sinusoidal: fixed, added to embeddings, no parameters, weak extrapolation in practice. Learned absolute: a vector per position, flexible, but capped at the trained length. RoPE: rotates queries and keys so scores depend on relative position; the default in modern LLMs; extendable with frequency scaling. ALiBi: adds a linear distance penalty per head to the scores; extrapolates well beyond the training length but imposes a recency bias.

What does the feed-forward network in a Transformer block do?

It's a two-layer MLP applied to each token independently, usually widening to about \(4d\) with a GELU or SwiGLU non-linearity. Attention mixes information across tokens; the FFN transforms each token's representation, adding non-linear capacity. It holds most of the block's parameters, and interpretability research suggests FFN layers store much factual knowledge as key–value-like associations. MoE layers replace it with many expert FFNs.

Why does the Transformer use residual connections and layer normalization?

Residual connections give each sublayer an identity path, so gradients reach early layers directly and each sublayer only needs to learn a refinement; without them, deep stacks are very hard to train. Normalization keeps activations at a stable scale across layers, which allows higher learning rates. Pre-LN (normalizing each sublayer's input) preserves a clean residual path and is more stable for deep models than Post-LN.

Encoder-only vs decoder-only vs encoder–decoder: when do you use each?

Encoder-only (BERT): bidirectional context, ideal for classification, entity extraction, embeddings and rerankers; small and fast. Decoder-only (GPT, LLaMA): causal attention and next-token prediction, ideal for generation and general-purpose assistants. Encoder–decoder (T5, BART, Whisper): a bidirectional encoder for the input plus a decoder with cross-attention, strong when input and output are different sequences, as in translation, summarization and speech recognition.

Why are most LLMs decoder-only?

Next-token prediction turns every token of raw text into a training example and scales smoothly with data and compute. Any task can be phrased as text in, text out, so one model handles everything. The architecture is simpler (one stack, one objective), generation is natural, and the KV cache makes inference efficient. At large scale it matched or beat encoder–decoder models on most tasks, so the field converged on it.

What is cross-attention?

Attention where the queries come from one sequence and the keys and values from another. In an encoder–decoder model, each decoder layer has a cross-attention sublayer whose queries come from the decoder's states and whose keys and values come from the encoder's output, letting the decoder consult the source while generating. Multimodal models use the same mechanism to attend from text to image features, and diffusion models use it to condition on text.

How does BPE tokenization work?

Start with a vocabulary of characters (or bytes). Repeatedly find the most frequent adjacent pair of tokens in the training corpus and merge it into a new token, recording the merge, until the vocabulary reaches the target size. To tokenize new text, apply the merges in the learned order. Frequent words become single tokens and rare words split into subwords, so there's no unknown-word problem (with byte-level BPE, any string is representable).

Why can LLMs struggle to count the letters in a word?

They don't see letters. "strawberry" might be tokenized as two or three subword tokens, so the model must have memorized the spelling of each token to count characters, and that information is only indirectly present in training data. The same applies to digits in arithmetic (numbers split into irregular chunks). Reasoning step by step, spelling the word out, or using a code tool works around it.

How does vocabulary size affect a model?

A larger vocabulary encodes text in fewer tokens, so more fits in the context window and attention is cheaper per document, and multilingual coverage improves. But the embedding and output matrices grow (\(V \times d\) each), the output softmax costs more, and rare tokens get little training signal. Smaller vocabularies mean longer sequences. Modern LLMs use roughly 32k to 256k tokens.

What is weight tying?

Using the same matrix for the input token embeddings and the output projection to vocabulary logits (transposed). It saves \(V \times d\) parameters, which is significant for small models with large vocabularies, and often improves quality because both directions learn a shared representation of each token. Larger models often untie them for extra capacity.

Estimate the parameter count of a 32-layer Transformer with d = 4096.

Each block has about \(12d^2\) parameters (\(4d^2\) attention, \(8d^2\) FFN): \(12 \times 4096^2 \approx 201\) million per layer, so about 6.4 billion for 32 layers. Add embeddings: vocabulary × \(d\), for example \(32{,}000 \times 4096 \approx 131\) million (twice that if the output head is untied). Total about 6.7 billion, matching LLaMA-7B.

How many FLOPs does it take to train a model?

Roughly \(6N\) FLOPs per training token for \(N\) parameters: about \(2N\) for the forward pass and \(4N\) for the backward pass. So training cost ≈ \(6ND\) for \(D\) tokens. For a 7B model on 2T tokens: \(6 \times 7\times10^9 \times 2\times10^{12} = 8.4\times10^{22}\) FLOPs. At a sustained \(4\times10^{14}\) FLOP/s per GPU that's about \(2.1\times10^8\) GPU-seconds, roughly 58,000 GPU-hours. This ignores attention's extra cost for long contexts.

How is a Transformer trained versus how it generates text?

In training, the entire sequence is fed at once and the causal mask lets every position predict its next token in parallel with teacher forcing; the loss is the average cross-entropy. In generation, the model produces one token at a time: run the prompt (prefill), sample a token, append it, and repeat. To avoid recomputing keys and values for all previous tokens at every step, they're cached (KV cache), so each new token costs time proportional to the context length.

How does attention compare with convolution and recurrence in its built-in assumptions?

Convolution assumes locality and translation equivariance; recurrence assumes sequential order and a compressed running state. Attention assumes almost nothing: any token can interact with any other, with content-dependent weights. That flexibility makes it powerful and general but data-hungry, and position must be added explicitly. With enough data, the weaker assumptions win; with little data, the stronger biases of CNNs or RNNs can help.

What are induction heads?

A pair of attention heads, often in consecutive layers, that implement "find where the current token appeared before and predict the token that followed it". The first head copies information about the previous token into each position; the second searches for earlier positions whose previous token matches the current one and copies what came next. They appear abruptly during training and are thought to underlie much of in-context learning, such as repeating patterns and copying from the prompt.

Common mistakes

  • Saying the scaling is by \(d_{model}\) instead of \(\sqrt{d_k}\).
  • Claiming multi-head attention has more parameters than single-head attention of the same width.
  • Applying the causal mask after the softmax.
  • Forgetting that self-attention is permutation-invariant without positional information.
  • Confusing cross-attention with self-attention.
  • Quoting attention as \(O(n^2)\) without mentioning the \(O(nd^2)\) terms that dominate short sequences.

docs.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimates
docs.text:
Interviewers love these because they show you understand where cost comes from. Say the formula, plug in round numbers, and state the assumption.

Training computeServing memoryDecode speedFine-tuning memoryEmbedding storage

How long to train a 7B model on 2T tokens?

\(C \approx 6ND = 6 \times 7\times10^9 \times 2\times10^{12} \approx 8.4\times10^{22}\) FLOPs. At a sustained \(4\times10^{14}\) FLOP/s per GPU (about 40% of a modern accelerator's BF16 peak): \(2.1\times10^{8}\) GPU-seconds ≈ 58,000 GPU-hours, about 25 days on 100 GPUs.

What does it take to serve a 70B model?

Weights: \(70\times10^9 \times 2\) bytes ≈ 140 GB in BF16, 70 GB in 8-bit, 35 GB in 4-bit. KV cache with GQA (80 layers, 8 KV heads of 128): \(2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 \approx 0.33\) MB per token, so 32 concurrent 4K-token requests add about 43 GB. BF16 therefore needs at least two 80 GB GPUs, and realistically four for that load; 4-bit weights fit on one.

What's the fastest a 7B model can generate at batch size 1?

Each token reads all the weights: 14 GB in FP16. At about 3 TB/s of memory bandwidth that's at least 4.7 ms per token, so ≈ 210 tokens/s at most. 4-bit weights (3.5 GB) raise the ceiling about fourfold; batching shares each weight read across sequences.

Can you fully fine-tune 7B on one 80 GB GPU?

Not with plain Adam: 16 bytes per parameter ≈ 112 GB before activations. Options: shard across GPUs (FSDP or ZeRO), 8-bit optimizers and gradient checkpointing, or LoRA (≈ 14 GB BF16 base plus small extras) or QLoRA (≈ 4–6 GB base).

How much memory for 1 billion item embeddings?

\(10^9 \times 128\) dimensions × 4 bytes ≈ 512 GB in float32. Product quantization to 32 bytes per item ≈ 32 GB, small enough for a few machines, at the cost of approximate distances (rerank the top results with full vectors).

docs.text: Quantity Value English text per token ≈ 4 characters ≈ 0.75 words Starting loss of a classifier ≈ \(\ln K\) for \(K\) classes (\(\ln 10 \approx 2.3\); 50K-token vocabulary ≈ 10.8) z-values 1.96 for 95%, 2.58 for 99% (two-sided) Distinct rows in a bootstrap sample ≈ 63.2% (\(1 - 1/e\)) Transformer MLP width 4 × \(d\); ≈ \(\frac{8}{3}\) × \(d\) with SwiGLU to keep the parameter count A 7B Llama-style model 32 layers, \(d = 4096\), 32 heads of 128 KV cache per token 7B with MHA ≈ 0.5 MB; 70B with GQA ≈ 0.33 MB (FP16) Bytes per parameter 4 (FP32), 2 (BF16), 1 (INT8/FP8), 0.5 (INT4) Full fine-tuning with Adam ≈ 16 bytes per parameter + activations QLoRA headline 65B fine-tuned on one 48 GB GPU Chinchilla-optimal data ≈ 20 tokens per parameter PPO clip, DPO β \(\epsilon \approx 0.2\); β typically 0.1–0.5 RRF constant \(k = 60\) Agent error compounding 95% per step over 20 steps ≈ 36% end to end

docs.title: Classical models at a glance
docs.text: Model Strengths Weaknesses Cost Linear / logistic regression Fast, interpretable, well-calibrated (logistic) Linear boundary; needs feature work \(O(nd)\) per epoch kNN No training; flexible boundary Slow queries; curse of dimensionality; needs scaling \(O(nd)\) per query Naive Bayes Works with little data; strong text baseline Independence assumption; poor probabilities \(O(nd)\) SVM Max margin; kernels for non-linear boundaries Kernel SVMs slow beyond ~100K rows; no native probabilities \(O(n^2)\)–\(O(n^3)\) training Decision tree Interpretable; no scaling; mixed types Overfits; unstable \(O(d\, n \log n)\) Random forest Robust; little tuning; parallel Large; slower inference; extrapolates poorly Trees × tree cost Gradient boosting (XGBoost, LightGBM) Best accuracy on tabular data Needs tuning; sequential training The tabular default k-means Simple; fast Round, similar-size clusters only; choose \(k\) \(O(nkd)\) per iteration DBSCAN Any cluster shape; flags outliers One density scale; sensitive to \(\epsilon\) \(O(n \log n)\) with an index PCA Fast; linear; invertible Linear only; high variance ≠ useful \(O(nd^2)\), or randomized SVD

docs.title: Optimizers
docs.text: Optimizer Idea Strength Weakness SGD Step against the gradient Simple; often generalizes well Slow in ravines; sensitive to learning rate Momentum, Nesterov Running average of gradients Faster, damps oscillation One more hyperparameter AdaGrad Per-parameter rate from summed \(g^2\) Good for sparse features Learning rate decays toward zero RMSProp Moving average of \(g^2\) Fixes AdaGrad's decay No momentum by default Adam Momentum + RMSProp + bias correction Robust default; fast Two extra states per parameter; L2 interacts badly AdamW Adam with decoupled weight decay Standard for Transformers Same memory as Adam

docs.title: Normalization layers
docs.text: BatchNorm LayerNorm RMSNorm Normalizes over The batch, per channel Each token's features Each token's features, without subtracting the mean Depends on batch size Yes; running statistics at inference No No Typical use CNNs Transformers (original, BERT, GPT-2) Modern LLMs (Llama and most since)

docs.title: Attention variants
docs.text: MHA MQA GQA MLA Key/value heads \(h\) 1 \(g\) groups, \(1 < g < h\) Compressed latent per token KV cache Largest ÷ \(h\) ÷ \(h/g\) Much smaller than GQA Quality Reference Some loss Close to MHA Close to MHA Examples Original Transformer, GPT-3 PaLM, Falcon Llama 2 70B, Llama 3, Mistral DeepSeek-V2, V3

docs.title: Distributed training
docs.text: Strategy Splits Communication Use when Data parallel (DDP) The batch; full replica per GPU All-reduce gradients The model fits on one GPU ZeRO / FSDP Optimizer state, gradients and weights across data-parallel ranks All-gather weights, reduce-scatter gradients Model state doesn't fit on one GPU Tensor parallel Matrices inside each layer All-reduce in every layer (needs fast links) Very wide layers, within a node Pipeline parallel Layers into stages Activations between stages; idle "bubbles" Very deep models, across nodes Sequence / context parallel The sequence dimension Attention blocks exchanged between GPUs (ring attention) Very long contexts Expert parallel MoE experts across GPUs All-to-all token routing Mixture-of-experts models

docs.title: Fine-tuning methods
docs.text: Method Trains Memory Notes Full fine-tuning All weights ≈ 16 bytes per parameter Highest ceiling; risk of forgetting LoRA Low-rank adapters, typically 0.1–1% of parameters BF16 base + small optimizer state Mergeable; swap adapters per task QLoRA LoRA on a frozen 4-bit (NF4) base ≈ 0.5–0.6 bytes per base parameter Close to 16-bit LoRA quality Adapters, prefix and prompt tuning Small inserted modules or virtual tokens Tiny Mostly superseded by LoRA Distillation A small student on a teacher's outputs Student-sized Cheap serving for a narrow task

docs.title: Alignment methods
docs.text: Method Needs Strength Weakness SFT Demonstrations Simple and stable Imitates; capped by data quality RLHF with PPO Preferences → reward model → on-policy RL Flexible; optimizes any reward Four models in memory; unstable; reward hacking DPO Preference pairs No reward model or sampling; simple Offline; can over-fit the preference data RLAIF / Constitutional AI Written principles + AI feedback Scales labeling Inherits the judge's biases GRPO with verifiable rewards Checkable tasks (tests, final answers) No critic; drives reasoning Only where answers can be verified; shortcut hacking

docs.title: Decoding strategies
docs.text: Strategy How Use Greedy Most likely token each step Deterministic; prone to repetition Beam search Keep the best \(B\) partial sequences Translation and short outputs; bland for chat Temperature Divide logits by \(T\) The creativity knob Top-k Sample from the \(k\) most likely tokens Fixed cut that ignores confidence Top-p (nucleus) Smallest set with probability mass ≥ \(p\) Adapts to the model's confidence Constrained decoding Mask tokens that would break a schema or grammar Guaranteed parseable output

docs.title: Vector indexes
docs.text: Index How Strength Weakness Flat Compare with every vector Exact \(O(n)\) per query IVF Cluster; search the nearest nprobe lists Compact, fast Recall depends on nprobe; retrain on drift HNSW Layered proximity graph, greedy search High recall at low latency Memory-heavy; slow builds and deletes PQ, IVF-PQ Compress vectors into short codes Many times smaller Approximate distances; rerank with full vectors

docs.title: Which approach for an LLM application?
docs.text: Need Reach for The model lacks facts or private knowledge RAG Format, tone or style is wrong Prompting first, then SFT or LoRA A narrow, high-volume task where cost matters Fine-tune or distill a small model A small, stable corpus that fits in the window Long context plus prompt caching Steps that can't be known in advance An agent with tools; otherwise a fixed workflow Many tools across many applications MCP servers Untrusted content reaching a model with tools Least privilege, approvals, isolation

docs.title: Flashcard Drill
docs.text:
Every interview question on every page of this site is in this deck, so new questions show up here on their own. Pick a section or a single page, answer out loud before you reveal the answer, then mark it honestly.

Loading questions…

docs.title: How the drill works
docs.text:
You do What happens Show answer (Space) Reveals the full answer from the topic page, with math and tables Review again (1) The question is marked weak and comes back about twice as often as an unseen one I knew it (2) The question is marked known and comes back rarely, so you still revisit it Skip (3) Moves on without changing anything
  • With Ask unseen and "review again" questions more often switched on, the drill weights its picks: review again ×6, unseen ×3, known ×1. Switch it off for uniform random picks.
  • The link above each card opens the topic page, where the question sits in context with diagrams and the questions around it.
  • Your marks are saved in this browser only. To move them to another browser or device, use Export and Import on My Progress.

A 15-minute daily routine

  1. Five minutes on All sections to keep everything warm.
  2. Ten minutes on the section you're studying this week.
  3. In the last week before an interview, drill only the sections the role emphasizes; the study plans list them by role.

Answer the way you would in the room

Mark I knew it only when your spoken answer covered the core idea, the mechanism, and at least one trade-off or failure mode. Recognizing the answer when you see it doesn't count: interviews test recall, not recognition.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Short definitions of the terms used on this site. Each links to the page that explains it in context. Abbreviations also show their expansion when you hover over them anywhere on the site.

A · B · C · D · E · F · G · H · I · K · L · M · N · O · P · Q · R · S · T · U · V · W · X–Z

docs.title: A
docs.text: A/B test A randomized experiment that compares a control and a treatment on live traffic, sized in advance for a minimum detectable effect. Evaluation A2A (Agent2Agent) An open protocol for agents to discover each other through agent cards and delegate tasks, with streamed status updates and artifacts. It complements MCP, which connects an agent to tools and data. MCP & A2A Activation function The non-linearity after a layer (ReLU, GELU, SiLU, tanh, sigmoid). Without it, stacked layers collapse into one linear map. Neural networks Adam, AdamW An adaptive optimizer that combines momentum with per-parameter step sizes and bias correction. AdamW applies weight decay separately from the adaptive step, and is the default for Transformers. Training Advantage How much better an action is than the policy's average in that state, \(A = Q - V\). Policy-gradient methods weight updates by it. RL essentials Agent An LLM running in a loop that chooses its own next action, calls tools, observes the results, and stops when the goal is met. Contrast with a fixed workflow. AI agents Agent harness Everything around the model in an agent: the loop, tools, sandbox, permissions, context management, verification, state, tracing and evals. Harness engineering ALiBi A position method that adds a distance-proportional penalty to attention scores instead of position embeddings, which helps with longer inputs than seen in training. Transformer Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search Index structures such as HNSW, IVF and product quantization that find close vectors quickly by giving up exactness. Embeddings Attention A weighted average of value vectors, with weights from the similarity of a query to each key. It lets every token read directly from every other token. Transformer AUC (ROC-AUC) The area under the ROC curve: the probability that a random positive is scored above a random negative. Evaluation Autoencoder A network trained to reconstruct its input through a narrow bottleneck, which forces a compressed representation. Generative models Autoregressive model A model that generates one token at a time, each conditioned on everything before it. GPT-style LLMs are autoregressive. Pretraining

docs.title: B
docs.text: Backpropagation Reverse-mode automatic differentiation: the chain rule applied backward through the network, giving the gradient for every parameter in one pass. Neural networks Bagging Training models on bootstrap samples of the data and averaging them to reduce variance. Random forests are bagged trees. Trees & ensembles Batch normalization Normalizing activations with the mean and variance of the current batch, per channel, then rescaling. It speeds up and stabilizes CNN training. Training Beam search Decoding that keeps the \(B\) most likely partial sequences at each step. Good for translation; bland for open-ended chat. Pretraining BERT An encoder-only Transformer pretrained by predicting masked tokens from both sides. Strong for classification, extraction and embeddings. Pretraining Bias–variance trade-off Expected error splits into bias squared (the model is too simple), variance (it's too sensitive to the training sample) and irreducible noise. ML fundamentals BM25 A keyword ranking function built from term frequency (with saturation), inverse document frequency and document-length normalization. RAG Boosting Adding weak learners one at a time, each correcting the errors of the ensemble so far, which reduces bias. Trees & ensembles Bradley–Terry model Models the probability that response A is preferred over B as \(\sigma(r_A - r_B)\). It's the loss used to train reward models on preference pairs. Post-training Byte-pair encoding (BPE) A tokenizer that starts from bytes or characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token. Transformer

docs.title: C
docs.text: Calibration Whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies: of all cases predicted at 0.8, about 80% should be positive. Fixed with Platt scaling, isotonic regression or temperature scaling. Evaluation Catastrophic forgetting Losing earlier capabilities when fine-tuning on new data. Reduced with lower learning rates, mixing in general data, or PEFT. Fine-tuning Chain-of-thought (CoT) Having a model write intermediate reasoning steps before its answer, through prompting or training. Reasoning Chinchilla scaling The finding that compute-optimal training scales parameters and data together, about 20 tokens per parameter. Pretraining Chunking Splitting documents into retrievable pieces for RAG, ideally along their structure and with some overlap. RAG Classifier-free guidance Steering a diffusion model toward its condition by extrapolating from the unconditional prediction toward the conditional one. Generative models CLIP Image and text encoders trained contrastively so matching pairs embed close together, which enables zero-shot image classification. CNNs & vision Cold start Recommending for new users or new items that have no interaction history. Recommender systems Collaborative filtering Recommending from the interaction patterns of similar users or similar items, without item content. Recommender systems Compaction Summarizing an agent's history when the context window fills, keeping decisions and open issues and dropping raw tool output. Context engineering Concept drift A change in \(P(y \mid x)\): the same inputs now lead to different outcomes. MLOps Constitutional AI Alignment that uses a written set of principles, with the model critiquing and revising its own outputs and AI feedback replacing much human labeling (RLAIF). Post-training Context engineering Choosing what enters the model's context window at each step (instructions, tools, retrieved data, memory, history, tool results) to get the most signal per token. Context engineering Context rot The drop in a model's recall and reasoning quality as its context window fills with more tokens. Context engineering Continuous batching Adding and removing requests from the running batch at every decode step, so the GPU stays busy. Inference Contrastive learning Learning embeddings by pulling matching pairs together and pushing non-matching pairs apart, for example with the InfoNCE loss. Embeddings Convolution Sliding a small learned filter over the input. It gives locality, weight sharing and translation equivariance. CNNs & vision Covariate shift A change in the input distribution \(P(x)\) while \(P(y \mid x)\) stays the same. MLOps Cross-encoder A model that reads the query and a document together to score relevance. Accurate but too slow for first-stage retrieval, so it's used for reranking. Embeddings Cross-entropy The negative log of the probability given to the correct class, averaged over examples: the negative log-likelihood for classification. Math for ML Cross-validation Estimating generalization by training and validating on several different splits; for time series, always train on the past and validate on the future. ML fundamentals Curse of dimensionality In high dimensions data becomes sparse and distances between points become similar, so nearest neighbors carry less information. ML fundamentals

docs.title: D
docs.text: Data leakage Information unavailable at prediction time leaking into training, such as future data or preprocessing fitted on the full dataset. It inflates offline results. ML fundamentals DBSCAN Density-based clustering that finds clusters of any shape and labels points in sparse regions as noise. Unsupervised Decision tree A model that splits data on feature thresholds, choosing each split to reduce impurity the most. Trees & ensembles Decoder-only Transformer A stack of causal self-attention blocks trained to predict the next token: the architecture of GPT-style LLMs. Transformer Diffusion model A generative model that learns to reverse a gradual noising process, and generates by denoising step by step from pure noise. Generative models Distillation Training a smaller student model to match a larger teacher's outputs or reasoning traces. Fine-tuning DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) Aligning a model on preference pairs with a classification-style loss, with no separate reward model and no RL sampling. Post-training Dropout Randomly zeroing activations during training so the network can't rely on any single unit; switched off at inference. Training

docs.title: E
docs.text: Early stopping Stopping training when the validation metric stops improving, a simple and effective regularizer. Training ELBO The evidence lower bound a VAE maximizes: reconstruction quality minus the KL divergence of the latent distribution from the prior. Generative models Embedding A dense vector representation in which similar items are close together. Embeddings Encoder–decoder An architecture in which an encoder reads the input and a decoder generates the output while attending to it, as in the original Transformer and T5. Sequence models Ensemble Combining several models' predictions to beat any single one, by bagging, boosting or stacking. Trees & ensembles Evals Test suites for LLM systems: a dataset of cases, graders (code, model or human) and metrics tracked across versions. Evaluating LLM systems Exploding gradients Gradients that grow exponentially through layers or time steps. Fixed with gradient clipping, careful initialization and normalization. Neural networks

docs.title: F
docs.text: F1 score The harmonic mean of precision and recall, a single number for an imbalanced positive class. Evaluation Feature store A system that serves the same feature definitions for training (point-in-time correct) and for online inference, preventing training–serving skew. MLOps Few-shot prompting Putting a few worked examples in the prompt to show the task and output format. Prompting Fine-tuning Continuing to train a pretrained model on task- or domain-specific data. Fine-tuning FlashAttention Exact attention computed in on-chip memory tiles with an online softmax, so the \(n \times n\) score matrix is never written to GPU memory. Efficient attention Flow matching Training a model to follow a velocity field that carries noise to data along near-straight paths, which allows fewer sampling steps than classic diffusion. Generative models FSDP, ZeRO Sharding optimizer state, gradients and weights across data-parallel GPUs, so models too large for one GPU can be trained. Fine-tuning Function calling See tool calling.

docs.title: G
docs.text: GAN A generator and a discriminator trained against each other. Produces sharp samples, but training is unstable and prone to mode collapse. Generative models GELU, SiLU Smooth, ReLU-like activation functions used in Transformers. Neural networks Gradient boosting Boosting in which each new tree fits the negative gradient of the loss; XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost are implementations. Trees & ensembles Gradient checkpointing Saving memory by storing only some activations and recomputing the rest during the backward pass. Fine-tuning Gradient clipping Rescaling gradients whose norm exceeds a threshold, preventing a single huge update. Training Gradient descent Repeatedly moving parameters a small step against the gradient of the loss. Math for ML Grounding Basing an answer on supplied sources, with citations, rather than on the model's memorized knowledge. RAG GQA (grouped-query attention) Groups of query heads share one key/value head, which shrinks the KV cache with little quality loss. Efficient attention Greedy decoding Always choosing the most likely next token. Deterministic but prone to repetition. Pretraining GRPO Group Relative Policy Optimization: PPO-style RL that samples a group of answers per prompt and uses each answer's reward, normalized within the group, as its advantage, with no critic model. Reasoning Guardrails Checks around an LLM (input and output classifiers, validators, policy filters, permission limits) that block or repair unsafe or invalid behavior. Security

docs.title: H
docs.text: Hallucination Fluent, confident output that is false or not supported by the provided sources. Pretraining Hinge loss The SVM loss \(\max(0, 1 - y f(x))\): zero for points beyond the margin on the correct side. kNN, NB & SVM HNSW A layered proximity-graph index for approximate nearest-neighbor search: high recall at low latency, but memory-heavy. Embeddings Human in the loop Requiring a person to approve high-impact actions, or to review predictions the system is unsure about. AI agents Hybrid search Combining keyword (BM25) and dense vector retrieval, usually merged with reciprocal rank fusion. RAG HyDE Hypothetical document embeddings: the LLM writes a plausible answer, and that answer's embedding is used to search. RAG Hyperparameter A setting chosen before training, such as learning rate, depth or regularization strength, tuned on validation data. ML fundamentals

docs.title: I
docs.text: In-context learning Performing a new task from instructions and examples in the prompt, with no weight updates. Prompting Inductive bias The assumptions built into a model's design, such as locality and weight sharing in CNNs. CNNs & vision Instruction tuning Supervised fine-tuning on instruction–response pairs so a base model follows instructions. Post-training IVF index An inverted-file index that clusters vectors and searches only the clusters nearest the query. Embeddings

docs.title: K
docs.text: k-means Clustering that alternates between assigning points to their nearest centroid and moving each centroid to the mean of its points. Unsupervised k-nearest neighbors (kNN) Predicting from the labels of the \(k\) closest training points. kNN, NB & SVM Kernel trick Computing dot products in a high-dimensional feature space through a kernel function, without ever building the features. kNN, NB & SVM KL divergence An asymmetric measure of how one probability distribution differs from another. Used as a penalty in RLHF and inside the VAE objective. Math for ML KV cache The stored keys and values of past tokens, so each decode step computes attention only for the new token. Efficient attention

docs.title: L
docs.text: L1 and L2 regularization Penalizing the absolute size (L1, which zeroes weights) or squared size (L2, which shrinks them) of weights to reduce overfitting. ML fundamentals Label smoothing Training on softened targets, such as 0.9 for the true class, to reduce overconfidence. Training Layer normalization Normalizing each token's features to zero mean and unit variance, independent of the batch; the standard in Transformers, often as RMSNorm. Training Learning-rate schedule Changing the learning rate during training, typically a short warmup followed by cosine or linear decay. Training LLM-as-judge Grading outputs with a language model and a rubric. Scales well, but has position, length and self-preference biases, so calibrate it against human labels. Evaluating LLM systems Logistic regression A linear score passed through a sigmoid and trained with log loss, for classification. Linear models Logit An unnormalized score before a sigmoid or softmax; for logistic regression, the log-odds. Linear models LoRA Fine-tuning by learning a low-rank update \(\Delta W = BA\) on frozen weights; the update can be merged in, so serving has no added latency. Fine-tuning LSTM A recurrent network with gated memory cells that update additively, preserving gradients over long sequences. Sequence models

docs.title: M
docs.text: Mamba A selective state-space model: a linear recurrence whose parameters depend on the input, giving linear time and constant memory per token. Efficient attention MAP estimation Choosing parameters that maximize likelihood times prior; regularization is a prior in disguise. Math for ML Masked language modeling Predicting randomly hidden tokens from the context on both sides: BERT's pretraining objective. Pretraining MCP (Model Context Protocol) An open protocol through which applications connect models to tools, resources and prompts exposed by servers, turning N × M integrations into N + M. MCP & A2A Memory (agents) What an agent keeps beyond the current context window: summaries, notes and to-do files, or a store of facts it searches when relevant. AI agents Mixed precision Computing in 16-bit floats while keeping 32-bit master weights, for speed and memory savings. Fine-tuning Mixture of experts (MoE) Layers with many expert networks and a router that sends each token to a few of them, growing parameters without growing compute per token. Efficient attention MLA (multi-head latent attention) Compressing keys and values into a small latent vector per token, shrinking the KV cache well below GQA's. Used in DeepSeek-V2 and V3. Efficient attention MLE (maximum likelihood estimation) Choosing the parameters that make the observed data most probable. Math for ML MLOps Practices and tools for getting models into production and keeping them working: pipelines, registries, deployment, monitoring and retraining. MLOps Model registry A versioned store of trained models with their metrics, lineage and approval status. MLOps MQA (multi-query attention) All query heads share a single key/value head: the smallest KV cache, with some quality loss. Efficient attention Multi-head attention Several attention heads in parallel, each with its own projections, so the model can track several relationships at once. Transformer Multimodal model (VLM) A model that takes images (or audio) and text, usually a vision encoder connected to an LLM through a projection. Generative models

docs.title: N
docs.text: Naive Bayes A classifier that applies Bayes' rule assuming features are independent given the class. kNN, NB & SVM NDCG A ranking metric with graded relevance and a logarithmic discount by position, normalized by the ideal ordering. Evaluation Next-token prediction The pretraining objective of GPT-style models: maximize the probability of each token given all the tokens before it. Pretraining

docs.title: O
docs.text: Out-of-bag error A random forest's built-in validation estimate, computed on the rows each tree didn't see in its bootstrap sample. Trees & ensembles Overfitting Fitting noise in the training data: training error keeps falling while validation error rises. ML fundamentals

docs.title: P
docs.text: PagedAttention Storing the KV cache in fixed-size blocks, like virtual-memory pages, to avoid fragmentation and share common prefixes; introduced by vLLM. Inference PCA Projecting data onto the orthogonal directions of greatest variance: the top eigenvectors of the covariance matrix. Unsupervised PEFT Parameter-efficient fine-tuning: training a small set of added or selected parameters, such as LoRA adapters, instead of all weights. Fine-tuning Perplexity The exponential of the average per-token cross-entropy; lower means the model finds the text less surprising. Pretraining Policy gradient RL methods that move a policy's parameters along \(\nabla \log \pi(a \mid s)\), weighted by how good the action turned out. RL essentials Position bias Users click higher-ranked items more regardless of relevance, so logged clicks overstate what was shown first. ML system design Positional encoding Order information added to attention, which is otherwise order-blind: sinusoidal, learned, RoPE or ALiBi. Transformer PPO Proximal Policy Optimization: policy-gradient RL with a clipped objective that keeps each update close to the previous policy. RL essentials Precision and recall Precision: the share of flagged items that are truly positive. Recall: the share of true positives that were flagged. Evaluation Prefill and decode Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel (compute-bound, sets time to first token); decode generates one token at a time (memory-bound, sets time per token). Inference Prefix (prompt) caching Reusing the KV cache of a repeated prompt prefix across requests, cutting latency and cost. Keep stable content at the start of the prompt. Inference Pretraining Self-supervised training on huge amounts of unlabeled data before any task-specific training. Pretraining PRM and ORM A process reward model scores each reasoning step; an outcome reward model scores only the final answer. Reasoning Product quantization (PQ) Compressing vectors by splitting each into parts and storing a short codebook index for every part. Embeddings Prompt engineering Designing instructions, examples, structure and output formats so a model behaves reliably. Prompting Prompt injection Instructions hidden in user input or in content the model reads (web pages, documents, tool results) that hijack its behavior. Security

docs.title: Q
docs.text: QLoRA LoRA training on top of a frozen base model quantized to 4 bits (NF4). Fine-tuning Quantization Storing weights, and sometimes activations, in fewer bits (8 or 4) for cheaper, faster serving. Fine-tuning Query, key, value The three projections of each token in attention: what it's looking for, what it offers to match, and what it passes on. Transformer

docs.title: R
docs.text: RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) Retrieving relevant documents at query time and putting them in the prompt, so the model answers from them and can cite them. RAG Random forest Bagged decision trees that also consider a random subset of features at each split, to de-correlate the trees. Trees & ensembles ReAct An agent pattern that interleaves reasoning, actions (tool calls) and observations in a loop. AI agents Reasoning model An LLM trained, usually with reinforcement learning, to think at length before answering, trading inference compute for accuracy. Reasoning Recall@k The share of all relevant items that appear in the top \(k\) results; it caps what a RAG generator can use. Evaluation Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) Merging ranked lists by summing \(1/(k + \text{rank})\) for each item across lists, usually with \(k = 60\). RAG Red teaming Deliberately attacking a system with adversarial inputs to find failures before users or attackers do. Security Regularization Anything that discourages fitting noise: weight penalties, dropout, early stopping, data augmentation. ML fundamentals Reinforcement learning (RL) Learning a policy that maximizes reward by interacting with an environment. RL essentials Reranker A slower, more accurate model, often a cross-encoder, that reorders the top retrieved candidates. RAG Residual connection Adding a block's input to its output, \(x + F(x)\), so gradients flow directly and the identity is easy to learn. CNNs & vision Reward hacking A policy exploiting flaws in its reward signal to score well without the intended behavior, such as longer answers or special-cased tests. Post-training Reward model A model trained on human preference pairs to score responses; the optimization target in RLHF. Post-training RLHF Reinforcement learning from human feedback: supervised fine-tuning, then a reward model trained on preferences, then RL (classically PPO) with a KL penalty. Post-training RLVR Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards: training on tasks whose results can be checked automatically, such as math answers or code tests. Reasoning RNN A network that processes a sequence one step at a time, carrying a hidden state forward. Sequence models ROC curve True-positive rate plotted against false-positive rate across all thresholds. Evaluation RoPE Rotary position embedding: rotates query and key vectors by an angle that depends on position, so attention scores depend on relative distance. Transformer

docs.title: S
docs.text: Sandbox An isolated environment where an agent's code and commands run, with limited file, network and credential access. Harness engineering Scaling laws Power-law relationships between a model's loss and its parameters, training data and compute. Pretraining Self-attention Attention in which queries, keys and values all come from the same sequence. Transformer Self-consistency Sampling several reasoning paths and taking the most common final answer. Reasoning Self-supervised learning Learning from labels derived from the data itself, such as the next token or a hidden image patch. Pretraining SFT (supervised fine-tuning) Fine-tuning on curated input–output demonstrations; the first post-training stage. Post-training Shadow deployment Running a new model on live traffic without acting on its predictions, to compare it with the current model safely. MLOps SHAP Feature attributions based on Shapley values from game theory, with consistency guarantees. Responsible AI Softmax Turns a vector of logits into probabilities: \(e^{z_i} / \sum_j e^{z_j}\). Neural networks Sparse vs dense retrieval Matching keywords over sparse term vectors (BM25) versus comparing learned dense embeddings. Embeddings Speculative decoding A small draft model proposes several tokens and the large model checks them in one pass, keeping the large model's output distribution exactly. Inference State-space model (SSM) A sequence model built on a linear recurrence that trains in parallel and runs with constant memory per token, such as S4 and Mamba. Efficient attention Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) Gradient descent that estimates the gradient from a random mini-batch at each step. Training Structured outputs Constraining generation to a JSON schema or grammar so the output always parses. Prompting Sub-agent A separate agent with its own clean context that handles one subtask and returns a condensed result to the main agent. Context engineering Support vector machine (SVM) A classifier that maximizes the margin between classes; kernels make it non-linear. kNN, NB & SVM System prompt The instructions an application gives the model to set its role, rules, tools and context for a conversation. Prompting

docs.title: T
docs.text: t-SNE and UMAP Non-linear methods that map high-dimensional data to 2D or 3D for visualization, preserving local neighborhoods; distances between clusters aren't meaningful. Unsupervised Teacher forcing Training a sequence model on the true previous tokens rather than its own predictions. Sequence models Temperature Dividing logits by \(T\) before the softmax: lower is more deterministic, higher is more varied. Pretraining Tensor and pipeline parallelism Splitting the matrices inside each layer across GPUs, or splitting the layers into stages across GPUs. Fine-tuning TF-IDF Term weights that rise with a word's frequency in a document and fall with its frequency across documents. Sequence models Tokenization Splitting text into the model's vocabulary units, usually subwords learned with BPE or a similar method. Transformer Tool calling The model emits a structured request to call a function described by a schema; the application runs it and returns the result to the model. Tool calling Top-k and top-p sampling Sampling only from the \(k\) most likely tokens, or from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to \(p\). Pretraining Training–serving skew Differences between how features are computed in training and in production, which silently degrade a deployed model. MLOps Transfer learning Reusing a model trained on one task or dataset as the starting point for another. Pretraining Transformer An architecture built from self-attention and feed-forward blocks, with residual connections and normalization. Transformer TTFT (time to first token) Queueing time plus prefill time: how long a user waits before output starts streaming. Inference

Generative models Vanishing gradients Gradients shrinking exponentially through many layers or time steps, so early layers stop learning.
