docs.title: ML Coding from Scratch
docs.text:
TL;DR

ML coding rounds ask you to implement a model, layer, loss or metric cleanly, usually in NumPy or PyTorch, while explaining shapes and trade-offs. The implementations below are tested: they live in code/ml_from_scratch.py, which includes self-tests (python code/ml_from_scratch.py), and this page includes that exact code. Practise writing each one from memory in 10–15 minutes.

Where this fits

Each exercise links back to its concept page. Use the Interview Playbook approach: clarify, state the approach, write the simple version, narrate shapes, test on a tiny example, then discuss improvements.

docs.title: How to approach each exercise
docs.text:
1. Clarify: input shapes and types, edge cases (empty input, ties, all one class), and whether vectorization or a loop is expected.
  2. State the math in one or two lines before coding.
  3. Write the simple, correct version, vectorized with NumPy.
  4. Narrate shapes: "X is (n, d), w is (d,), so X @ w is (n,)."
  5. Test on a tiny example you can verify by hand.
  6. Discuss: numerical stability, complexity, regularization, and how you'd scale it.
Exercise Concept page Frequently asked follow-up Linear regression Linear models Why use lstsq instead of inverting \(X^\top X\)? Logistic regression Linear models Why a stable sigmoid? Add L2 and class weights Softmax and cross-entropy Neural networks Derive the \(p - y\) gradient k-means Unsupervised learning Handle empty clusters; choose \(k\) k-nearest neighbors kNN, NB & SVM Make it fast for millions of points Decision-tree split Trees & ensembles Grow a full tree recursively; regression splits Two-layer MLP with backprop Neural networks Check gradients numerically; add momentum Attention The Transformer Add a padding mask; KV cache Sampling Pretraining & LLMs Combine with repetition penalties BPE The Transformer Encode new text with the learned merges Metrics Evaluation & metrics Compute AUC in \(O(n \log n)\) Cosine retrieval Embeddings Replace brute force with an ANN index

docs.title: Linear regression
docs.text:
Closed form via least squares, and gradient descent on MSE. Gradient: \(\frac{2}{n}X^\top(Xw + b - y)\).

def linear_regression_normal_equation(X, y):
    """Closed form: w = (X^T X)^-1 X^T y. A bias column is added. Returns (w, b)."""
    Xb = np.hstack([X, np.ones((X.shape[0], 1))])
    theta = np.linalg.lstsq(Xb, y, rcond=None)[0]   # more stable than an explicit inverse
    return theta[:-1], theta[-1]


def linear_regression_gd(X, y, lr=0.1, epochs=1000):
    """Batch gradient descent on mean squared error. X: (n, d), y: (n,)."""
    n, d = X.shape
    w, b = np.zeros(d), 0.0
    for _ in range(epochs):
        error = X @ w + b - y              # (n,)
        w -= lr * (2 / n) * (X.T @ error)  # dMSE/dw
        b -= lr * (2 / n) * error.sum()    # dMSE/db
    return w, b

Say: solving with lstsq (QR/SVD) is more stable than computing \((X^\top X)^{-1}\) explicitly; the closed form costs \(O(nd^2 + d^3)\), so use gradient descent or SGD for large \(d\); scale features for gradient descent.

docs.title: Logistic regression
docs.text:
Sigmoid of a linear score, trained on log loss. Gradient: \(\frac{1}{n}X^\top(p - y)\).

def sigmoid(z):
    """Numerically stable sigmoid."""
    out = np.empty_like(z, dtype=float)
    pos = z >= 0
    out[pos] = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z[pos]))
    ez = np.exp(z[~pos])
    out[~pos] = ez / (1 + ez)
    return out


def log_loss(y, p, eps=1e-12):
    p = np.clip(p, eps, 1 - eps)
    return -np.mean(y * np.log(p) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p))


def logistic_regression(X, y, lr=0.1, epochs=2000, l2=0.0):
    """Gradient descent on log loss with optional L2. Labels y in {0, 1}."""
    n, d = X.shape
    w, b = np.zeros(d), 0.0
    for _ in range(epochs):
        p = sigmoid(X @ w + b)
        w -= lr * (X.T @ (p - y) / n + l2 * w)   # gradient is (p - y) x
        b -= lr * np.mean(p - y)
    return w, b

Say: the naive 1 / (1 + exp(-z)) overflows for large negative \(z\), hence the two-branch sigmoid; clip probabilities in the loss to avoid \(\log 0\); L2 keeps weights finite on separable data; for imbalance, weight each example's gradient by its class weight.

docs.title: Softmax and cross-entropy
docs.text:
def softmax(z, axis=-1):
    z = z - z.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)      # subtract the max: no overflow
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)


def cross_entropy_with_grad(logits, labels):
    """logits: (n, k), labels: (n,) integer classes. Returns (loss, dL/dlogits)."""
    n = logits.shape[0]
    shifted = logits - logits.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    log_probs = shifted - np.log(np.exp(shifted).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True))  # log-softmax
    loss = -log_probs[np.arange(n), labels].mean()
    grad = np.exp(log_probs)
    grad[np.arange(n), labels] -= 1               # p - y
    return loss, grad / n

Say: subtracting the row maximum doesn't change softmax but prevents overflow; computing log-softmax directly avoids \(\log 0\); the gradient with respect to logits is \((p - y)/n\). The self-test checks it against finite differences.

docs.title: k-means
docs.text:
def kmeans(X, k, iters=100, seed=0):
    """Lloyd's algorithm with k-means++ initialization. Returns (centroids, labels)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    centroids = [X[rng.integers(len(X))]]
    for _ in range(1, k):                          # k-means++: spread the starting points
        d2 = np.min([((X - c) ** 2).sum(axis=1) for c in centroids], axis=0)
        centroids.append(X[rng.choice(len(X), p=d2 / d2.sum())])
    centroids = np.array(centroids)
    for _ in range(iters):
        dists = ((X[:, None, :] - centroids[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=2)  # (n, k)
        labels = dists.argmin(axis=1)
        new = np.array([X[labels == j].mean(axis=0) if np.any(labels == j) else centroids[j]
                        for j in range(k)])
        if np.allclose(new, centroids):
            break
        centroids = new
    return centroids, labels

Say: k-means++ initialization; each iteration is \(O(nkd)\); the broadcasted distance matrix uses \(O(nk)\) memory (chunk it for large \(n\)); handle empty clusters (here: keep the old centroid; alternatives re-seed it with a far point); run several seeds and keep the lowest inertia.

docs.title: k-nearest neighbors
docs.text:
def knn_predict(X_train, y_train, X_query, k=5):
    """Majority vote among the k nearest training points (Euclidean)."""
    d2 = ((X_query[:, None, :] - X_train[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=2)  # (m, n)
    nearest = np.argpartition(d2, kth=k - 1, axis=1)[:, :k]
    return np.array([Counter(y_train[row]).most_common(1)[0][0] for row in nearest])

Say: argpartition finds the \(k\) smallest in \(O(n)\) per query instead of sorting; brute force is \(O(mnd)\); scale features first; for millions of points use an approximate index (HNSW, IVF); for ties, use distance weighting or an odd \(k\).

docs.title: Best decision-tree split
docs.text:
def gini(y):
    _, counts = np.unique(y, return_counts=True)
    p = counts / counts.sum()
    return 1 - np.sum(p ** 2)


def best_split(X, y):
    """Return (feature, threshold, gain) of the best Gini split, or None if no split helps."""
    n, d = X.shape
    parent = gini(y)
    best = None
    for j in range(d):
        values = np.unique(X[:, j])
        for t in (values[:-1] + values[1:]) / 2:  # midpoints between distinct values
            left = X[:, j] <= t
            n_left = left.sum()
            child = (n_left * gini(y[left]) + (n - n_left) * gini(y[~left])) / n
            gain = parent - child
            if best is None or gain > best[2]:
                best = (j, t, gain)
    return best if best and best[2] > 0 else None

Say: candidate thresholds are midpoints between sorted distinct values; this version is \(O(d \cdot n^2)\); sorting once per feature and sweeping with running class counts makes it \(O(d\, n \log n)\); to grow a tree, recurse on each side until a depth limit, a minimum leaf size, or no positive gain.

docs.title: Two-layer network with backprop
docs.text:
def train_mlp(X, y, hidden=16, k=2, lr=0.5, epochs=2000, seed=0):
    """Two-layer network (ReLU hidden layer, softmax output) trained with full-batch GD."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    d = X.shape[1]
    W1 = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / d), (d, hidden)); b1 = np.zeros(hidden)   # He init
    W2 = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / hidden), (hidden, k)); b2 = np.zeros(k)
    for _ in range(epochs):
        Z1 = X @ W1 + b1                 # (n, h)
        A1 = np.maximum(0, Z1)
        Z2 = A1 @ W2 + b2                # (n, k)
        loss, dZ2 = cross_entropy_with_grad(Z2, y)
        dW2 = A1.T @ dZ2; db2 = dZ2.sum(axis=0)
        dA1 = dZ2 @ W2.T
        dZ1 = dA1 * (Z1 > 0)             # ReLU derivative
        dW1 = X.T @ dZ1; db1 = dZ1.sum(axis=0)
        W1 -= lr * dW1; b1 -= lr * db1
        W2 -= lr * dW2; b2 -= lr * db2
    predict = lambda Xn: (np.maximum(0, Xn @ W1 + b1) @ W2 + b2).argmax(axis=1)  # noqa: E731
    return predict, loss

Say: He initialization for ReLU; the backward pass mirrors the forward pass (\(\partial W = A^\top \partial Z\), pass back \(\partial Z\,W^\top\), multiply by the ReLU mask); the self-test trains it on an XOR-like problem a linear model can't solve; next steps would be mini-batches, momentum or Adam, and a held-out set.

docs.title: Attention
docs.text:
def scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V, causal=False):
    """Q: (..., n, d_k), K: (..., m, d_k), V: (..., m, d_v) -> (..., n, d_v)."""
    d_k = Q.shape[-1]
    scores = Q @ np.swapaxes(K, -1, -2) / np.sqrt(d_k)
    if causal:
        n, m = scores.shape[-2:]
        scores = np.where(np.triu(np.ones((n, m), dtype=bool), k=1), -1e9, scores)
    return softmax(scores, axis=-1) @ V


def multi_head_attention(X, W_q, W_k, W_v, W_o, num_heads, causal=True):
    """X: (n, d_model); each W: (d_model, d_model)."""
    n, d_model = X.shape
    d_head = d_model // num_heads
    split = lambda T: T.reshape(n, num_heads, d_head).transpose(1, 0, 2)  # noqa: E731
    Q, K, V = split(X @ W_q), split(X @ W_k), split(X @ W_v)
    heads = scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V, causal)            # (h, n, d_head)
    return heads.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(n, d_model) @ W_o

Say: scale by \(\sqrt{d_k}\); mask with a large negative number before the softmax; heads are split by reshaping \((n, d)\) to \((h, n, d/h)\); the self-test checks causality (changing later tokens doesn't change earlier outputs). For a padding mask, combine a key mask with the causal mask. In PyTorch:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn


class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model: int, n_heads: int):
        super().__init__()
        assert d_model % n_heads == 0
        self.n_heads, self.d_head = n_heads, d_model // n_heads
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model)
        self.out = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)

    def forward(self, x):                                   # x: (B, T, C)
        B, T, C = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).split(C, dim=2)
        q, k, v = (t.view(B, T, self.n_heads, self.d_head).transpose(1, 2) for t in (q, k, v))
        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / self.d_head ** 0.5      # (B, h, T, T)
        mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool, device=x.device), diagonal=1)
        att = att.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf")).softmax(dim=-1)
        y = (att @ v).transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(B, T, C)
        return self.out(y)
        # Production code would call torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)

docs.title: Sampling: temperature, top-k, top-p
docs.text:
def sample_next_token(logits, temperature=1.0, top_k=None, top_p=None, rng=None):
    """Temperature, then top-k, then top-p (nucleus) filtering, then sample one token id."""
    rng = rng or np.random.default_rng()
    if temperature == 0:
        return int(np.argmax(logits))                 # greedy
    probs = softmax(np.asarray(logits, dtype=float) / temperature)
    order = np.argsort(probs)[::-1]                    # most likely first
    keep = np.ones(len(probs), dtype=bool)
    if top_k is not None:
        keep[order[top_k:]] = False
    if top_p is not None:
        cumulative = np.cumsum(probs[order])
        cutoff = np.searchsorted(cumulative, top_p) + 1   # smallest set reaching top_p
        keep[order[cutoff:]] = False
    probs = np.where(keep, probs, 0)
    return int(rng.choice(len(probs), p=probs / probs.sum()))

Say: temperature 0 means greedy; apply temperature before filtering; top-p keeps the smallest set of tokens whose probability reaches \(p\); renormalize after filtering; repetition penalties would adjust logits before all of this.

docs.title: Byte-pair encoding
docs.text:
def train_bpe(word_counts, num_merges):
    """word_counts: {"low": 5, ...}. Returns the list of merges, most frequent pair first."""
    vocab = {tuple(word): count for word, count in word_counts.items()}
    merges = []
    for _ in range(num_merges):
        pairs = Counter()
        for symbols, count in vocab.items():
            for a, b in zip(symbols, symbols[1:]):
                pairs[(a, b)] += count
        if not pairs:
            break
        best = max(pairs, key=lambda p: (pairs[p], p))   # ties broken deterministically
        merges.append(best)
        new_vocab = {}
        for symbols, count in vocab.items():
            out, i = [], 0
            while i < len(symbols):
                if i < len(symbols) - 1 and (symbols[i], symbols[i + 1]) == best:
                    out.append(symbols[i] + symbols[i + 1]); i += 2
                else:
                    out.append(symbols[i]); i += 1
            new_vocab[tuple(out)] = count
        vocab = new_vocab
    return merges

Say: each iteration counts adjacent pairs weighted by word frequency and merges the most frequent; real tokenizers work on bytes, pre-split text on whitespace and punctuation, and use efficient data structures; to encode new text, apply the merges in the learned order.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
def precision_recall_f1(y_true, y_pred):
    tp = np.sum((y_pred == 1) & (y_true == 1))
    fp = np.sum((y_pred == 1) & (y_true == 0))
    fn = np.sum((y_pred == 0) & (y_true == 1))
    precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0
    recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0
    f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) if precision + recall else 0.0
    return precision, recall, f1


def roc_auc(y_true, scores):
    """Probability a random positive outranks a random negative (ties count half)."""
    pos, neg = scores[y_true == 1], scores[y_true == 0]
    greater = (pos[:, None] > neg[None, :]).sum()
    ties = (pos[:, None] == neg[None, :]).sum()
    return (greater + 0.5 * ties) / (len(pos) * len(neg))


def ndcg_at_k(relevances, k):
    """relevances: graded relevance of results in ranked order."""
    rel = np.asarray(relevances, dtype=float)
    discounts = 1 / np.log2(np.arange(2, k + 2))
    dcg = np.sum(rel[:k] * discounts[: len(rel[:k])])
    ideal = np.sort(rel)[::-1][:k]
    idcg = np.sum(ideal * discounts[: len(ideal)])
    return dcg / idcg if idcg > 0 else 0.0

Say: guard against division by zero; this AUC is the pairwise definition, \(O(n_{pos} \cdot n_{neg})\); the \(O(n \log n)\) version ranks all scores and uses the Mann–Whitney formula \(\frac{R_{pos} - n_{pos}(n_{pos}+1)/2}{n_{pos}\,n_{neg}}\), where \(R_{pos}\) is the sum of positive ranks; NDCG divides by the ideal ordering's DCG.

docs.title: Cosine similarity retrieval
docs.text:
def top_k_cosine(query, doc_matrix, k=3):
    """query: (d,), doc_matrix: (n, d). Returns indices and scores of the k most similar docs."""
    q = query / np.linalg.norm(query)
    D = doc_matrix / np.linalg.norm(doc_matrix, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    scores = D @ q
    idx = np.argsort(-scores)[:k]
    return idx, scores[idx]

Say: normalize once at indexing time so retrieval is a single matrix–vector product; argpartition gives the top \(k\) in \(O(n)\) before sorting just those; beyond about a million documents, use an ANN index; for RAG, add BM25 and a reranker.

docs.title: Most-Asked Questions
docs.text:
How to use this page

Each row is a question that comes up again and again, with the one-line core of a good answer. Cover the answer column, say your answer out loud, then compare. If your answer is weaker than the line, open the linked page; its interview section has the full answer. For spaced practice with every question on the site, use the Flashcard Drill.

docs.title: Foundations
docs.text: Question Core of the answer Page Explain the bias–variance trade-off. Error = bias² + variance + noise; simple models underfit, flexible ones overfit; diagnose with train vs validation error. ML Fundamentals L1 vs L2: why is L1 sparse? The L1 ball has corners on the axes, and its gradient doesn't shrink near zero, so weights hit exactly zero. ML Fundamentals What is data leakage? Examples? Information unavailable at prediction time reaching training: preprocessing before splitting, future data, target-derived features, duplicate users. ML Fundamentals How do you cross-validate time series? Forward-chaining splits: train on the past, validate on the next period; never shuffle. ML Fundamentals How do you handle imbalanced data? Right metric (PR-AUC, recall at fixed FPR), class weights or resampling on the training fold only, threshold tuning, recalibration. ML Fundamentals MLE vs MAP; priors and regularization? MAP adds a log prior; Gaussian prior = L2, Laplace prior = L1. Math for ML Why cross-entropy rather than MSE for classification? It's the correct likelihood, convex for logistic regression, and its gradient \(p - y\) doesn't vanish when confidently wrong. Math for ML What is a p-value? P(data at least this extreme given the null is true); not P(null is true). Math for ML Precision vs recall: when does each matter? Recall when misses are costly (screening, fraud); precision when false alarms are costly (spam, blocking). Evaluation What does ROC-AUC mean; when is it misleading? P(random positive scored above random negative); misleading under heavy imbalance, so use PR-AUC. Evaluation What is calibration and how do you fix it? Predicted 0.8 should mean 80% positive; fix with Platt scaling, isotonic regression or temperature scaling. Evaluation Explain NDCG. Position-discounted graded relevance, \(\sum rel_i/\log_2(i+1)\), divided by the ideal ordering's DCG. Evaluation How do you size an A/B test? \(n \approx 16\,p(1-p)/\delta^2\) per group for α = 0.05 and power 0.8; run whole weeks; don't peek. Evaluation Offline metric up, online metric down: why? Metric misaligned with the goal, leakage, training–serving skew, logged-data bias, latency, novelty, broken test. Evaluation

docs.title: Classical ML
docs.text: Question Core of the answer Page Assumptions of linear regression? Linearity, independent errors, constant variance, roughly normal errors (for inference), no perfect multicollinearity. Linear models Interpret a logistic regression coefficient. Change in log-odds per unit; \(e^w\) is the odds ratio, not a probability multiplier. Linear models Why not MSE for logistic regression? Non-convex through the sigmoid and vanishing gradients when wrong; log loss is convex and correct. Linear models What are support vectors and the kernel trick? Points on or inside the margin define the boundary; kernels compute dot products in a feature space without building it. kNN, NB & SVM Why is Naive Bayes "naive", and why does it work? Assumes conditional independence; probabilities are off but class rankings often survive; great with little data. kNN, NB & SVM Bagging vs boosting? Bagging averages independent deep trees to cut variance; boosting adds shallow trees sequentially to cut bias. Trees & ensembles Why does a random forest sample features? To de-correlate trees: averaging only cancels variance that isn't shared. Trees & ensembles What makes XGBoost better than plain gradient boosting? Second-order optimization, regularized leaves, sparsity-aware splits, subsampling, fast parallel systems work. Trees & ensembles Trees vs neural nets on tabular data? GBDTs usually win on heterogeneous, medium-sized tabular data; nets win on raw text, images and huge ID spaces. Trees & ensembles How do you choose k in k-means? When does it fail? Elbow, silhouette, stability, usefulness; fails on non-round clusters, varied densities, outliers, unscaled features. Unsupervised Derive PCA; relation to SVD? Maximize projected variance → top eigenvectors of the covariance; the right singular vectors of centered data. Unsupervised Can you trust distances in t-SNE plots? No: cluster sizes and gaps are not meaningful; use for exploration only. Unsupervised Collaborative vs content-based filtering; cold start? Interactions vs item features; cold start with content features, popularity, onboarding and exploration. Recommender systems Why candidate generation then ranking? Latency: cheap high-recall retrieval over millions, expensive precise ranking over hundreds. Recommender systems

docs.title: Deep learning
docs.text: Question Core of the answer Page Why non-linear activations? Without them stacked layers collapse into one linear map. Neural networks Derive backprop for two layers. \(\partial Z_2 = P - Y\); \(\partial W = A^\top \partial Z\); pass back \(\partial Z\,W^\top\); multiply by the activation derivative. Neural networks Vanishing gradients: cause and fixes? Products of small per-layer factors; ReLU, good init, normalization, residuals, gated RNNs, clipping for explosions. Neural networks Xavier vs He initialization? Keep activation variance constant: \(2/(n_{in}+n_{out})\) for tanh, \(2/n_{in}\) for ReLU. Neural networks Explain Adam; why AdamW? Momentum + per-parameter scaling + bias correction; AdamW decouples weight decay from the adaptive step. Training Why learning-rate warmup? Early Adam statistics and random weights make big steps unstable, especially in Transformers. Training BatchNorm vs LayerNorm? Batch statistics per channel vs per-token feature statistics; LayerNorm doesn't depend on batch, so Transformers use it. Training Dropout at train vs test time? Randomly zero and rescale during training; off at inference. Training How do you debug a model that won't train? Check initial loss ≈ ln K, overfit one batch, inspect data and labels, check gradients and learning rate. Training Conv output size and parameters? \(\lfloor (W - k + 2p)/s \rfloor + 1\); parameters \((k^2 C_{in} + 1) C_{out}\). CNNs & vision How does ResNet solve degradation? Learn residuals \(F(x) + x\); identity is easy and gradients flow through skips. CNNs & vision ViT vs CNN? Patches as tokens, weak inductive bias, needs more data, scales better; CNNs are data-efficient. CNNs & vision How does CLIP do zero-shot classification? Compare the image embedding with text embeddings of "a photo of a {label}". CNNs & vision Why do RNNs struggle? Vanishing gradients, no parallelism over time, a fixed-size state bottleneck. Sequence models Walk through the LSTM gates. Forget, input, candidate, output; additive cell update keeps gradients alive. Sequence models How did attention fix seq2seq? The decoder takes a relevance-weighted mix of all encoder states at each step. Sequence models

docs.title: Transformers and LLMs
docs.text: Question Core of the answer Page Explain Q, K, V. Query = what I'm looking for, key = what I offer to match, value = what I pass on; weights from softmax of \(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}\). Transformer Why divide by √d_k? Dot products grow with dimension; large scores saturate softmax and kill gradients. Transformer Why multi-head attention? Several relationships at once at the same total cost. Transformer Why positional encodings? Explain RoPE. Attention is order-blind; RoPE rotates Q and K by position so scores depend on relative distance. Transformer Why are most LLMs decoder-only? One scalable objective over all text, every task as generation, efficient KV-cached inference. Transformer Parameters of a 32-layer, d = 4096 model? ≈ \(12d^2 \times 32 \approx 6.4\)B plus embeddings ≈ 6.7B. Transformer What is the KV cache; how big is it? Stored past keys and values; \(2 \times L \times h_{kv} \times d_h \times T \times\) bytes per sequence. Efficient attention MHA vs MQA vs GQA? Shared keys and values across heads shrink the cache; GQA keeps near-MHA quality. Efficient attention How does FlashAttention work? Exact attention in SRAM tiles with an online softmax; never writes the n×n matrix. Efficient attention How does MoE work; total vs active parameters? A router sends each token to top-k experts; memory follows total, compute follows active. Efficient attention BERT vs GPT objectives? Masked tokens with bidirectional context vs next token with causal context. Pretraining What did Chinchilla show? Scale data with parameters (~20 tokens per parameter for compute-optimal training). Pretraining Top-k vs top-p; temperature? Fixed candidate count vs probability mass; temperature divides logits to sharpen or flatten. Pretraining Why do LLMs hallucinate; how to reduce it? Trained for plausibility, not truth; ground with RAG and citations, allow abstaining, verify, evaluate. Pretraining Explain LoRA; why B = 0 at init? Learn low-rank \(\Delta W = BA\) on frozen weights; zero B starts exactly at the base model; merges with no latency. Fine-tuning Memory to fully fine-tune 7B? ≈ 16 bytes per parameter with Adam in mixed precision ≈ 112 GB plus activations. Fine-tuning Quantization: FP16 vs INT4 for 70B? ≈ 140 GB vs ≈ 35 GB of weights; PTQ methods such as GPTQ and AWQ. Fine-tuning DDP vs FSDP; tensor vs pipeline parallelism? Replicate vs shard training state; split matrices within layers vs split layers into stages. Fine-tuning Prefill vs decode? Prompt processed in parallel (compute-bound, TTFT) vs one token at a time (memory-bound, per-token latency). Inference Continuous batching and PagedAttention? Swap requests in and out every step; store the KV cache in pages to avoid waste. Inference How does speculative decoding preserve quality? A draft proposes tokens; the target verifies with rejection sampling, so outputs follow the target distribution exactly. Inference VAE vs GAN vs diffusion? Stable but blurry vs sharp but unstable vs high quality and stable but slow to sample. Generative models What is classifier-free guidance? Extrapolate from unconditional toward conditional noise predictions with scale \(w\). Generative models

docs.title: Alignment and reasoning
docs.text: Question Core of the answer Page Walk through RLHF. SFT → reward model from preference pairs (Bradley–Terry) → PPO maximizing reward minus KL to the reference. Post-training Why the KL penalty? The reward model is an imperfect proxy; KL limits reward hacking and drift. Post-training DPO vs PPO? DPO optimizes preferences directly with a classification-style loss, no reward model or sampling; PPO is on-policy and handles arbitrary rewards. Post-training What is Constitutional AI / RLAIF? AI feedback guided by written principles replaces much human labeling. Post-training What is reward hacking? Maximizing the proxy reward without the intended behavior: length, flattery, special-casing tests. Post-training Explain PPO's clipping. Clip the new/old probability ratio to \([1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon]\) so updates stay small. RL essentials What is GRPO? PPO-style updates with group-normalized rewards as advantages; no critic. Reasoning What is test-time compute scaling? Better answers by spending more inference compute: longer reasoning, best-of-N with verifiers, search. Reasoning PRM vs ORM? Step-level rewards vs final-answer rewards. Reasoning

docs.title: AI engineering and agents
docs.text: Question Core of the answer Page How do you get reliably parseable output? Structured outputs or tool schemas with constrained decoding, then validate and retry. Prompting Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder? Separate embeddings for fast retrieval vs joint scoring for accurate reranking. Embeddings How does HNSW work; IVF vs HNSW? Layered proximity graph with greedy search; IVF clusters and is compact; HNSW has better recall and more memory. Embeddings Walk through a RAG pipeline. Parse → chunk → embed + BM25 → hybrid retrieval with ACL filters → rerank → prompt with citations → evaluate. RAG How do you choose a chunk size? Start from structure at a few hundred tokens with overlap; tune on retrieval recall with real questions. RAG Why hybrid search and reranking? Dense misses exact terms, BM25 misses meaning; rerankers add precision on a shortlist. RAG How do you evaluate RAG? Retrieval recall@k and MRR; faithfulness and correctness of answers; end-to-end success. RAG RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context? Knowledge vs behavior vs small stable corpora; combine them. RAG How does function calling work? Tools described by schema; the model emits a structured call; your code executes and returns the result. Tool calling How do you design good tools? Few, well-scoped, clearly described, typed, concise results, helpful errors, user-scoped permissions. Tool calling Workflow vs agent? Fixed code paths vs the model choosing the path; use agents only when steps can't be known upfront. Agents Explain ReAct. Alternate reasoning, actions and observations in a loop. Agents Why do agents fail on long tasks? Errors compound (\(0.95^{20} \approx 0.36\)), context fills, goals drift; verify, checkpoint, compact. Agents What problem does MCP solve? N × M integrations become N + M with a standard protocol for tools, resources and prompts. MCP & A2A Host vs client vs server; tools vs resources vs prompts? App, per-server connector, capability provider; model-, app- and user-controlled primitives. MCP & A2A MCP vs A2A? Agent-to-tools/data vs agent-to-agent with tasks and artifacts. MCP & A2A What is context engineering? Curating the smallest high-signal context at each step: just-in-time retrieval, compaction, notes, sub-agents. Context engineering What is an agent harness? The loop, tools, sandbox, permissions, context, verification, state, tracing and evals around the model. Harness engineering pass@k vs pass^k? At least one success in k tries (capability) vs all k succeed (reliability). Harness engineering Pros and cons of LLM-as-judge? Scales subjective grading; biased by position, length and self-preference; calibrate against humans. LLM evals Direct vs indirect prompt injection; defenses? User-typed vs hidden in content; limit capabilities, approvals, isolate untrusted content, restrict egress. Security

docs.title: Production and design
docs.text: Question Core of the answer Page Notebook to production? Reproducible pipeline, registry, packaging, shadow → canary → A/B, monitoring, rollback, retraining. MLOps Training–serving skew? Features computed differently offline and online; shared definitions, point-in-time joins, logging served features. MLOps Covariate shift vs concept drift? \(P(x)\) changes vs \(P(y \mid x)\) changes; detect with distribution tests and delayed labels. MLOps ML system design framework? Clarify, frame, data, features, model, training, evaluation, serving and monitoring. ML system design Position bias and delayed labels? Model position and correct with propensities; train on matured labels, use proxies, monitor leading indicators. ML system design Design an enterprise RAG assistant. Connectors, parsing, chunking, hybrid index with ACLs, rerank, cite or abstain, eval set, monitoring, cost. GenAI system design SHAP vs LIME? Shapley-value attributions with consistency guarantees vs local linear surrogates. Responsible AI Two fairness metrics that conflict? Demographic parity vs equalized odds (or calibration) when base rates differ. Responsible AI

docs.title: GenAI System Design
docs.text:
TL;DR

GenAI design rounds test judgment: start with the simplest architecture that could work (a prompt, then RAG, then tools, then an agent, then fine-tuning), choose models by measured quality, latency and cost, and spend real time on evaluation, guardrails, permissions, cost and latency. Strong answers define success metrics early, propose an evaluation set before building, and explain how the system improves after launch.

Where this fits

Before: the whole AI Engineering section, Inference & Serving, MLOps & LLMOps. This page: putting it together under interview conditions.

docs.title: A framework for GenAI designs
docs.text: Step What to cover 1. Clarify Users and tasks; what a good answer looks like; risk level; latency target (TTFT and total); cost per request; data sources and permissions; languages; volume and peaks; compliance 2. Choose the architecture Prompt only → RAG → tool calling → workflow → agent; fine-tuning only where behavior or cost demands it. Justify each step up. 3. Choose models Hosted vs open weights; size tiers; routing between a small and a large model; embedding and reranking models; measured on your eval set 4. Knowledge and data Ingestion, parsing, chunking, indexing, freshness, permissions, PII handling 5. Context and prompts System prompt, retrieved context, tools, memory; layout for prompt caching 6. Evaluation An offline set from real tasks; programmatic checks, calibrated judges, human review; online metrics and A/B tests 7. Safety Prompt injection, data leakage, output handling, approvals for actions, abuse, over-refusal 8. Serving and operations Streaming, caching, batching, rate limits, fallbacks, tracing, cost and quality monitoring, rollout of prompt and model versions

docs.title: Worked design: an enterprise knowledge assistant
docs.text:
Clarify. Employees ask questions over 1 million internal documents (wikis, policies, tickets, PDFs, slides) in several languages. Answers must cite sources and respect document permissions. Target: first token under 2 s, full answer under 8 s; cost under a few cents per question; 50,000 questions a day.

Architecture.

flowchart LR
    subgraph ING["Ingestion (offline)"]
        direction TB
        S["Connectors: wiki, drive,<br/>tickets, email archives"] --> P["Parse + OCR<br/>layout, tables"]
        P --> C["Structural chunking<br/>+ contextual headers"]
        C --> E["Embed + BM25"]
        E --> IDX[("Hybrid index<br/>with ACL metadata")]
    end
    subgraph Q["Retrieval (online)"]
        direction TB
        U["User question<br/>+ identity"] --> RW["Rewrite with<br/>chat history"]
        RW --> R["Hybrid retrieval<br/>filtered by ACLs"]
        R --> RR["Rerank<br/>top 50 → 8"]
    end
    subgraph GEN["Generation and feedback"]
        direction TB
        G["LLM: answer with<br/>citations or abstain"] --> GR["Output checks:<br/>PII, groundedness"]
        GR --> UI["Streamed answer<br/>+ sources"]
        UI --> FB["Feedback + traces<br/>→ eval set, dashboards"]
    end
    ING --> Q --> GEN

Key decisions.

  • Permissions: sync ACLs from each source into chunk metadata; filter in the retrieval query by the user's groups; re-sync on permission changes. The model never sees what the user can't.
  • Retrieval quality: hybrid search (names, acronyms and ticket IDs need BM25), a cross-encoder reranker, contextual chunk headers, query rewriting for follow-ups, routing to specialized indexes (HR policies vs engineering docs).
  • Generation: cite every claim with source links; abstain when sources are insufficient; prefer newer documents when they conflict; a mid-sized model for most questions, escalating to a stronger model for complex synthesis.
  • Freshness: incremental re-indexing from change feeds; show document dates.
  • Evaluation: a few hundred real questions labeled with the documents that answer them (retrieval recall@k) and reference answers or key facts (faithfulness and correctness judged by a calibrated LLM judge), unanswerable questions, and permission tests with users of different roles.
  • Cost: about 4,000 input tokens (instructions plus 8 passages) and 400 output tokens per question; stable instructions cached; repeated questions answered from a semantic cache scoped by permissions.
  • Online: thumbs up/down, citation clicks, "no answer" rates by topic (to find content gaps), latency per stage, cost per answer.

docs.title: Worked design: a support agent that takes actions
docs.text:
Clarify. Handle customer chats for an e-commerce company: answer questions, track orders, process returns and refunds within policy, escalate otherwise. Success: resolution rate, customer satisfaction, correct actions, and no unauthorized refunds.

Architecture.

  • Router (workflow): classify intent; simple FAQs go to a RAG answer; account actions go to the agent; sensitive cases (legal threats, safety) go straight to humans.
  • Agent with tools: lookup_customer, get_order, search_policy, create_return, issue_refund(order_id, amount, reason), escalate_to_human(summary), all acting with the authenticated customer's scope.
  • Policy enforcement in code: refunds above a threshold, outside the return window, or repeated within 30 days require human approval regardless of what the model says; idempotency keys prevent double refunds.
  • Context: customer profile and order summary loaded up front; policies retrieved on demand; conversation compacted for long chats.
  • Handoff: escalation includes a structured summary so the human doesn't restart the conversation.

Evaluation. Replay historical conversations with known correct outcomes in a simulator with mocked tools; check end states (correct refund amount, correct order, policy followed) over several runs per case; red-team with manipulative customers ("my manager said I get a full refund") and injected instructions in order notes. Rollout: shadow mode (agent proposes, humans act), then autonomous on low-risk intents, then wider.

docs.title: Worked design: a coding agent for internal repositories
docs.text:
Clarify. Engineers assign issues (bug fixes, small features, test additions) to an agent that opens pull requests for review. Success: share of PRs merged with little rework; safety: no secrets leaked, no unreviewed changes to protected branches.

Harness.

  • Sandbox: a container per task with the repository checked out, dependencies installed, network limited to package mirrors, no production credentials.
  • Tools: code search, file read, edit by diff, run tests and linters, run a command (allow-listed), create a branch and PR. Pushing to protected branches is denied by policy.
  • Context: a repository instructions file (build and test commands, conventions); search on demand rather than loading the repository; truncated test output; compaction for long sessions; sub-agents for broad exploration.
  • Verification: run relevant tests before declaring done; add or update tests; run the linter and type checker; summarize changes and test evidence in the PR description.
  • Budgets: step, time and cost limits per task; escalation with a summary when stuck.

Evaluation. A suite of past issues with their hidden tests (SWE-bench-style) from your own repositories; measure resolution rate (pass@1 and pass^k), review rework, time and cost per task; monitor merged-PR revert rates in production.

docs.title: Worked design: document extraction at scale
docs.text:
Clarify. Extract fields (supplier, dates, line items, totals, tax IDs) from 2 million invoices a month in varied layouts and languages, some scanned; feed an accounting system; accuracy above 99% on totals, with human review for uncertain cases.

Pipeline.

  1. Ingest and classify document type; route known templates to cheap template extractors.
  2. Extract with a vision-language model (or OCR plus an LLM) using structured output against a strict schema.
  3. Validate with business rules: line items sum to the subtotal, tax rates valid, dates plausible, supplier exists in the vendor master data, totals match purchase orders.
  4. Confidence routing: auto-accept when validations pass and confidence is high; otherwise send to a human review queue showing the document with highlighted fields.
  5. Learn from corrections: reviewer fixes become evaluation cases and fine-tuning data (a fine-tuned smaller model can cut cost at this volume).

Cost and throughput. Batch processing through batch APIs or self-hosted models; measure cost per document and straight-through-processing rate; field-level precision and recall per document type and language.

docs.title: Worked design: an LLM gateway for many teams
docs.text:
Clarify. Dozens of internal teams want LLM access with consistent security, cost control and observability across several model providers and self-hosted models.

Components.

  • Unified API with authentication per team and per application.
  • Routing: by model name, capability, cost tier and availability; fallback to another provider on errors or rate limits.
  • Policies: PII redaction, data-residency rules per request, allowed models per team, content safety checks.
  • Quotas and rate limits per team; budgets with alerts.
  • Caching: provider prompt caching passthrough, plus optional response caching scoped per application.
  • Observability: traces with tokens, latency, cost and model version per request; dashboards per team; sampled quality evaluations.
  • Evaluation service: teams register eval suites; model upgrades are tested against them before rollout.

Trade-offs: an extra network hop (a few milliseconds), a central dependency (needs high availability and graceful degradation), and the balance between central control and team flexibility.

docs.title: Back-of-envelope for GenAI designs
docs.text:
Tokens, cost and capacity

For 50,000 requests a day at 4,000 input and 400 output tokens each: 200M input and 20M output tokens a day. With hosted prices of P₁ and P₂ per million input and output tokens, daily cost ≈ 200·P₁ + 20·P₂; if 3,000 of the input tokens are a cached prefix, most of the input cost is billed at the cached rate.

Self-hosting: 20M output tokens a day is about 230 output tokens per second on average; with peaks of 5× and a target of 50 tokens per second per user, size GPUs for roughly 1,200 tokens per second of decode plus prefill capacity for 1M input tokens per hour at peak, then add headroom and redundancy.

Latency: TTFT ≈ queueing + retrieval and reranking (100–400 ms) + prefill (grows with prompt length); total ≈ TTFT + output tokens × time per token (for example 400 × 20 ms = 8 s), which is why streaming matters.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
How do you decide between prompting, RAG, tools, an agent or fine-tuning in a design?

Start with the simplest thing that might work and measure it on an evaluation set. Add RAG when the problem is knowledge that's private, large or changing. Add tools when the system must read live data or take actions. Use a workflow when the steps are known, and an agent only when the path depends on what's discovered. Fine-tune when you need consistent behavior or format that prompting can't reach, or to replace a large model with a cheaper small one at high volume. Each step adds cost and complexity, so justify it with evidence.

How do you reduce the latency of a RAG assistant?

Stream tokens so users see progress; parallelize retrieval sources; use a fast embedding model and cache query embeddings; rerank fewer candidates or use a smaller reranker; trim the prompt (fewer, better passages) and cache stable prefixes; route simple questions to a smaller, faster model; keep services close together; and set per-stage latency budgets with tracing to find the slowest step.

How do you handle multi-tenancy in an LLM application?

Isolate data per tenant: separate indexes or namespaces, ACL filters enforced in retrieval, caches keyed by tenant (and user where needed), and per-tenant encryption where required. Isolate resources with per-tenant quotas and rate limits. Keep per-tenant configuration (prompts, allowed tools, models) and per-tenant observability and cost attribution. Test isolation explicitly, including prompt-injection attempts to reach other tenants' data.

How do you roll out a new model or prompt version safely?

Run the offline evaluation suite (including safety and slice metrics) and compare with the current version; check cost and latency; deploy in shadow mode or to internal users; then canary to a small share of traffic with online metrics and guardrails monitored; expand gradually with the ability to roll back instantly. Version prompts and models together, and record which version served each request.

What would you log for an LLM application, and how do you handle privacy?

Per request: inputs, retrieved context IDs, tool calls and results, outputs, model and prompt versions, tokens, latency per stage, cost, guardrail decisions and user feedback, linked as a trace. For privacy: redact or tokenize PII before logging, restrict access, set retention limits, honor deletion requests, avoid logging content from restricted sources, and make sure provider agreements cover data use.

Hosted API or open-weights model for a new product?

Measure quality on your evaluation set first. Hosted APIs offer the strongest models, no infrastructure, and fast iteration, priced per token with less control over data location and model changes. Open models give control over deployment, data residency, latency and fine-tuning, and can be cheaper at steady high volume, but need serving expertise, GPU capacity and upgrades. Many products start hosted, then move high-volume, narrow tasks to fine-tuned open models, keeping a hosted model for hard cases.

How do you design for hallucination risk in a high-stakes domain such as healthcare or finance?

Ground every answer in approved sources with citations and require abstention when sources are insufficient; restrict scope to supported questions; add verification (groundedness checks, rule checks on numbers); keep a human in the loop for decisions; show confidence and sources in the UI; evaluate with domain experts on representative and adversarial cases; monitor in production with sampled expert review; and meet regulatory requirements for audit trails.

Common mistakes

  • Proposing an agent or fine-tuning before showing why prompting and RAG aren't enough.
  • No evaluation plan until the end of the interview.
  • Enforcing permissions or policies only in the prompt.
  • Ignoring cost per request and latency budgets.
  • No rollout or fallback plan for model and prompt changes.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:
• Recite the GenAI design framework
  • Design the enterprise knowledge assistant with permissions, evaluation and cost
  • Design the support agent with policy enforcement and safe rollout
  • Design the coding agent's harness and evaluation
  • Design document extraction with validation and confidence routing
  • Do token, cost and latency estimates

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
• Anthropic: Building effective agents
  • Chip Huyen: Building A Generative AI Platform
  • Eugene Yan: Patterns for Building LLM-based Systems & Products

docs.title: ML System Design
docs.text:
TL;DR

Design rounds reward structure and trade-offs more than any single algorithm. Use the same eight steps every time: clarify requirements and scale, frame it as an ML problem with metrics, design data and labels, features, a model that starts simple, training, evaluation offline and online, then serving and monitoring. Most designs reuse the same blocks: multi-stage retrieval and ranking, implicit labels with delays and biases, a feature store, calibrated scores, A/B tests and drift monitoring.

Where this fits

Before: every modeling page, Evaluation & Metrics, Recommender Systems, MLOps. This page: combining them under interview conditions. Next: GenAI System Design for LLM-based systems.

docs.title: The eight-step framework
docs.text:
Step What to cover Time (45 min) 1. Clarify The business goal; users; scale (users, items, QPS); latency budget; freshness; constraints (privacy, fairness, cost, regions) 5 min 2. Frame Input, output and ML task type (classification, ranking, regression); the business metric and the offline metric that tracks it; what a mistake costs 5 min 3. Data and labels Sources; explicit vs implicit labels; label delay and noise; sampling and class imbalance; leakage risks; privacy 5 min 4. Features User, item, context, interaction and cross features; embeddings; real-time vs batch features 5 min 5. Model A baseline (heuristic or logistic regression), then a stronger model (GBDT, two-tower, deep ranker); multi-stage if the candidate set is large 8 min 6. Training Loss, negative sampling, imbalance handling, time-based validation, retraining cadence 4 min 7. Evaluation Offline metrics and slices; online A/B test with primary and guardrail metrics 5 min 8. Serving and monitoring Architecture, latency budget per stage, caching, feature store, ANN index, fallbacks; drift, feedback loops, retraining, fairness 8 min

Habits that score well: state assumptions with numbers, propose a baseline before a complex model, say what you'd measure, name trade-offs explicitly ("this improves recall at the cost of 20 ms"), and keep the interviewer involved ("should I go deeper on features or serving?").

docs.title: Building blocks you'll reuse
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    REQ["Request: user + context"] --> CG["Candidate generation<br/>ANN over embeddings,<br/>heuristics, popular"]
    REQ --> FS["Feature store<br/>(online)"]
    CG -->|"~1,000"| RK["Ranking model<br/>(GBDT or deep)"]
    FS --> RK
    RK -->|"~100"| RR["Re-ranking<br/>diversity, rules, policy"]
    RR --> OUT["Response"]
    OUT --> LOG["Logs: impressions,<br/>actions, features used"]
    LOG --> TR["Training pipeline<br/>(offline store, labels)"]
    TR -.->|"retrain"| RK
    TR -.->|"retrain"| CG
Block Key points Multi-stage funnel Cheap, high-recall retrieval narrows millions of items; an expensive, precise ranker orders hundreds Implicit labels Clicks, watch time, purchases: abundant but biased (position, exposure) and sometimes delayed Negative sampling and downsampling Sample negatives to manage imbalance and cost; recalibrate probabilities afterwards if they're used directly Feature store Same feature definitions offline and online; point-in-time-correct training data Calibration Required whenever scores feed money or thresholds (bids, risk limits) Exploration A small share of traffic for new items and to break feedback loops Evaluation Time-based offline splits; online A/B tests with guardrails; long-term holdouts Monitoring Data quality, drift, prediction distribution, delayed-label performance, latency, cost Back-of-envelope numbers to have ready
  • 100 million daily active users × 20 requests a day ≈ 2 billion requests a day ≈ 23,000 QPS on average; plan for peaks of 2–5×.
  • 1 billion items × 128-dimensional float32 embeddings ≈ 512 GB; product quantization to 32 bytes per item ≈ 32 GB.
  • A latency budget of 200 ms might split into: feature fetch 20 ms, retrieval 30 ms, ranking 80 ms, re-ranking and business logic 20 ms, network and overhead the rest.
  • Logging 1 KB per impression at 10 billion impressions a day ≈ 10 TB a day of training data.

docs.title: Worked design: video or news feed recommendations
docs.text:
Clarify. Personalized home feed; 100M+ daily users, millions of items, many new items per day; goal: long-term engagement and satisfaction, not just clicks; latency about 200 ms.

Frame. Rank candidates by predicted value, combining several predicted outcomes: \(\text{score} = w_1 P(\text{click}) + w_2\, \mathbb{E}[\text{watch time}] + w_3 P(\text{like}) - w_4 P(\text{skip or hide})\). Offline: recall@k for retrieval; NDCG and AUC per objective for ranking. Online: watch time per user, retention, satisfaction surveys; guardrails: latency, creator diversity, report rates.

Data and labels. Impressions with outcomes (click, watch time, likes, shares, hides), user history, item metadata and content embeddings. Biases: position bias, exposure bias (only shown items get labels), and popularity bias. Label delay for long-term signals.

Features. User (history embeddings, preferences, demographics if allowed), item (topic, creator, age, quality signals, content embeddings), context (time, device, session), and cross features (user–creator affinity, similarity between item and recent history).

Model. Retrieval from several sources (two-tower embeddings with ANN, recent creators followed, trending, fresh items) merged to about 1,000; a multi-task deep ranker (shared bottom with heads per objective, or mixture-of-experts heads) or a GBDT baseline; re-ranking for diversity, freshness and policy.

Training. In-batch negatives with popularity correction for retrieval; impressions as negatives for ranking; position as a training feature set to a constant at serving; daily or continuous training; time-based validation.

Evaluation. Offline per objective and per segment (new users, heavy users, regions); online A/B test with long enough duration to see retention; holdout groups for long-term effects.

Serving and monitoring. Precomputed item embeddings in an ANN index refreshed frequently; user embedding computed per request; ranking on GPU or CPU with batching; caching for repeated requests; fallback to popular items. Monitor engagement, diversity, creator exposure, drift and feedback loops; reserve exploration traffic for new items.

Follow-ups to expect: cold start for new users and items; clickbait (optimize satisfaction, not clicks); filter bubbles (diversity constraints, exploration); how to choose the objective weights (business trade-offs, experiments).

docs.title: Worked design: e-commerce search ranking
docs.text:
Clarify. Query → ranked products; tens of millions of products; latency about 100–300 ms; goal: purchases and successful searches.

Frame. Learning to rank. Relevance labels from clicks, add-to-cart and purchases (graded), plus human relevance judgments for a sample. Offline: NDCG@10, MRR; online: conversion per search, revenue per search, zero-result rate, query reformulation rate.

Data. Query logs with impressions and actions; product catalog; human-rated query–product pairs. Biases: position bias (use randomization or propensity weighting), presentation bias.

Pipeline.

  1. Query understanding: spelling correction, tokenization, category and attribute extraction ("red running shoes size 9"), query embeddings.
  2. Retrieval: BM25 over titles and attributes plus dense retrieval with a bi-encoder, merged; filters for availability and region.
  3. Ranking: LambdaMART (GBDT with a ranking objective) using text match scores, embedding similarity, product popularity, price, ratings, personalization features; optionally a cross-encoder on the top candidates.
  4. Re-ranking: business rules (sponsored slots, diversity across brands), deduplication.

Trade-offs and follow-ups: relevance vs revenue (keep relevance primary, guard with quality metrics); long-tail queries (dense retrieval helps); latency of cross-encoders (only on the top 20–50); evaluating rankers efficiently (interleaving).

docs.title: Worked design: payment fraud detection
docs.text:
Clarify. Score every card transaction in real time (under ~100 ms) to approve, decline or send to review; fraud rate about 0.1–1%; review team capacity is limited; costs differ sharply between missed fraud and blocked good customers.

Frame. Binary classification with extreme imbalance, used with thresholds: auto-decline above a high threshold, review in a middle band, approve below. Offline: PR-AUC, recall at a fixed false-positive rate, and expected money saved; online: fraud losses, false decline rate, review queue size.

Data and labels. Transactions, account history, device and network signals, merchant data. Labels come from chargebacks and investigations with delays of weeks, and are noisy; declined transactions have no outcome label (selection bias).

Features. Velocity features (transactions per card, device or IP in the last minute, hour, day), deviation from the customer's usual amount and location, merchant risk, device fingerprint, graph features (shared devices, cards and addresses linking accounts), time of day.

Model. Rules as a baseline and safety net; GBDT with class weights; graph-based features or models for fraud rings; anomaly detection to catch new patterns. Calibrate scores so thresholds map to costs.

Training and evaluation. Time-based splits; wait for label maturity or use partial labels carefully; evaluate per segment (new accounts, merchant categories); test against recent attacks.

Serving and monitoring. Streaming feature computation for velocity counts; low-latency online feature store; model scoring service with rule overrides; explanations (top contributing features) for reviewers; feedback from reviews flowing into labels. Monitor drift closely, because fraudsters adapt; keep a small random sample of approvals for unbiased estimates.

docs.title: Worked design: ad click-through prediction
docs.text:
Clarify. Predict \(P(\text{click} \mid \text{user, ad, context})\) for ad auctions; billions of requests per day; latency of a few milliseconds per candidate; the prediction directly sets prices.

Frame. Binary classification where calibration matters: expected value = bid × predicted click probability (or conversion probability), so a model that's 20% over-confident overcharges or overspends. Offline: log loss and calibration (alongside AUC); online: revenue, advertiser ROI, user experience guardrails.

Data. Impressions and clicks (and delayed conversions), very sparse categorical features (user IDs, ad IDs, publisher, keywords). Massive volume, so negatives are downsampled; correct probabilities afterward with \(p = \frac{p'}{p' + (1 - p')/w}\), where \(w\) is the negative sampling rate.

Model. Logistic regression with hashed feature crosses as the classic baseline; factorization machines; deep CTR models (Wide & Deep, DeepFM, DCN) with embeddings for sparse IDs; frequent or online updates because ads and users change quickly.

Follow-ups: delayed conversion feedback; position and auction bias; cold-start ads (content features, exploration budget); privacy changes reducing user-level signals.

docs.title: Worked design: content moderation
docs.text:
Clarify. Detect policy-violating posts (hate, harassment, violence, spam, nudity) across text, images and video, in many languages; millions of posts per day; some need action within minutes; human reviewers are the scarce resource.

Frame. Multi-label classification per policy, with thresholds per policy and action (remove automatically, down-rank, send to review). Metrics: precision and recall per policy and language; prevalence of violating content actually seen by users; reviewer workload; appeal overturn rate.

Data. Reviewer decisions (expensive, inconsistent between reviewers), user reports (noisy), policy definitions that change over time; severe class imbalance; adversarial users who adapt (misspellings, images of text).

Model. Fine-tuned multilingual text encoders and vision models, or a multimodal model; LLM classifiers prompted with the policy text, which adapt quickly when policies change; hash matching for known harmful media; ensembles with rules for spam.

Serving. Pre-publication checks for the most severe categories, post-publication scanning, prioritized review queues ordered by predicted severity and reach; active learning to send uncertain cases to reviewers.

Follow-ups: fairness across languages and dialects (per-group error rates), policy changes (update prompts or relabel), adversarial evasion, reviewer wellbeing, transparency and appeals.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
How do you choose the offline metric for a system design problem?

Start from the business goal and what a mistake costs, then pick the offline metric that best tracks it and can be computed from available labels: NDCG or recall@k for ranking and retrieval; PR-AUC or recall at a fixed false-positive rate for rare-event detection; log loss and calibration when probabilities drive money; per-objective metrics for multi-task rankers. State the online metric it's a proxy for, and the guardrails that must not get worse.

Why propose a baseline before a complex model?

It sets a reference point for whether complexity pays off, ships value quickly, exposes data and pipeline problems early, and is easier to debug and monitor. In interviews it shows judgment. A heuristic, logistic regression or a GBDT often captures most of the achievable value; you then add complexity where measurements show the baseline falls short.

How do you handle delayed labels, like chargebacks that arrive weeks later?

Train on data old enough for labels to have matured, accepting some staleness; use early proxy signals (customer disputes, reviewer decisions) as provisional labels; model the delay explicitly or weight recent examples; evaluate on matured periods; and monitor leading indicators (score distributions, rule hit rates) while waiting. Mention the selection bias from declined transactions that never get labels, and keep a small random sample to estimate it.

What is position bias and how does it affect a ranking system design?

Items in higher positions get more clicks regardless of relevance, so training on raw clicks teaches the model to reproduce its previous ranking. Handle it by including position as a training feature (set to a fixed value when serving), weighting clicks by inverse propensity estimated from randomization experiments, using interleaving for evaluation, and collecting human relevance labels for a sample.

When do you need calibrated probabilities in a design?

Whenever the score is used as a probability rather than just for ordering: expected-value calculations such as ad bidding, pricing and credit limits; thresholds tied to costs or review capacity; combining scores from several models or objectives; and showing confidence to users. Downsampling, class weights and boosting all distort calibration, so recalibrate on held-out data (Platt scaling, isotonic regression) and monitor calibration in production.

How do you handle a multi-objective ranking problem?

Predict each objective separately (click, watch time, like, hide) with a multi-task model, then combine them in a scoring formula with weights reflecting business priorities, tuned through online experiments. Alternatives: constrained optimization (maximize engagement subject to quality or diversity constraints), or Pareto analysis of trade-offs. Keep the objectives observable separately in dashboards so a regression in one isn't hidden by the combined score.

How would you scale a design from one country to global?

Data: language and regional differences in features and labels, and data-residency laws. Models: multilingual encoders, regional fine-tuning or features, and per-region evaluation slices (fairness across languages). Serving: regional deployments to meet latency, replicated feature stores and indexes, and capacity for different traffic peaks. Operations: per-region monitoring and gradual rollouts by region.

How do you prevent feedback loops in a recommender or fraud system?

Keep a small share of traffic for exploration or random selection so you observe outcomes the model wouldn't have chosen; log propensities so you can correct for selection with inverse propensity weighting; monitor diversity and coverage; and evaluate with holdouts unaffected by the model. In fraud, approve a small random sample of borderline cases (within risk limits) to measure true fraud rates.

Common mistakes

  • Jumping to a model architecture before clarifying the goal and scale.
  • Choosing accuracy for imbalanced problems, or AUC when calibration matters.
  • Ignoring label delay, position bias and feedback loops.
  • Random splits in time-dependent systems.
  • Designing without latency budgets or monitoring.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:

  • Draw the retrieval → ranking → re-ranking architecture with logging and training
  • Do the back-of-envelope numbers for QPS, embedding storage and logs
  • Walk through each worked design in under 10 minutes
  • Explain position bias, delayed labels, calibration and feedback loops

docs.title: MLOps & LLMOps
docs.text:
TL;DR

Model code is a small part of a production ML system; most failures come from data and infrastructure. MLOps makes the lifecycle reliable: version data, code and models; compute features the same way in training and serving; deploy gradually (shadow, canary, A/B); monitor inputs, predictions, outcomes and system health; detect drift and retrain. LLMOps adds prompts and retrieval as versioned artifacts, tracing of every call, evaluation in CI, and tracking cost, latency and quality per request.

Where this fits

Before: every modeling page, plus Evaluation & Metrics and Evaluating LLM Systems. This page: running models in production. Next: ML System Design and GenAI System Design put it all together.

docs.title: The ML lifecycle
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph BUILD["Build"]
        direction TB
        A["Frame the problem<br/>business → ML metric"] --> B["Data<br/>collect, label, validate"]
        B --> C["Features"]
        C --> D["Train and tune"]
    end
    subgraph RUN["Ship and operate"]
        direction TB
        E["Evaluate offline"] --> F["Register and package"]
        F --> G["Deploy<br/>shadow → canary → full"]
        G --> H["Monitor data, predictions,<br/>outcomes; retrain on drift"]
    end
    BUILD --> RUN
  • Framing: map the business goal to an ML metric and decide whether ML is needed at all; a rules-based baseline is often the right first release.
  • Data: sources, labeling (human, weak supervision, LLM-assisted with review), data validation (schemas, ranges, null rates) before training.
  • Training pipelines: reproducible, parameterized, automated (orchestrated with tools like Airflow, Kubeflow, or managed platforms).
  • Registry: each model version stored with its data snapshot, code commit, hyperparameters, metrics and approval status.

Hidden technical debt (Sculley et al., 2015) names recurring problems: glue code, pipeline jungles, undeclared consumers of model outputs, feedback loops, configuration sprawl, and dependence on unstable data.

docs.title: Reproducibility and versioning
docs.text: Artifact How to version Code Git Data Immutable snapshots, data versioning tools (DVC, lakeFS, table formats with time travel) Features Feature definitions in code; feature store with versions Models Model registry (MLflow, cloud registries) with lineage Experiments Tracking of parameters, metrics and artifacts (MLflow, Weights & Biases) Environment Pinned dependencies, containers Prompts and retrieval config (LLM apps) Stored and versioned like code, with evaluation results

docs.title: Feature stores and training–serving skew
docs.text:
Training–serving skew: the model sees features computed differently in production than in training, and quietly underperforms. Common causes: separate code paths (SQL for training, Java for serving), different handling of missing values or time zones, stale online features, and future data leaking into training features.

Feature stores address it:

  • One feature definition, used to build both the offline store (historical values in a warehouse, for training) and the online store (low-latency key-value lookups, for serving).
  • Point-in-time-correct joins: when building training data, take each feature's value as of the prediction time of each example, never a later value.
  • Reuse across teams, monitoring of freshness, and lineage. Examples: Feast, Tecton, and the feature stores in cloud ML platforms.

docs.title: Deployment patterns
docs.text:
Pattern When Batch prediction Scores needed periodically (nightly churn scores, weekly recommendations); simplest and cheapest Online (real-time) inference Per-request predictions with latency budgets (fraud checks, ranking) behind a REST or gRPC service Streaming Features from event streams (Kafka, Flink) for fresh signals such as velocity counts Edge / on-device Privacy, offline use, or ultra-low latency; requires compression and quantization Rollout strategy How Shadow The new model receives live traffic but its predictions aren't used; compare outputs, latency and errors Canary Route a small percentage of traffic to the new model; expand if healthy A/B test Randomized split to measure business impact Blue–green Two full environments; switch traffic and switch back instantly if needed Rollback Always keep the previous version ready

Serving concerns: latency budgets (p95, p99), batching, caching, autoscaling, model servers (Triton, TorchServe, KServe, BentoML), hardware choice, and graceful fallbacks (a simpler model or a rule) when the model service fails.

docs.title: Monitoring and drift
docs.text:
What to monitor Examples Data quality Schema violations, null rates, out-of-range values, missing features Input drift Feature distributions vs training (PSI, KL or Jensen–Shannon divergence, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test) Prediction drift Distribution of scores and predicted classes Model performance Accuracy, precision and recall once labels arrive (often delayed) Business metrics Conversion, losses prevented, user satisfaction System health Latency, throughput, errors, resource use, cost

Types of shift:

  • Covariate (data) drift: \(P(x)\) changes (new user demographics, a new device type).
  • Label (prior) shift: \(P(y)\) changes (fraud rate doubles during holidays).
  • Concept drift: \(P(y \mid x)\) changes (fraudsters change tactics, so the same features mean something new).

Population stability index: \(\text{PSI} = \sum_i (a_i - e_i)\ln\frac{a_i}{e_i}\) over bins, with expected (\(e\)) and actual (\(a\)) proportions. A common rule of thumb: below 0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 moderate shift, above 0.25 significant.

When labels are delayed or absent: monitor input and prediction drift as leading indicators, use proxy labels (early outcomes), and sample cases for human labeling.

docs.title: Retraining
docs.text:
• Scheduled (daily, weekly) for steadily changing domains; triggered by drift or performance alerts; online / incremental for fast-moving signals such as ads.
  • Validate every retrained model against the current production model on recent data before promotion (champion vs challenger).
  • Watch for feedback loops: a model's predictions shape the data it's retrained on (recommendations, fraud blocking that hides outcomes). Keep exploration or holdout traffic to collect unbiased data.

docs.title: CI/CD for ML
docs.text:
• Continuous integration: unit tests for data processing and features, data validation tests, training smoke tests on small samples, evaluation thresholds that block bad models.
  • Continuous delivery: automated packaging, registry promotion with approvals, staged rollout, automatic rollback on alerts.
  • Continuous training: pipelines that retrain and validate on fresh data.

docs.title: What changes for LLM applications (LLMOps)
docs.text: Concern In practice New versioned artifacts Prompts, tool definitions, retrieval settings (chunking, embedder, reranker), model and version, decoding parameters Tracing Every request as a trace: prompt, retrieved context, tool calls, outputs, tokens, latency, cost, model version Evaluation in CI Evaluation suites run on every change to prompts, retrieval, tools or model (see Evaluating LLM Systems) Quality monitoring Sampled LLM-judge scores, user feedback, guardrail trigger rates, hallucination checks Cost and latency Tokens per request, cache hit rates, cost per successful task, p95 latency per stage Provider changes Pin model versions, re-run evals before upgrading, have a fallback provider or model Data handling PII redaction in logs, retention policies, data-processing agreements with providers Index operations Freshness of RAG indexes, re-embedding on model changes, permission sync

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Walk me through taking a model from a notebook to production.

Turn the notebook into a reproducible pipeline: versioned data snapshot, feature code shared with serving, training script with tracked parameters and metrics, and tests. Evaluate against the current baseline on a time-based holdout; register the model with lineage; package it (container) behind a serving API or batch job with latency and throughput tests. Roll out with shadow traffic, then canary, then an A/B test on the business metric. Add monitoring for data quality, drift, predictions, outcomes and system health, plus alerts, a rollback path and a retraining plan.

What is training–serving skew, and how do you prevent it?

A difference between how features are computed or what data looks like in training versus production, which silently degrades performance. Causes: separate implementations of feature logic, different missing-value handling, time-zone or unit bugs, stale online features, and leakage of future data into training features. Prevent it with shared feature definitions (a feature store), point-in-time-correct training data, logging the exact features used at serving time and training on those logs, and monitoring feature distributions online vs offline.

What is a point-in-time-correct join?

When assembling training examples, each feature value is taken as it was at the moment the prediction would have been made, not its latest value. For a fraud label on a transaction at 10:00, the "transactions in the last hour" feature must count only transactions before 10:00. Using later values leaks future information, inflating offline metrics and causing skew in production. Feature stores implement these as-of joins.

Batch vs real-time inference: how do you decide?

Batch when predictions can be computed ahead of time and reused (nightly risk scores, weekly recommendations, email campaigns): simpler, cheaper, easy to monitor. Real-time when the prediction depends on fresh context or must happen at request time (fraud checks on a payment, search ranking, conversational responses), at the cost of latency budgets, online feature infrastructure and higher availability requirements. Hybrids are common: precompute candidates in batch, re-rank in real time.

Shadow vs canary deployment.

In a shadow deployment the new model receives copies of live requests and its outputs are logged but not used, so you can compare predictions, latency and errors with zero user impact. In a canary, a small share of real traffic actually uses the new model, exposing real effects on a few users and letting you expand gradually or roll back. Shadow first to catch technical issues, canary and A/B to measure impact.

Covariate shift vs concept drift, with examples.

Covariate shift: the input distribution changes but the relationship between inputs and labels stays the same, for example an app launching in a new country brings different user profiles. Concept drift: the relationship itself changes, for example fraudsters change tactics so transactions that looked safe are now fraudulent, or a pandemic changes what purchase patterns mean. Covariate shift can sometimes be handled by reweighting or retraining on new inputs; concept drift requires new labels.

How do you detect drift without labels?

Compare current input feature distributions with the training reference using PSI, KS tests or divergence measures per feature and over time; monitor the distribution of model scores and predicted classes; track data quality signals; detect drift in embedding space for text or images; and watch business proxies. Then confirm with delayed labels or a labeled sample. Alert on sustained, meaningful shifts rather than every statistical blip.

What would you monitor for an LLM application?

Per request: traces of prompts, retrieved context, tool calls and outputs; tokens, cost and latency per stage; errors and timeouts; guardrail triggers. Quality: sampled LLM-judge scores on key criteria (faithfulness, helpfulness, policy compliance), user feedback (ratings, regenerations, escalations), refusal and over-refusal rates. Data: input topic and language drift, retrieval hit rates and index freshness. Business: task completion and cost per successful task. Plus alerts when any of these shift.

How do you decide when to retrain a model?

Combine a schedule matched to how fast the domain changes with triggers: a performance drop when labels arrive, significant input or prediction drift, a major product change, or new labeled data. Before promoting, compare the retrained challenger against the current champion on recent data, including slices, and roll it out gradually. Watch for feedback loops that bias new training data.

How does LLMOps differ from traditional MLOps?

The core lifecycle is the same, but the artifacts and signals change. You version prompts, tool definitions, retrieval settings and model versions rather than (or in addition to) trained weights; you often depend on an external model provider whose updates you must evaluate; quality is judged with evaluation suites and LLM judges rather than one accuracy number; every request is traced across retrieval and tool calls; cost and latency per token are first-class metrics; and security concerns such as prompt injection and data leakage are part of operations.

Common mistakes

  • Separate feature code for training and serving.
  • Random train/test splits for time-dependent problems, then surprise in production.
  • Monitoring only system metrics, not data and predictions.
  • Retraining automatically without validating against the current model.
  • Unpinned LLM model versions and no evaluation before upgrades.

docs.title: Revision checklist
docs.text:

  • Explain training–serving skew, feature stores and point-in-time joins
  • Compare batch, online, streaming and edge deployment, and rollout strategies
  • Define covariate shift, label shift and concept drift, and PSI
  • Design monitoring with delayed labels
  • List what LLMOps adds: versioned prompts, tracing, evals in CI, cost tracking
