docs.title: Responsible AI
docs.text:
TL;DR

Responsible AI covers whether people can understand, trust and safely use a model. Explainability attributes predictions to inputs (permutation importance, SHAP, LIME, counterfactuals), with the caveat that explanations aren't causal. Fairness measures outcomes across groups (demographic parity, equal opportunity, equalized odds, calibration), and those definitions can't all hold at once, so the choice is a policy decision. Privacy protects personal data in training and use (minimization, differential privacy, federated learning, defenses against memorization). Governance documents and oversees models (model cards, risk assessments, regulation such as the EU AI Act).

Where this fits

Before: models across the site, MLOps and Guardrails & Security. This page: making systems trustworthy, a frequent topic in senior and regulated-industry interviews.

docs.title: Explainability
docs.text:
Question Methods Which features matter overall? (global) Coefficients of linear models, permutation importance, mean absolute SHAP values, partial dependence plots Why this prediction? (local) SHAP values, LIME, counterfactual explanations, saliency and integrated gradients for neural nets What would change the outcome? Counterfactuals: "the loan would be approved if income were 8% higher"
  • Intrinsically interpretable models (linear models, small trees, rule lists, generalized additive models) are often good enough for high-stakes tabular decisions and are easier to audit.
  • Permutation importance: shuffle one feature on validation data and measure the drop in performance. Model-agnostic and more reliable than impurity-based tree importance, but misleading with correlated features (shuffling one leaves its correlated twin intact).
  • Partial dependence and ICE plots: average and per-example predicted outcome as one feature varies.
  • LIME: perturb the input around one example, fit a simple weighted linear model to the black box's outputs, and read its coefficients. Fast, but results can be unstable across runs and depend on how perturbations are sampled.
  • SHAP: attributes a prediction among features using Shapley values from cooperative game theory: each feature's average marginal contribution over all orders in which features could be added. Properties: contributions sum to the prediction minus the baseline (local accuracy), consistent, and fair. TreeSHAP computes exact values efficiently for tree ensembles; KernelSHAP approximates for any model.
  • Neural networks: gradient-based saliency, integrated gradients (integrate gradients along a path from a baseline input), attention visualizations (which are not reliable explanations by themselves).
  • LLMs: mechanistic interpretability studies internal circuits and features; sparse autoencoders decompose activations into interpretable features. Chain-of-thought text isn't a faithful explanation (Reasoning Models).

Explanations aren't causation

SHAP and similar tools explain the model, not the world. A feature with high importance may be a proxy for something else, and changing it may not change the real outcome. Correlated features split or swap credit unpredictably.

docs.title: Where bias comes from
docs.text: Source Example Historical Past hiring decisions reflect discrimination, and the model learns it Representation A group is under-represented in training data, so error rates are higher for it Measurement Labels or features are measured differently across groups (arrests as a proxy for crime) Proxies Removing a protected attribute doesn't help when ZIP code or name encodes it Aggregation One model for groups with genuinely different relationships Evaluation and deployment Benchmarks that don't reflect real users; use in contexts the model wasn't built for

docs.title: Fairness metrics
docs.text:
With prediction \(\hat Y\), label \(Y\) and group \(A\):

Metric Requires Intuition Demographic parity \(P(\hat Y = 1 \mid A = a)\) equal across groups Equal selection rates Equal opportunity Equal true positive rates across groups Qualified people are selected at equal rates Equalized odds Equal true positive and false positive rates Equal error rates both ways Predictive parity Equal precision across groups A positive prediction means the same thing for everyone Calibration within groups Among people scored 0.7, 70% are positive in every group Scores mean the same thing across groups

The impossibility result: when base rates differ between groups, a classifier generally can't satisfy calibration and equal error rates at the same time (except in trivial cases). So choosing a fairness criterion is a value judgment about which harm matters most in context, made with stakeholders, domain experts and legal input, not purely a technical choice.

docs.title: Mitigation
docs.text:
• Pre-processing: collect more representative data, reweight or resample, fix label problems.
  • In-processing: add fairness constraints or penalties to training; adversarial training that prevents predicting the group from the representation.
  • Post-processing: adjust thresholds per group to equalize a chosen metric (legal constraints vary by jurisdiction and domain).
  • Process: audit error rates by group and intersections of groups, document decisions, monitor in production, and provide human review and appeals for consequential decisions.

LLMs: test for stereotyped associations, unequal quality across languages and dialects, and different refusal rates by group, using targeted evaluation sets.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
Technique What it protects Notes Data minimization Collect and keep only what's needed The simplest, strongest control Pseudonymization and anonymization Remove direct identifiers Re-identification is often possible by linking quasi-identifiers (ZIP code, birth date, gender) Access control and encryption Who can see data In transit, at rest, in logs Differential privacy (DP) Guarantees that any one person's data barely changes the output Formal: for neighboring datasets \(D, D'\), \(P[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon P[M(D') \in S] + \delta\). Smaller ε means stronger privacy and more noise DP-SGD Training with DP Clip each example's gradient, add calibrated Gaussian noise, track the privacy budget; costs accuracy and compute Federated learning Raw data stays on devices or at institutions Only model updates are shared; combine with secure aggregation and DP, since updates can still leak information

Attacks to know: membership inference (was this record in the training set?), model inversion (reconstruct sensitive attributes), and training-data extraction from LLMs, which can regurgitate memorized text, especially duplicated sequences. Mitigations: deduplicate and scrub PII from training data, DP for sensitive fine-tunes, output filters, and testing for regurgitation. Machine unlearning (removing a person's influence after training) is an open problem; retraining without the data is the reliable but expensive option.

docs.title: Governance and regulation
docs.text:
• Model cards document intended use, out-of-scope uses, training data, evaluation results (including by group), limitations and ethical considerations. Datasheets for datasets document how data was collected and its known gaps.
  • Risk assessments before deployment: who could be harmed, how, how likely, and what mitigations and human oversight exist.
  • Human oversight for consequential decisions, with the ability to override and appeal.
  • Regulation: the EU AI Act classifies systems by risk (prohibited practices; high-risk systems with requirements for risk management, data governance, documentation, human oversight and accuracy; transparency obligations for some systems such as chatbots and generated content; and obligations for general-purpose AI model providers). GDPR governs personal data (lawful basis, minimization, rights of access and erasure, safeguards for automated decision-making). The NIST AI Risk Management Framework offers a voluntary structure: govern, map, measure, manage. Sector rules (credit, hiring, healthcare) add more.

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
SHAP vs LIME.

Both explain individual predictions. LIME fits a simple local surrogate (usually linear) to the model's behavior on perturbed samples around the instance: fast and model-agnostic, but explanations can vary between runs and depend on the perturbation scheme. SHAP assigns each feature its Shapley value, the average marginal contribution across all feature orderings, which satisfies properties such as contributions summing to the prediction; TreeSHAP computes it exactly and fast for tree models. SHAP is generally more consistent and is the common choice, especially for tree ensembles.

Why is impurity-based feature importance biased, and what would you use instead?

It's computed on training data and rewards features offering many split points (continuous or high-cardinality features, even random IDs), and it splits credit arbitrarily between correlated features. Use permutation importance on held-out data or SHAP values, check stability across resamples, and handle correlated features by grouping them. And remember importance shows what the model uses, not what causes the outcome.

Is attention an explanation?

Not reliably. Attention weights show where information was mixed at one layer and head, but outputs depend on values, many heads and layers, residual paths and MLPs, and studies have found that very different attention patterns can produce the same prediction. Attention can be a useful diagnostic, but faithful attribution needs methods like integrated gradients, ablations or mechanistic analysis.

Name two fairness metrics and explain how they can conflict.

Demographic parity requires equal positive prediction rates across groups; equalized odds requires equal true positive and false positive rates. If the groups' true base rates differ, a classifier with equal error rates will select the groups at different rates, violating demographic parity, and enforcing equal selection rates forces different error rates. Similarly, calibration within groups and equal error rates can't both hold when base rates differ. Which criterion to prioritize depends on the context and the harm you're trying to prevent.

How would you audit a hiring model for bias?

Define the decision and the harms (qualified candidates rejected, unequal selection), identify protected and proxy attributes, and gather representative evaluation data with outcomes. Measure selection rates, true and false positive rates and calibration by group and by intersections of groups; check feature attributions for proxies; test counterfactuals (change only the name or gender cue in a resume and compare scores). Investigate data sources, mitigate (data, constraints, thresholds, removing proxies), document everything, involve legal and domain experts, keep humans in the decision, and monitor after deployment.

What is differential privacy?

A formal guarantee that an algorithm's output distribution barely changes whether or not any single person's data is included: probabilities differ by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\) (plus a small δ). An observer therefore can't confidently tell if a given person contributed. It's achieved by adding calibrated noise; in training, DP-SGD clips each example's gradient and adds Gaussian noise. Smaller ε gives stronger privacy at the cost of accuracy, and the budget accumulates over repeated queries or training steps.

How can an LLM leak its training data, and how do you reduce the risk?

Large models memorize some training sequences, especially ones duplicated many times, and can reproduce them when prompted with a prefix or via extraction attacks; membership inference can reveal whether a record was in training. Reduce it by deduplicating and scrubbing PII and secrets from training data, using differential privacy for sensitive fine-tuning, filtering outputs for PII and verbatim regurgitation, limiting access to raw probabilities, and testing models with extraction attacks before release.

What goes into a model card?

The model's purpose and intended users; out-of-scope uses; training data and preprocessing; evaluation data and metrics, broken down by relevant groups and conditions; known limitations, failure modes and biases; ethical considerations and risks; and maintenance information (version, owners, update cadence). It helps users decide whether the model fits their use, and supports audits and regulatory documentation.

Why doesn't removing the protected attribute make a model fair?

Other features act as proxies: ZIP code, school, name, purchase patterns and many more correlate with race, gender or age, so the model can reconstruct the attribute's effect. Removing it also makes it harder to measure and correct disparities. Better: keep the attribute for auditing (where legally allowed), measure outcomes by group, look for proxies, and apply explicit mitigation.

Common mistakes

  • Treating feature importance or SHAP values as causal effects.
  • Claiming a model is fair after removing protected attributes.
  • Picking a fairness metric without discussing why it fits the context.
  • Calling pseudonymized data anonymous.
  • Treating responsible AI as a launch checklist rather than ongoing monitoring.

docs.text:

  • List sources of bias and five fairness metrics
  • Explain the impossibility result and the three families of mitigation
  • Define differential privacy and DP-SGD; explain federated learning and memorization risks

docs.title: The Big Picture
docs.text:
TL;DR

AI/ML moved through four acts. Act I: people design features and algorithms learn weights on top of them. Act II: neural networks learn the features themselves. Act III: attention and scale turn next-token prediction into general-purpose models. Act IV: post-training, retrieval and tools make those models helpful, grounded and able to act. Each act began because the previous one hit a specific wall.

docs.title: Evolution lines
docs.text: Each line is one idea evolving. Every station states the weakness that pushed the field to the next station. Station names link to the page that covers them.

docs.title: Act I lines
docs.text:
Tree & ensemble line: trees, then two ways to fix them: average them, or chain them.

  • Decision tree 1984Readable and non-linear, but high variance: small data changes give a different tree.
  • Bagging 1996Average trees trained on bootstrap samples to cut variance.
  • Random forest 2001Random feature subsets de-correlate the trees. Bias stays where it was.
  • AdaBoost 1995Chain learners instead: each one focuses on the previous one's mistakes. Sensitive to noisy labels.
  • Gradient boosting 2001Each tree fits the gradient of any differentiable loss. Accurate, but sequential.
  • XGBoost · LightGBM · CatBoost 2014–2017Second-order, regularized, fast, handles missing values and categories. Still the tabular default.

Classifier line: from one neuron to deep networks, with SVMs winning the years in between.

  • Perceptron 1958Learns a line, but only for linearly separable data. Fails on XOR.
  • Logistic regression 1958Probabilities and a convex loss. Still a linear boundary.
  • MLP + backprop 1986Hidden layers learn features, but deep versions were hard to train with 1990s data and compute.
  • SVM + kernels 1992–1995Maximum margin plus the kernel trick beat shallow nets. Training cost grows faster than n².
  • Deep networks 2012GPUs, ReLU, dropout and big datasets made depth work. Features are learned, not designed.

docs.title: Act II lines
docs.text:
Vision line: hand-made features to CNNs to Transformers to vision–language models.

  • SIFT · HOG + SVM 1999–2005Experts design the features, and accuracy plateaus.
  • LeNet 1998Learned convolution filters for digits. Too small for natural images with the compute of the time.
  • AlexNet 2012GPUs, ReLU and dropout: ImageNet top-5 error fell from about 26% to 15%.
  • VGG · Inception 2014Deeper and wider. Past about 20 layers, plain networks got worse, not better.
  • ResNet 2015Skip connections let 152-layer networks train. Reused in every Transformer block.
  • Vision Transformer 2020Image patches as tokens. Scales with data but needs a lot of it.
  • CLIP 2021Learns from 400M image–caption pairs and classifies zero-shot.
  • Multimodal LLMs 2023+Vision encoders feed an LLM, so you can ask questions about images, charts and screens.

Training line: the tricks that made deep networks trainable.

  • Sigmoid + SGD 1980sGradients vanish through saturating activations; one learning rate for everything.
  • ReLU · Xavier/He init 2010–2015No saturation for positive inputs; weights start at the right scale.
  • Momentum → Adam → AdamW 1964–2017Velocity damps zig-zags; per-parameter step sizes; decoupled weight decay.
  • BatchNorm 2015Stable, fast training, but depends on batch size and is awkward for sequences.
  • Residual connections 2015An identity path carries gradients through hundreds of layers.
  • LayerNorm → Pre-LN → RMSNorm 2016–2019Per-token normalization; the standard inside every LLM.

Text representation line: from counting words to embedding meaning.

  • Bag of words · TF-IDF · BM25 1950s–1994Counts words, ignoring order and meaning. BM25 still powers keyword search.
  • word2vec · GloVe · fastText 2013–2016Dense vectors from context. One vector per word, so "bank" is ambiguous.
  • ELMo 2018Contextual vectors from a bi-LSTM: "bank" differs by sentence.
  • BERT 2018Deep bidirectional context from a Transformer encoder.
  • Sentence embeddings → LLM embedders 2019–2025One vector per passage, trained contrastively. The retrieval half of RAG.

docs.title: Act III lines
docs.text:
Sequence line: the main storyline, language modeling from counting to LLMs.

  • n-gram language models 1980sCount word sequences. No meaning, short window.
  • RNN 1990Carries a hidden state, but gradients vanish and it runs one step at a time.
  • LSTM · GRU 1997 · 2014Gates protect memory over hundreds of steps. Still sequential.
  • Seq2seq 2014Encoder–decoder for translation. The whole input is squeezed into one vector.
  • Attention 2014The decoder looks back at every input state. Still built on slow RNNs.
  • Transformer 2017Attention only, fully parallel. Cost grows with the square of the length.
  • BERT · GPT 2018Pretrain once on raw text, then adapt to any task.
  • LLMs at scale 2020+Few-shot learning appears with scale. Still needs alignment and grounding.

Efficiency line: fighting the quadratic cost and the memory wall.

  • Full multi-head attention 2017Quadratic in length; every head stores its own keys and values.
  • KV cache 2017+Reuse past keys and values when generating. Memory grows with context length.
  • MQA → GQA → MLA 2019–2024Share or compress keys and values across heads to shrink the cache.
  • FlashAttention 2022Exact attention computed in on-chip tiles; never stores the full n×n matrix.
  • PagedAttention · continuous batching 2023Serve many requests at once without wasting cache memory.
  • Mixture of experts 2017–2024Many parameters, few active per token.

Adaptation line: ever cheaper ways to specialize a pretrained model.

  • Train from scratch classicNeeds lots of labeled data for every task.
  • Full fine-tuning 2018Best quality, but a full copy of the weights per task.
  • Adapters · prompt tuning 2019–2021Train a few new parameters; adapters add latency.
  • LoRA 2021Low-rank weight updates that merge back in: no added latency.
  • QLoRA 2023LoRA on a 4-bit base model: fine-tune 65B on one 48 GB GPU.

Generative line: each generator fixed the last one's blur, instability or speed.

  • Autoencoder 1980sCompress and reconstruct. The latent space has holes, so random samples look bad.
  • VAE 2013A smooth Gaussian latent space; easy sampling, blurry outputs.
  • GAN 2014Sharp images, but unstable training and mode collapse.
  • Diffusion 2020Learn to remove noise step by step. Stable and diverse, but slow to sample.
  • Latent diffusion · DiT · flow matching 2022+Diffuse in a compressed space with Transformer denoisers and straighter paths.

docs.title: Act IV lines
docs.text:
Alignment line: from text predictor to assistant to reasoner.

  • Pretrained LM 2020Continues text. Doesn't reliably follow instructions.
  • Instruction tuning (SFT) 2021–2022Imitates good demonstrations. Can't learn from "this answer is worse".
  • RLHF with PPO 2022Learns from human preferences. Complex: four models in memory, unstable.
  • Constitutional AI · RLAIF 2022AI feedback guided by written principles scales oversight.
  • DPO 2023Learns from preference pairs directly: no reward model, no RL loop.
  • RL with verifiable rewards 2024–2025Rewards checkable answers, so models learn to reason longer (GRPO, R1).

Grounding line: how models got access to knowledge they were never trained on.

  • Knowledge in weights 2020Frozen at the cutoff, can't cite sources, fills gaps with plausible text.
  • Prompt stuffing 2022Paste documents into the prompt. Limited by context size and cost.
  • RAG 2020–2023Retrieve relevant chunks at query time and answer from them with citations.
  • Hybrid search + reranking 2023Keywords plus vectors, then a cross-encoder picks the best passages.
  • GraphRAG · agentic RAG 2024+Entity graphs for global questions; the model decides what to search and checks itself.

Agent line: from asking well to engineering the whole system around the model.

  • Prompting 2020Ask well and give examples. One shot, no actions.
  • Chain-of-thought 2022Think step by step before answering. Still no access to the world.
  • ReAct 2022Interleave reasoning with actions and observations.
  • Function calling 2023Structured tool calls with JSON schemas, supported natively by models.
  • Agents 2023–2024The model chooses its next step until the goal is met.
  • MCP · A2A 2024–2025Open protocols connect any AI app to any tool, and agents to each other.
  • Context engineering 2025Curate the smallest high-signal context at every step.
  • Harness engineering 2025–2026Design the loop, tools, permissions, checks and evals around the model.

docs.title: Where the lines cross
docs.text:
The same few ideas reappear across decades. Making these connections out loud is what makes answers sound senior.

docs.title: Three narratives to have ready
docs.text:
Interviewers often ask for a history in one or two minutes. These are the shapes of strong answers.

“Walk me through how NLP models evolved.”

We started by counting: bag-of-words and TF-IDF for documents, n-grams for language modeling. They had no notion of meaning. word2vec (2013) learned dense vectors where similar words sit close, but gave one vector per word. RNNs and LSTMs read sequences with memory, but one step at a time and with fading long-range memory. Seq2seq with attention (2014) let the decoder look back at every input word, fixing the single-vector bottleneck. The Transformer (2017) kept only attention, which made training parallel and long-range interactions direct. Pretraining (ELMo, BERT, GPT in 2018) learned from raw text and transferred to any task. Scale (GPT-3, 2020) produced in-context learning. Alignment (InstructGPT and ChatGPT, 2022) made models follow instructions. Retrieval and tools (2023 on) grounded them in fresh data and actions, and RL with verifiable rewards (2024–25) produced reasoning models.

“How did computer vision get from hand-made features to multimodal models?”

Before 2012, pipelines used hand-designed features such as SIFT and HOG fed into an SVM. AlexNet (2012) showed a CNN trained on GPUs with ReLU and dropout could cut ImageNet error from about 26% to 15%. VGG and Inception went deeper, but plain deep networks degraded until ResNet (2015) added skip connections. Detection (Faster R-CNN, YOLO) and segmentation (U-Net, Mask R-CNN) built on those backbones. The Vision Transformer (2020) treated image patches as tokens and scaled better with data. CLIP (2021) trained image and text encoders together on captions, enabling zero-shot classification, and those vision encoders now feed multimodal LLMs that answer questions about images, documents and screens.

“How did we get from GPT-3 to agents?”

GPT-3 predicted text well but didn't reliably follow instructions. Instruction tuning and RLHF (InstructGPT, 2022) turned it into an assistant, and ChatGPT made that conversational. Models still lacked fresh knowledge and actions, so RAG put retrieved documents in the prompt and function calling let models request tool calls with structured arguments. ReAct-style agents put those calls in a loop: reason, act, observe, repeat. MCP (2024) standardized how applications connect models to tools and data, so integrations are built once. As agents ran longer, the bottleneck moved to what's in the context window (context engineering) and to the system around the model: loop, tools, permissions, verification and evals (harness engineering).

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Why did Transformers replace RNNs?

Three reasons. Parallelism: an RNN must process token t before token t+1, while self-attention processes all tokens of a sequence at once, so training uses GPUs far better. Path length: in an RNN information between distant tokens passes through many steps and fades (vanishing gradients); in attention any two tokens interact directly in one step. Scaling: because training is parallel and stable, Transformers could be scaled to billions of parameters and trillions of tokens, and quality kept improving with scale. The cost is attention's \(O(n^2)\) time and memory in sequence length, which motivated FlashAttention, sparse attention and state-space models.

Why does deep learning dominate images and text, while gradient boosting still wins on tabular data?

Images, audio and text are raw, high-dimensional signals with local structure (pixels near each other, words in order). Deep networks learn hierarchical features from them, which beats anything hand-designed. Tabular data is already featurized: columns are meaningful, heterogeneous (prices, categories, counts), often small, and have irregular, axis-aligned decision boundaries. Tree ensembles handle mixed types, missing values and monotonic thresholds natively, need little tuning, and are robust to uninformative features. Neural nets on tabular data tend to need much more tuning and data to match them. Many production systems therefore use GBDTs for tabular signals and neural networks for embeddings of text or images, sometimes feeding one into the other.

What changed between GPT-3 and ChatGPT?

Mostly post-training, not architecture. GPT-3 was a base model trained to continue internet text, so a question might be answered, ignored, or continued with more questions. InstructGPT and ChatGPT added supervised fine-tuning on human-written demonstrations, then RLHF: a reward model trained on human preference comparisons, and PPO to optimize the model against it with a KL penalty to stay close to the SFT model. The result follows instructions, holds a conversation, refuses some harmful requests, and was preferred by people even at much smaller sizes (a 1.3B InstructGPT model was preferred over 175B GPT-3 in the paper's evaluations).

Why did diffusion models overtake GANs for image generation?

GANs produce sharp images but train as an adversarial game, which is unstable and prone to mode collapse (covering only part of the data distribution). Diffusion models train with a simple, stable regression loss (predict the noise that was added), cover the distribution well, and are easy to condition on text through cross-attention and classifier-free guidance. Their weakness, slow sampling over many denoising steps, was reduced by better samplers, latent-space diffusion (Stable Diffusion), distillation and flow matching.

What is the difference between a language model, an assistant and an agent?

A language model predicts the next token; a base model just continues text. An assistant is a language model post-trained (SFT plus preference tuning) to follow instructions and converse safely. An agent is an assistant placed in a loop with tools: it decides which action to take, observes the result, and continues until a goal is met. What makes it an agent is that the model chooses the control flow, rather than a fixed sequence of calls written by a developer (which is a workflow).

What is self-supervised learning, and why was it the key to LLMs?

Self-supervised learning creates labels from the data itself, for example "predict the next word" or "fill in the masked word". It needs no human annotation, so the training set can be the whole internet. Next-token prediction at that scale forces a model to learn grammar, facts, reasoning patterns and code, which then transfer to downstream tasks with little or no labeled data. The same idea powers contrastive image models such as CLIP and masked autoencoders in vision.

Where does knowledge live in pretraining, fine-tuning and RAG?

Pretraining stores broad knowledge in the weights; it is expensive and frozen at a cutoff date. Fine-tuning adjusts the weights, which is good for behavior, format, style and domain language, but unreliable and costly for teaching many new facts. RAG keeps knowledge outside the model in a searchable store and inserts relevant passages at query time, so it is fresh, private, citable and access-controlled, but limited by retrieval quality. Production systems often combine them: a fine-tuned model for behavior plus RAG for facts.

Where does classical ML still beat LLMs in production?

On structured prediction at scale with tight latency and cost budgets: fraud scoring, credit risk, demand forecasting, ad click prediction, ranking. Gradient-boosted trees or logistic regression run in microseconds, are cheap, calibrated, explainable, and easy to monitor and retrain. LLMs are better for unstructured inputs (text, documents, conversation) and open-ended generation. A strong answer mentions combining them: for example LLM-generated features or embeddings feeding a GBDT, or a classical model routing requests before an LLM is called.

docs.title: How to Use This Site
docs.text:
TL;DR

Read the whole map once, quickly. Then go deep one page at a time in the order of the left sidebar. Then drill questions every day. When a topic sends you backward, step back one topic, read only its Weaknesses, and return.

docs.title: The problem this solves
docs.text:
Most people prepare for AI/ML interviews by jumping between topics: Transformers today, then RNNs because attention mentions them, then LSTMs, then suddenly RAG and MCP because a job description listed them. Each topic makes sense on its own, but nothing connects, so every new session feels like starting over.

This site fixes that with three ideas:

  1. One storyline. Every technique on this site exists because an earlier one failed at something. The navigation follows that story, from 1805 (least squares) to 2026 (agent harnesses). See The Big Picture.
  2. The same seven questions on every topic. You always know where you are on a page, and you practise answering in a fixed order.
  3. Evolution lines. Short chains such as RNN → LSTM → attention → Transformer show which idea replaced which and why. Going backward becomes navigation, not a restart.

docs.title: The three passes
docs.text:
Pass 1 · Map (one weekend)Pass 2 · Depth (8–12 weeks)Pass 3 · Drill (daily, and the last 2 weeks)

Goal: be able to place any topic in the story. Don't go deep.

  • Read The Big Picture and every evolution line on it.
  • Skim each page's TL;DR and Where this fits box, in sidebar order.
  • Don't open the interview questions yet.

You are done when someone can name a technique and you can say what came before it, what problem it fixed, and what replaced it.

Goal: be able to explain every topic in your own words, with the math and trade-offs.

  • Work through the pages in sidebar order. The study plans split them into weeks.
  • For each page: read it, then build or derive the key piece (the ML Coding page has exercises), then answer the page's interview questions out loud before opening each answer.
  • Set the page's status: Learning until you can answer every question without peeking, then Confident.

Goal: fast, confident recall under interview pressure.

  • Open the Flashcard Drill for 15 minutes a day. It favours questions you haven't seen or marked Review again.
  • Use the Interview Playbook answer frames out loud.
  • In the final week, read only Most-Asked Questions, the Cheat Sheet, and pages still marked Learning.

docs.title: The seven questions on every topic
docs.text:
Every concept is written to answer these, in this order. Use the same order when you answer in an interview.

# Question What a strong answer includes 1 What problem came before it? The previous method and the specific way it failed 2 What is the core idea? One sentence a non-specialist could follow 3 How does it work? Mechanism first, then the key equation or diagram 4 What are its strengths? Why people use it, with conditions 5 What are its weaknesses? Where it breaks: interviewers almost always ask this as a follow-up 6 What came next, and why? The bridge to the next technique 7 What do interviewers ask? The page's question bank Worked example: the LSTM in seven answers
  1. Problem before it: plain RNNs forget after roughly ten steps because gradients shrink exponentially through time (vanishing gradients).
  2. Core idea: a separate cell state carries memory forward by addition, with gates deciding what to forget, write and expose.
  3. How it works: forget, input and output gates; \(c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{c}_t\), and \(h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t)\).
  4. Strengths: remembers over hundreds of steps; dominated speech and translation from about 2014 to 2017.
  5. Weaknesses: still processes one step at a time (slow on GPUs), four weight matrices per layer, still struggles with very long ranges.
  6. What came next: GRU made it lighter; attention let the decoder look back at every input; the Transformer removed recurrence entirely.
  7. Interview questions: walk through each gate; why does the cell state help gradients flow; LSTM vs GRU.

docs.title: How each page is laid out
docs.text:
• Study bar under the title: the act it belongs to, interview priority, reading time, number of questions, and your status.
  • TL;DR: the page in a few lines. Read it first, and again the night before an interview.
  • Where this fits: what came before, what came after, with links.
  • Concept sections: each built around the seven questions, with diagrams and comparison tables.
  • Interview questions: click a question to reveal the answer. Answer out loud first.
  • Common mistakes: answers that cost candidates points.
  • Revision checklist: tick items in your head; if you can't, re-read that section.

Medium Asked in some loops, or as a follow-up to a Critical topic. Good to know Completes the picture. Rarely asked directly, but it makes your answers sound senior.

docs.title: Role tags
docs.text: Tags above each title show which roles the page matters most for: ML Engineer, AI Engineer (building LLM applications), Agentic AI Engineer, Data Scientist, Applied / Research Scientist and MLOps Engineer. The study plans give a page order for each role, and Pages by role lists every page under each tag.

docs.title: When a topic sends you backward
docs.text:
This is the habit that keeps preparation from restarting:

  1. Open the page's Where this fits box, or the evolution line on The Big Picture.
  2. Step back one station.
  3. Read only that topic's Weaknesses. That is the reason the topic you were reading exists.
  4. Return to where you were.

One station per sitting. If you need more, note it and schedule it; don't follow the chain all the way back to 1958.

docs.title: Tools on the site
docs.text:
• Search (press / or S): searches every page, including hidden answers.
  • Previous and next (press P and N): move along the study path.
  • Your status on every page, totalled on My Progress. Export it there to move between devices.
  • Flashcard Drill: every interview question on the site, filterable by section and page. Keys: Space shows the answer, 1 review again, 2 I knew it, 3 skip.
  • Tooltips: hover over abbreviations such as RLHF or NDCG for their expansion.
  • Dark mode: the sun and moon icon in the header.

docs.title: Habits that make it stick
docs.text:
• Answer out loud before reading the answer. Recognising an answer is not the same as producing one.
  • Write one line per topic in your own words. Problem, idea, one trade-off. These notes are your best last-week revision.
  • Revisit on a schedule. Re-answer a page's questions 1, 3, 7 and 21 days after first studying it.
  • Build the key pieces. Implementing attention or logistic regression from scratch makes every explanation more concrete, and ML coding rounds ask for exactly that.
  • Connect topics. Interviewers are impressed when you link ideas across eras, for example that LoRA is the low-rank idea from SVD, or that RLHF's KL penalty is the same KL divergence from information theory.

docs.title: Interview Playbook
docs.text:
TL;DR

Most AI/ML loops combine five or six rounds: ML fundamentals, ML coding, ML or GenAI system design, a project deep dive, standard coding, and behavioral. Each rewards a repeatable structure. Use the six-step frame for concept questions, clarify → baseline → improve for coding, the eight-step frame for system design, and STAR for behavioral.

docs.title: What each round tests
docs.text: Round What they test What strong looks like Prepare with ML fundamentals Concepts and judgment: bias–variance, metrics, regularization, trees vs nets, Transformers, LLM training Explains the why and the trade-offs, not just definitions Foundations to Alignment pages; Flashcard Drill ML coding Implement a model, loss, metric or layer from scratch, cleanly Vectorized code, correct shapes, edge cases, talks while coding ML Coding from Scratch ML system design Open-ended: recommendations, search, fraud, ads, moderation Clarifies, frames the ML problem, picks metrics, designs data and serving, covers monitoring ML System Design GenAI system design RAG assistants, agents, LLM serving, evaluation, safety Starts simple, measures, adds complexity only with evidence; discusses cost and latency GenAI System Design Project deep dive Your own work, end to end Clear problem, honest trade-offs, numbers, what you'd do differently The project frame below Coding (DSA) Algorithms and data structures Standard; usually separate from ML prep Not covered on this site Behavioral Ownership, ambiguity, conflict, failure Specific stories with your actions and measured results STAR frame below

docs.title: Answering a concept question: the six-step frame
docs.text:
Use this for "What is X?", "Explain X", "Why X instead of Y?".

  1. Define it in one sentence.
  2. Name the problem it solved: what came before, and why it failed.
  3. Explain how it works: intuition first, then the key equation or a quick sketch.
  4. Give strengths and weaknesses.
  5. Say when you'd use it, and what you'd choose instead.
  6. Ground it in an example, ideally from your own work.

Aim for 60–90 seconds, then stop and let the interviewer steer. Depth on demand beats a five-minute monologue.

Worked example: “What is LoRA?”
  1. Definition: LoRA fine-tunes a large model by learning a small low-rank update to its weight matrices while the original weights stay frozen.
  2. Problem: full fine-tuning of a 7B model with Adam needs roughly 112 GB for weights, gradients and optimizer states, plus a full copy of the model for every task.
  3. How: weight updates during fine-tuning tend to be low-rank, so learn \(\Delta W = BA\) with rank \(r \ll d\). \(B\) starts at zero, so training begins exactly at the base model. Usually well under 1% of parameters train.
  4. Trade-offs: cheap, and the update can be merged into \(W\) so inference adds no latency. It can trail full fine-tuning on large domain shifts, and rank and alpha need tuning.
  5. When: per-task or per-customer adaptation on limited GPUs; QLoRA when memory is tight; full fine-tuning or continued pretraining for a big domain shift.
  6. Example: name the model, the rank, which layers you adapted, the data size, and the metric it moved.
Worked example: “Why do we divide by √d in attention?”
  1. Definition: the scaling factor \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) in \(\text{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V\).
  2. Problem: if query and key components are roughly independent with unit variance, their dot product has variance \(d_k\). With \(d_k = 128\), scores have a standard deviation around 11.
  3. How: large scores push softmax toward a one-hot output, where its gradient is nearly zero, so learning stalls. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) brings the variance back to about 1.
  4. Trade-offs: cheap and effective; some models add other stabilizers such as QK-normalization at very large scale.
  5. Alternative framing: it's the same reason we initialize weights with variance scaled by fan-in: keep signals at unit scale.
  6. Example: mention seeing attention entropy collapse or loss spikes when the scale is wrong.

docs.title: Handling follow-ups
docs.text:
Interviewers push on the weakest point of your answer. Expect these shapes and prepare them for every topic:

  • "What are its limitations?" Every page's Weaknesses list.
  • "What would you use instead?" The What came next line.
  • "How would you know it's working?" The metric and the offline/online evaluation.
  • "What happens at 100× scale?" Memory, latency, cost, data volume, failure modes.
  • "Have you seen this fail?" A specific story with a number.

If you don't know: say what you do know, reason from first principles out loud, and state your assumption. "I haven't used X, but given it does Y, I'd expect Z" is a good answer. Guessing confidently is not.

docs.title: ML coding rounds
docs.text:
1. Clarify inputs, outputs, shapes, edge cases and constraints (time, memory, numerical stability).
  2. State the approach in two or three sentences before typing.
  3. Write the simple correct version first. Vectorize with NumPy; avoid Python loops over samples.
  4. Narrate shapes as you go: "X is (n, d), w is (d,), so X @ w is (n,)."
  5. Test on a tiny example you can check by hand.
  6. Discuss improvements: numerical stability (log-sum-exp), regularization, complexity, batching.

The most common asks are on the ML Coding page: linear and logistic regression with gradient descent, k-means, kNN, a decision-tree split, softmax and cross-entropy, backprop for an MLP, scaled dot-product and multi-head attention, top-k/top-p sampling, and metrics such as AUC and NDCG.

docs.title: System design rounds: the eight-step frame
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph P1["Frame the problem"]
        direction TB
        A["1 · Clarify<br/>goal, users, scale, latency"] --> B["2 · Frame as ML<br/>input, output, metric"]
        B --> C["3 · Data<br/>sources, labels, leakage"]
        C --> D["4 · Features"]
    end
    subgraph P2["Build and ship"]
        direction TB
        E["5 · Model<br/>baseline → better"] --> F["6 · Training<br/>loss, sampling, splits"]
        F --> G["7 · Evaluation<br/>offline → online A/B"]
        G --> H["8 · Serving<br/>and monitoring"]
    end
    P1 --> P2

Time budget for a 45-minute round: about 5 minutes clarifying, 5 framing, 10 on data and features, 10 on modeling and training, 5 on evaluation, 10 on serving, monitoring and trade-offs. For GenAI designs, replace steps 4–6 with prompt, retrieval, tools and model choice, and spend more time on evaluation, guardrails, cost and latency. Full worked designs are on ML System Design and GenAI System Design.

docs.title: Project deep dives
docs.text:
Prepare two or three projects with this structure, and rehearse each in 3 minutes and in 10:

Part What to say Problem The business goal and why it mattered, in one or two sentences Constraints Data size, latency, cost, labels, privacy, team Baseline What existed before and how good it was, with a number Approach Data, features, model, training, evaluation, and why you chose them over alternatives Results Offline metric and online impact, with numbers Trade-offs and failures What didn't work and what you learned Next steps What you'd do with more time or at 10× scale

Expect questions like "Why that metric?", "How did you split the data?", "How did you know it wasn't leakage?", "What was the hardest bug?", "What would you change?".

docs.title: Behavioral rounds: STAR
docs.text:
• Situation: context in two sentences.
  • Task: what you were responsible for.
  • Action: what you did. Use "I", and include the decisions and trade-offs.
  • Result: the measured outcome, plus what you learned.

Have six to eight stories ready, each mapped to several themes: a project you led, a disagreement, a failure, an ambiguous problem, a time you influenced without authority, a tight deadline, and a time you raised quality or safety concerns.

docs.title: Red flags interviewers notice
docs.text:
Answers that cost candidates points

  • Reciting a definition without the problem it solves or its trade-offs.
  • Choosing accuracy as the metric for an imbalanced problem.
  • Jumping to a deep model before proposing a baseline.
  • Ignoring data leakage, especially time-based leakage.
  • Designing a system with no evaluation or monitoring plan.
  • Saying "fine-tune it" for a knowledge problem that RAG would solve, or the reverse.
  • Treating an LLM's output as trusted input to tools or code.
  • Claiming experience you can't explain in depth when asked a follow-up.

docs.title: Questions to ask the interviewer
docs.text:
• What does success look like for this role in the first six months?
  • How do you evaluate models before and after launch?
  • What's the split between research, building, and operating systems?
  • What's the hardest ML problem the team is facing right now?
  • How are LLM features evaluated and monitored here?

docs.title: Interview questions
docs.text:
Tell me about a model you shipped. How did you choose the metric?

Structure: business goal → what a mistake costs (false positive vs false negative) → offline metric that reflects that cost → online metric that measures the business goal → guardrail metrics. Example shape: "For fraud, a missed fraud cost about 40 times a false alarm, so we optimized recall at a fixed false-positive rate of 1% offline, measured PR-AUC across thresholds, and tracked prevented losses and manual-review volume online." Then mention how you checked the metric moved together with the business outcome.

How do you approach an ML problem you've never seen before?

Clarify the goal and how success is measured; check whether ML is needed at all (rules or heuristics can be the baseline); look at the data (size, labels, leakage risks, time structure); build the simplest baseline end to end; choose an offline metric aligned with the business cost; iterate on data and features before model complexity; validate properly (time-based splits where relevant); plan the online test and monitoring. Interviewers want to hear "baseline first" and "measure before adding complexity".

Your model performs well offline but poorly in production. What do you check?

In order: training–serving skew (features computed differently online, missing values filled differently, stale features); data leakage in offline evaluation (future information, duplicates across splits, target leakage); distribution shift (population, seasonality, a new product flow); label definition or delay (online labels differ from training labels); feedback loops (the model changes the data it later trains on); and the metric mismatch (the offline metric doesn't track the business outcome). Compare feature distributions offline vs online, replay production traffic through the offline pipeline, and check the experiment setup itself (sample ratio mismatch).

How would you explain a complex model's decision to a non-technical stakeholder?

Start from the decision and its business impact, not the algorithm. Use global explanations (which factors matter most overall, from SHAP or permutation importance) and local ones (why this specific case got this score) in plain language, with examples. Be explicit about uncertainty and limits: correlation is not causation, and importance is not the same as "changing this will change the outcome". Offer guardrails: human review for borderline cases, monitoring, and an appeal path.

docs.title: Study Plans by Week and Role
docs.text:
TL;DR

Pick the plan that fits your timeline, then use the role track to decide which pages to go deep on and which to skim. Every week ends with something you built or derived, because building is what makes answers concrete.

docs.title: Choose your timeline
docs.text: Time until interviews Plan Daily time 3 months or more 12-week plan About 2 hours on weekdays, 4 on weekends About a month 4-week plan 3–4 hours Two weeks or less 2-week plan As much as you can; focus on Critical pages and drills

docs.title: 12-week plan
docs.text:
Week Pages Build or derive You're ready to move on when you can… 1 Big Picture, Math for ML, ML Fundamentals Derive MSE and log loss from maximum likelihood; linear regression with gradient descent in NumPy Explain bias–variance, L1 vs L2, and three kinds of data leakage 2 Evaluation & Metrics, Linear & Logistic Regression Logistic regression from scratch; compute ROC-AUC and PR-AUC by hand on 10 points Pick and defend a metric for fraud, search and churn 3 kNN, Naive Bayes & SVM, Trees & Ensembles Best Gini split from scratch; XGBoost on a tabular dataset with proper cross-validation Explain bagging vs boosting and why XGBoost wins on tabular data 4 Unsupervised Learning, Recommender Systems k-means from scratch; matrix factorization on a small ratings set Sketch a two-stage recommender and handle cold start 5 Neural Network Fundamentals, Training Deep Networks A tiny autograd engine, then an MLP in PyTorch; compare SGD, Adam and AdamW Derive backprop for two layers; explain Adam, BatchNorm vs LayerNorm 6 CNNs & Computer Vision, Sequence Models Small CNN on CIFAR-10; character-level LSTM Explain ResNet's skip connection and the LSTM gates from memory 7 The Transformer, Efficient Attention & MoE Scaled dot-product and multi-head attention in NumPy; a mini GPT Draw the block, explain √d, compute KV-cache size 8 Pretraining & LLMs, Fine-Tuning & Efficiency LoRA fine-tune of a small open model; training-memory math for 7B Explain scaling laws, LoRA, QLoRA and quantization trade-offs 9 Inference & Serving, Generative Models Implement top-k, top-p and temperature sampling; step through a tiny diffusion model Explain prefill vs decode, speculative decoding, diffusion vs GANs 10 RL Essentials, Post-Training, Reasoning Models Derive the policy gradient and the DPO loss Walk through RLHF end to end; compare PPO, DPO and GRPO 11 Prompting, Embeddings, RAG, Tool Calling, Agents, MCP RAG app with hybrid search, a reranker and an eval set; a small MCP server with one tool Design a RAG assistant; explain agent loops and MCP's architecture 12 Context and Harness Engineering, LLM Evals, Security, Production pages Four system-design problems out loud, 45 minutes each; mock interviews Run any design question through the frameworks without notes

Every day, not just every week

Spend the first 15 minutes of each session in the Flashcard Drill on pages you've already studied. Spaced recall is what turns reading into answers.

docs.title: 4-week plan
docs.text:
Week Focus Pages 1 Classical ML judgment ML Fundamentals, Evaluation & Metrics, Linear Models, Trees & Ensembles; skim the rest of Classical ML 2 Deep learning to Transformers Neural Network Fundamentals, Training Deep Networks, Sequence Models, The Transformer, Efficient Attention 3 LLMs end to end Pretraining & LLMs, Fine-Tuning & Efficiency, Inference & Serving, Post-Training, Reasoning Models 4 Applications and design RAG, Agents, MCP, Context Engineering, Evaluating LLM Systems, ML and GenAI System Design; two mock interviews

Cover everything else with TL;DRs and the Cheat Sheet.

docs.title: 2-week plan
docs.text:
1. Days 1–3: every page marked Critical for your role (see below). Read the TL;DR and answer the questions out loud.
  2. Days 4–8: the Most-Asked Questions list, then drill each section in the Flashcard Drill.
  3. Days 9–12: system design. Do two ML System Design or GenAI System Design problems a day, timed.
  4. Days 13–14: Cheat Sheet, your own notes, and questions you marked Review again.

docs.title: A two-hour session
docs.text:
1. 15 minutes, drill: five to ten questions in the Flashcard Drill, out loud. Mark Review again honestly.
  2. 45 minutes, one new section: read it, then its primary source or a good explainer.
  3. 40 minutes, build or derive: code it, derive the key equation, or redraw the diagram from memory.
  4. 10 minutes, write it: one or two lines in your own words: problem, idea, one trade-off.
  5. 10 minutes, walk the line: on The Big Picture, say why the previous station failed and why the next one exists.

docs.title: Revision schedule
docs.text:
• Days 1, 3, 7 and 21 after first study: answer the page's questions without looking. When you get them all twice in a row, mark the page Confident and leave it to the drill.
  • Weekly: redraw two evolution lines from memory, including each station's weakness.
  • Final week: one full pass over every TL;DR (about three hours), then drill only Review again questions.
  • Night before: your own notes and the Cheat Sheet. Nothing new.
